stories.Headline: University of Indianapolis uses $8.5 million Lilly grant to launch AI center for human performance
stories.Summary:
The University of Indianapolis received an $8.5 million grant from Lilly Endowment Inc. to establish a new Center for Artificial Intelligence for Human Performance. The award was announced on November 23, 2026, and the three-year initiative is expected to begin in January. The funding will significantly expand the use of artificial intelligence across the university's campus. University President Tanuja Singh said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how people live and work at breathtaking speeds. The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which supports Indiana colleges and universities.

The initiative calls for creating or revising up to 330 courses to incorporate artificial intelligence into the curriculum. The university will also develop nine AI-focused micro-credentials and provide students with opportunities to work on industry-sponsored projects. Faculty members will receive additional training and resources to incorporate AI into their teaching, with an emphasis on critical thinking and ethical decision-making. The university plans to introduce AI-powered tools to improve academic advising, student support services, transfer credit evaluations and data security. The new center will be located in a renovated section of Krannert Memorial Library on the university's campus.

University of Indianapolis President Tanuja Singh said higher education has a responsibility to prepare students not just to use new tools but to think critically about how and why they are used. She said the investment helps the university build on its strengths in experiential learning and student-centered education. Singh also said the university must ensure that technology serves people, not the other way around. UIndy Provost Chris Plouff said the center pairs faculty expertise with student creativity and problem-solving abilities to address real-world challenges facing Hoosier businesses and organizations. Plouff said students will benefit greatly from hands-on experience gained by applying classroom lessons to real-world problems.

Ted Maple, the Endowment's vice president for education, said the rapid rise and growing ubiquity of AI may be one of the most significant challenges higher education institutions have ever faced. Maple said faculty and staff are concerned about the potential for AI to impede original and independent thinking and threaten social connections. He also said colleges and universities have recognized that AI may present unprecedented opportunities to enhance teaching, learning, student services and research capabilities. Small businesses and nonprofits that lack the resources or expertise to implement AI independently will be able to access customized consulting services through the center. The center will serve two primary purposes: encouraging discussions about the relationship between artificial intelligence and human performance, and providing practical assistance to businesses and nonprofit organizations.

The grant is part of Lilly Endowment's Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education initiative, which is providing funding to 35 Indiana colleges and universities. The initiative is designed to help higher education institutions respond to the growing influence of artificial intelligence and prepare students, faculty and staff for technological changes. The University of Indianapolis has already begun exploring the technology's impact through events such as its inaugural AI Summit in April. That summit brought together business leaders, educators, technology experts and policymakers to explore the opportunities and challenges of AI. The university plans to hold another AI Summit in fall 2027.

The initiative is expected to begin in January and builds on the University of Indianapolis's ongoing work in artificial intelligence. One strategic pillar of the center will be thought leadership, serving as a hub for both campus and community conversations about how AI intersects with human performance. The other strategic pillar will focus on applied learning and consulting by providing customized services to nonprofits and small businesses. The articles do not specify which businesses or nonprofits will receive consulting services first. They also do not state how many students will participate in industry-sponsored projects or when the renovated library space will open.

stories.Headline: Nasscom proposes a three-year AI services transformation scheme for India's 2027-28 budget
stories.Summary:
Nasscom, India’s IT industry body, has urged the government to introduce a three-year AI Services Transformation and Innovation Scheme in the Union Budget 2027-28. The apex body made this request in its pre-Budget submission on Monday, November 23, 2026, from Bengaluru. The scheme is intended to strengthen India’s global competitiveness as generative and agentic artificial intelligence reshape global technology demand and business models. Nasscom said transitioning to AI-led service delivery models requires substantial upfront investments before generating commercial returns. The proposed scheme would be designed by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Finance in consultation with industry.

The scheme would support technology commercialisation developed in India, supervised project-based workforce retraining and shared technical infrastructure for smaller firms. It would cover AI services and products built and operated from India, including offerings based on licence fees, subscriptions, usage-based payments and outcome-linked revenues. Nasscom recommended that overseas specialist visits of up to 90 days in 12 months, genuine employee secondments and global leadership positions held by India-based executives should not trigger permanent establishment status. It also proposed deferring taxation of unlisted ESOPs until sale, listing or ten years after exercise, whichever is earlier. Further, Nasscom called for raising the monthly wage ceiling for additional employment deductions under Section 146 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, from ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

Nasscom said AI is fundamentally reshaping global technology demand, business models and the nature of employment, making it important for India to strengthen its technology capabilities and create high-skilled jobs. The industry body said developing reusable AI-based offerings and retraining employees require upfront investments, even before new business models start generating returns. It proposed that the scheme link employee training with supervised project deployment, allowing existing workers to take on new roles while giving new entrants practical experience. Nasscom also sought a dedicated cybersecurity programme, with a capped initial allocation, to help manufacturing and service-sector micro, small and medium enterprises establish and maintain basic cyber protections. The body said the recommendations are aimed at strengthening India’s global competitiveness, encouraging technology innovation and supporting employment as AI transforms the industry.

Smaller service providers face greater difficulties in financing development, accessing specialists and releasing employees for training while continuing client work, according to Nasscom. Shared technical facilities, specialist support and collaborative projects have been suggested for smaller companies to overcome these constraints. Employees currently face a salary tax liability before any sale is possible, even though they may not have received money from selling the shares, Nasscom said. The body also sought taxation based on the lower of the exercise benefit or actual realised gain for ESOPs. For corporate restructuring, it sought loss carry-forward benefits for IT and KPO firms undertaking amalgamations, tax neutrality for fast-track demergers and enforcement of the 10% pre-payment cap for disputed tax stays.

Building on transfer pricing reforms announced in the previous Budget, Nasscom’s recommendations cover four key areas aimed at improving the ease of doing business and attracting global mandates. With Global Capability Centres increasingly assuming global leadership and research and development responsibilities, Nasscom sought permanent establishment safeguards. On employee stock ownership plans, particularly for startups, the body proposed deferring taxation of unlisted ESOPs until sale, listing or ten years after exercise, whichever is earlier. It also called for codifying employer ESOP deductions and raising the monthly wage ceiling for additional employment deductions under Section 146 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The economics of AI services remain a challenge for service providers exploring new ways to monetise their capabilities, as Indian IT firms look to convert AI adoption and productivity gains into additional revenue.

The proposed scheme, to be designed by MeitY and the Finance Ministry in consultation with industry, would support the development and commercialisation of AI services and products built and operated from India. Nasscom has proposed that the scheme link employee training with supervised project deployment, allowing existing workers to take on new roles while giving new entrants practical experience. Other proposals include greater tax certainty for global capability centres, continuity of accumulated losses in qualifying IT-sector mergers and faster resolution of tax disputes. stories.Headline: Sarvam AI launches Dictate API for voice dictation in English and 22 Indian languages
stories.Summary:
Sarvam AI launched the Sarvam Dictate API for voice dictation in English and 22 Indian languages. This new service was released around November 24, 2026, to help developers integrate voice features. The AI unicorn created this tool to convert spoken inputs into text for various business records. It allows users to create messages, documents, and meeting minutes through a voice interface. The API supports both live dictation and uploaded recordings that last up to one hour.

The service costs developers 0.50 rupees per minute of audio and combines Saaras V4 with Sarvam 105B. Developers can provide up to 1,000 names and technical terms per request along with CRM records. Users can specify formatting preferences and choose output scripts for English and the 22 Indian languages. The system handles natural speech patterns, including false starts, self-corrections, and code-switching between different languages. It returns both raw and edited text for applications like chat messages, forms, and sales records.

Sarvam AI stated that the Dictate API has been tested through its own dictation application called Kivi. The company reported that users have dictated over 30 million words since the launch of Kivi. Sarvam claimed that Dictate required 40 per cent fewer character edits than Gemini 3.5 Transcribe for short English. For longer English dictations, the company claimed it required 11 per cent fewer edits than Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. It also claimed a 17 per cent reduction in character edits compared to the service from AssemblyAI.

The company claimed a 47 per cent reduction in edits across Hinglish and Indian languages in its tests. Developers are the primary group affected as they can now add multilingual voice dictation to their applications. The tool is designed for those needing to convert spoken words into professional documents or business records. It targets users who frequently switch between English and Indian languages during natural speech or professional dictation. These developers can now utilize a single API to manage complex voice inputs for their users.

The launch occurs as AI developers increasingly integrate voice interfaces for data entry and professional documentation. Nasscom projects that the voice AI market in India will reach 1.8 billion dollars by 2030. This growth is driving various startups to develop speech-to-text models for a wide range of multilingual applications. Sarvam AI is an AI unicorn that focuses on building homegrown models for the Indian market. The company previously released a 105-billion-parameter foundation model in February 2026 using government subsidized compute capacity.

Sarvam AI plans to release more models across speech, vision, and edge AI over the next two weeks. The company is working with partners to bring the latest training-grade computing infrastructure into the country. It aims to pursue larger models while building a sustainable commercial business for population-scale applications. The articles do not state when the next specific model release will occur after the two-week window. They also leave open how the API will evolve as the Indian voice AI market grows.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl and Argentum AI launch a $630 million Boulder data center deal with Nvidia chips
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl and Argentum AI announced on Tuesday that they had reached a 20-year agreement involving an initial 10 megawatts of capacity at Kyndryl's existing Boulder data center. The deal is valued at $630 million and will bring Nvidia B300 graphics processing systems to the facility, which are designed to handle demanding artificial intelligence workloads. Argentum has already begun deploying the equipment, and the companies described the project as an expansion of high-performance computing capacity for businesses using artificial intelligence.

Rather than building a new data center from the ground up, Argentum will use infrastructure operated by Kyndryl, which provides enterprise technology and information systems services. The companies say the Boulder site is equipped to support the high-density equipment Argentum plans to install. The initial 10-megawatt commitment is significant, but it does not establish how much electricity the facility will consume on a daily or annual basis. Actual usage depends on operating conditions, the amount of equipment deployed and the facility's cooling and power systems.

Argentum founder and CEO Andrew Sobko described the partnership as an important step in expanding the company's computing infrastructure. Kyndryl U.S. President Jamie Rutledge said the agreement would put the company's existing capacity to work while drawing on its experience operating large technology systems. The companies have not disclosed several details that would help residents assess the deal's local impact, including the number of jobs associated with the project, expected water consumption and whether additional electrical infrastructure will be necessary. The announcement also does not identify any new local tax incentives or public subsidies.

The announcement arrives as demand for AI computing continues to drive investment in specialized data centers, and as Colorado communities debate the costs and benefits of data center growth. Such facilities can attract long-term investment and expand the regional technology sector, but their utility requirements may also affect infrastructure planning. Kyndryl and Argentum said equipment deployment is already underway and that the companies may explore further collaboration. No completion date was given for the initial installation.

stories.Headline: International Bar Association names AI as the top priority for lawyers in its 2026 Legal Agenda
stories.Summary:
The International Bar Association published its Legal Agenda 2026 on Monday, November 23, 2026, to identify the most pressing issues for lawyers. This new report names artificial intelligence as the top priority facing legal professionals globally as technological advances reshape the delivery of services. The organization released this update to reflect the accelerating influence of AI and the urgent need for regulators and firms to respond. This latest edition marks a significant change from the 2025 Agenda, which had previously ranked the rule of law as the foremost concern. In that earlier 2025 list of seven priorities, artificial intelligence had been placed in second place rather than as the leading issue.

The 2026 Agenda lists seven priorities including AI governance, the rules-based international order, talent development, law firm business models, and ethical pressures. Other key priorities are cybersecurity and operational risk, as well as diversity, inclusion, and the evolution of the modern legal workplace culture. The report notes that divergent national and regional approaches to AI regulation create complexity for international businesses and firms in multiple jurisdictions. In March 2026, the Association and the Danish Bar and Law Society launched the IBA Rule of Law Educational Project in Denmark. Additionally, the organization established the IBA Artificial Intelligence Institute in June 2026 to serve as a reference point for the profession.

IBA President Claudio Visco stated that the adoption of artificial intelligence is becoming the most impactful technological advancement of the current time. He said that the legal community must embrace innovation without compromising the professional standards, ethical responsibilities, and independence that underpin the law. Visco added that lawyers have a crucial role in helping to regulate and promote the proper governance of these new technologies. Immediate Past-President Jaime Carey remarked that AI overtaking the rule of law does not diminish the fundamental importance of that legal principle. Carey stated that the legal profession must remain a steadfast defender of justice and individual rights during times of geopolitical uncertainty.

The report notes that young people entering the profession are affected as technology performs tasks historically undertaken by junior legal lawyers. Law firms are facing increased pressure from clients, employees, and the public to either accept or reject certain legal mandates. Some lawyers have reportedly left their firms due to disagreements over decisions made in response to government sanctions or political pressure. International firms face additional challenges due to differing moral and regulatory expectations in jurisdictions such as Russia and also in China. The Agenda also highlights a persistent gender imbalance at senior levels, which is explored through the Raising the Bar project.

The IBA Legal Agenda was first launched in 2023 by former President Almudena Arpón de Mendívil Aldama as a strategic roadmap. This annual update is part of a five-year strategic focus for the period between 2023 and 2028 to identify critical issues. The development of the Agenda built upon consultations held with leaders of major national and international law firms in London and New York. The International Bar Association was established in 1947 to contribute to global stability and peace through the administration of justice. The organization describes itself as the global voice of the legal profession and the foremost organization for international legal practitioners.

The priorities outlined in the 2026 Agenda will serve as the foundation for the strategic initiatives and partnerships of the IBA. The organization intends to unite and guide the global legal community to address the profound transformations currently facing the legal profession. The IBA will continue to play an active role in strengthening the rule of law globally through advocacy and closer coordination. Further consultations are scheduled to take place in 2027 to provide the necessary information to inform the next edition of the Agenda. The articles leave open how the profession will specifically adapt traditional career development pathways as AI continues to perform junior tasks.

stories.Headline: California Republican expects Congress to pass AI bill before January
stories.Summary:
Rep. Jay Obernolte, a California Republican, said on Sunday that he is optimistic Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence bill before the end of the year. He made the statement during an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” even though Democrats are preparing to take control of the House in January. Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said lawmakers have made significant progress on the Great American AI Act, known as GAIA. He noted that major pieces of the legislation have already passed through the relevant policy committees and are now queued for action on the House floor.

The Great American AI Act is a package of proposals that would establish federal safeguards for the rapidly developing technology. Obernolte said the legislation has six bipartisan co-sponsors, and portions of it have already attracted support from lawmakers in both parties. He acknowledged that any bill would require cooperation across party lines, regardless of which party controls Congress. He explained that anything passed would need 60 votes in the Senate to avoid the filibuster and would also require the signature of the president of the United States.

Obernolte has been among the leading voices in Congress pushing for federal AI legislation as states move ahead with their own regulations. He said all 50 states are going in 50 different directions on AI regulation, which has caused concerns in the industry over a patchwork of conflicting rules for tech companies operating nationwide. He added that lawmakers must strike a balance between protecting Americans from the misuse of AI and allowing the technology’s benefits to reach the economy. The push comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of the House following this month’s midterm elections, potentially complicating efforts to reach an agreement on AI oversight.

Obernolte said he is optimistic that lawmakers can get the job done before the current Congress ends. He told host Chris Stirewalt that the relevant policy committees have passed major pieces of GAIA and that the legislation is queued up for action on the House floor. He said, “We actually could get this done this year.” The California Republican did not provide a specific timeline for a floor vote or for Senate consideration of the bill.

stories.Headline: Google launches Gemini Task globally as a free daily automation agent
stories.Summary:
Google integrated its Spark AI agent into the Gemini interface and renamed it Task on November 24, 2026. The feature is available globally and free for some users, though certain capabilities are limited to the United States. Gemini Task lets users create automations that run in the background, such as managing Gmail or monitoring prices. It is not a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, according to Lifehacker. The tool works best when users have enabled Personal Intelligence and connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos.

To use Task, users open Gemini, create a new chat, and switch to the Task tab next to Chat. They can type a prompt or action and press Send, or choose from suggested options. Users can tag @Gmail to use their Gmail account or a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so a user can say "run this task once every day" and the AI adds it to Scheduled Tasks. The free plan only lets users run tasks once per day, with no granular control over exact timing.

The free plan allows only 10 tasks at the same time, while AI Pro users can run 50 tasks. Compute-based usage limits also apply based on the plan. Free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea. Some features are only for U.S. users, including calling businesses on a user's behalf and forwarding emails to [email protected] to turn contents into a task. U.S. users can also connect Google Wallet to set up payments at supported stores.

Khamosh Pathak, a freelance tech journalist, tested Gemini Task and found it works well with Gmail, though with quirks. He asked Gemini to locate marketing emails from the last week, unsubscribe from them, and create a report, but it could not unsubscribe without his consent. There was no way to individually uncheck email newsletters he wanted to keep. After the task, he received a formatted report in Google Sheets. He also asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing highlighting important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks, and it reminded him of an article due date, pitches to review, a credit card bill due soon, and upcoming holidays.

Pathak created an automation that collects all his coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. He then asked Task to create a subscription manager, which collated the services he pays for into one list in a few minutes. It accounted for currency differences, with some subscriptions in USD and some in INR, and gave a tally in INR along with average monthly cost. Pathak also asked Gemini to monitor the price of Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily, but Amazon blocked the remote browser instantly. It succeeded in opening Croma, a national retailer in India, but took almost a minute to determine the price had not dropped below his threshold.

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, and users still have to check the work and approve important steps. If a website blocks AI models, there is not much Gemini can do. Pathak sees value in the deep Gmail integration for someone all-in on the Google ecosystem. He recommends free plan users set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or research that run every morning. Paid AI Pro users can get a lot more done, but the articles do not specify what happens next for wider availability or feature expansion.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in a 43.9 billion dollar all-stock deal
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire the network security provider Zscaler on Monday, November 23, 2026. The company plans to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at 43.9 billion dollars. This transaction combines two significant security businesses while artificial intelligence is supercharging cyberattacks. The deal is expected to close during the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. This acquisition marks the biggest purchase for CrowdStrike to date.

Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they currently hold. The deal pushes the Austin, Texas-based vendor into the network security market. It unites endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to obtain greater control over AI agents. The transaction surpasses a 32 billion dollar Google acquisition of Wiz. It aims to give chief information security officers a single supplier for security controls.

CEO George Kurtz said the company is building a single control plane to deploy and control AI. He claimed the company sees a path to become the largest AI safety and security company ever. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said the combination allows them to go beyond existing partner integrations. CFO Burt Podbere stated the companies will operate independently until the deal closes. Kurtz also reiterated a commitment to a single-software agent architecture.

Analysts at JPMorgan wrote that the deal allows CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending. Analyst Frank Dickson said the combination fundamentally changes the competitiveness of the cybersecurity industry. Chief information security officers are affected by the shift toward broader platforms for security operations. Customers may wonder if the companies can turn existing integrations into unified enforcement. Some customers might worry about vendor lock-in when using these combined services.

Cybersecurity vendors have been on an acquisition spree to keep pace with AI-powered threats. Recent outages affecting JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, and the Federal Aviation Administration sparked anxiety for businesses. CrowdStrike shares soared about 80 percent this year due to demand for AI security. Zscaler shares were up about 5 percent year to date before the Monday surge. Their combined market value exceeded 265 billion dollars as of Friday's close.

CrowdStrike intends to bring Zscaler's offerings into Falcon Flex after the deal closes. The company expects to generate 1 billion dollars in annualized revenue savings within 30 months. CrowdStrike expects to introduce an agent identity provider around January to provide just-in-time access. The articles leave open whether the companies can preserve support for competing products. It remains unclear when a combined agent will be delivered to the customers.

stories.Headline: Experts warn AI infrastructure spending may burst if Nvidia shares fall 50 percent and chip ETF drops 40 percent
stories.Summary:
Investors and technology companies are committing hundreds of billions of dollars to artificial intelligence infrastructure, but some experts warn a bubble may burst. This expansion involves data centers, specialized chips, and power plants, which rely on optimistic assumptions about future revenue. Market volatility has increased recently, leading to debates about whether the industry is facing a collapse or a correction. Some traders are betting on a burst, while others believe the infrastructure remains stronger than ever. The situation is complicated by scandals involving the leadership of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.

A burst would be triggered if Nvidia shares fall 50 percent from their high and the iShares PHLX Semiconductor ETF drops 40 percent. In southern Ohio, SB Energy is developing the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus near Piketon at a former uranium enrichment site. AEP Ohio described 4.2 billion dollars in transmission investment for this project, which OpenAI has leased for computing capacity. SB Energy reported billions in accumulated deficits and project debt due soon, alongside 6 billion dollars in credit support. These developments require massive electricity, potentially demanding a fundamental enlargement of the entire United States electrical grid.

Lottie Nimmo, the CEO of iPredicta, stated that traders will only be paid if three hard markers are hit. She argued that a market correction might be required because AI stocks carry astronomical values based on massive expectations. US President Donald Trump claimed his intervention was very important in convincing Nvidia to reinstate its CEO, Jensen Huang. Trump stated on Truth Social that the government has no reason to believe Huang's return poses any national security risk. Jensen Huang said he was honored to return to his role with humility and a renewed commitment.

Residents across the country are organizing against data centers and power lines due to noise, water consumption, and electricity costs. These affected communities object to the conversion of residential countryside and farmland into corridors of towers and wire. Some people ask if promised economic benefits justify the costs and if companies will be answerable if projects fail. The Economist noted that AI model makers earn 200 billion dollars annually but need 3 trillion by 2030 for returns. This required revenue would equal about a tenth of all wages paid in the developed world.

The current boom follows a pattern similar to the 2000s when adjustable-rate mortgages created a vast structure of unreliable obligations. Like the 2007 collapse, the AI boom rests on commitments that could fail if anticipated demand does not arrive. The industry is responding to power needs by proposing natural gas turbines at or near the data centers. Some developers envision facilities that make their own electricity to avoid relying on the public electrical grid. However, these physical undertakings still require permits, pipelines, and regulatory approval that cannot be financed away.

Future outcomes depend on whether revenue growth, which slowed to 12 percent in October, can sustain the massive infrastructure costs. The articles leave open who will pay for regulated transmission lines if the primary customers disappear from the system. It remains unclear if the financial mechanisms used to allocate commercial risk will be exhausted by the accumulated deficits. The market continues to weigh whether current volatility is a sharp reset or the beginning of a total collapse. Finally, the actual termination payments for infrastructure may differ from the collateral posted in binding contract documents.

stories.Headline: Education founder Dmytro Korchevskyi proposes four assignment design methods to stop students offloading thinking to AI
stories.Summary:
Dmytro Korchevskyi wrote an opinion piece on November 25, 2026, about preventing students from offloading their thinking to artificial intelligence. He developed four specific approaches to assignment design with his curriculum team for a network of schools he founded. These methods aim to ensure students do the bulk of intellectual work even when AI answers are available. The author believes that banning the use of AI is not the correct solution for modern education. He argues that only a person can spark a student's interest, whereas a machine can only suggest things.

The first approach involves placing the student inside the story by framing lesson topics around the student as the protagonist. Teachers can ask students to imagine being in Caesar's shoes to force them to work out the situation. The second method adds oral presentations to assignments so students must explain their conclusions and reasoning aloud to teachers. The third approach replaces simple practice programs with the creation of working prototypes, such as a video service with features. Finally, teachers can set many short micro-tasks during a lesson that are too fiddly to delegate to AI.

Dmytro Korchevskyi, a doctor of pedagogical sciences, is the founder of STEP IT Academy and a network of schools in Ukraine. He stated that real learning takes place during discussions and presentations when students link facts and arguments from memory. He noted that students who work through material independently answer questions with ease compared to those reading generated text. Korchevskyi believes that basic skills remain important because they allow students to bring their own creative ideas to fruition. He claims that micro-tasks prevent students from disengaging from the learning process by requiring modest independent intellectual effort.

A Pew Research Center survey of students aged 13 to 17 found one in ten American teenagers use AI chatbots. This survey indicates that these students complete all or most of their schoolwork with the help of such tools. A separate study of nearly 300 teachers conducted two years ago found staff identified AI essays in only 37.8 percent. This suggests that AI output is often so convincing that teachers cannot always distinguish it from work written by humans. Students can now easily tailor their answers to the required tone and format using the latest AI models.

The author began his career giving private programming lessons as a student before opening his first training center in 1999. He personally wrote the first curricula and trained the first instructors for his educational ventures in the IT field. His academy now operates as a global network that provides IT education across 26 different countries around the world. He observes that students are more likely to study a subject if it helps them achieve a personal goal. This background informs his view that assignments must be structured to encourage active thinking rather than mere formality.

The proposed methods allow AI to be used for gathering material or drawing up a plan for a task. Teachers can use tricky questions during oral defenses to see if students understand the work they have submitted. The author suggests that students can use AI to produce a first version of a product more quickly. The articles do not state if these four approaches have been tested across all 26 countries of the academy. It remains open whether these specific design changes can fully stop students from offloading their thinking to machines.

stories.Headline: Together AI links prompt leak to AI coding agent committing credential to public GitHub repository
stories.Summary:
Together AI revealed that an AI coding agent caused a prompt leak by committing a credential to a public GitHub repository. An unauthorized party used this credential to download stored samples of customer prompts from a private Hugging Face repository. The intruder then searched these downloaded samples for credentials belonging to other services. Together AI notified its customers about this security incident on November 21, 2026. The leak involved requests made to the serverless inference service of the company.

The exposed samples came from requests to MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6, primarily on June 24 and July 4, 8 and 14, 2026. The AI coding agent committed the credential while working on xorl, which is a public GitHub project. Together AI stored these prompt samples in a private Hugging Face repository for the purpose of routine software testing. The company stated it was authorized to use the samples for this specific testing purpose. The intruder tested credentials found in the prompts, including five decoy canaries tied to a Dragos security experiment.

Together AI stated that automated scanning detected the exposure and the company reverted the commit. The company said it has found no evidence of additional prompt leaks. Together AI claimed it has no reason to believe the samples were shared further. The company stated it understands that the downloaded data has since been deleted. Together AI said it will contact affected customers directly as needed after reviewing the samples.

Dragos submitted about 2 million prompts containing traceable credentials and URLs to AI services between July and November 2026. Dragos researchers found evidence of data exposure involving at least three AI providers but did not identify them. The disclosure does not specify the number of affected customers or the number of prompts leaked. It is unclear if the intruder used the found credentials to access any other service. The identity of the AI coding agent was not disclosed in the security notice.

Together AI collected the prompt samples for routine software testing to check latency, formatting and model behavior. The company used a private Hugging Face repository to store these samples from June and July 2026. Public GitHub repositories are constantly scraped by bots that hunt for tokens and secrets. The company worked with law enforcement and an external forensic firm to investigate the incident. The leak occurred because a credential was committed to a public repository instead of being kept private.

Together AI now checks all pull requests for credentials and updated its processes for AI coding agents. The company uses keyless access, scoped credentials or short-lived credentials where these are supported. Zero data retention is now the default for new accounts, and customers are advised to enable this setting. The company is still reviewing the prompt samples for other customer data or sensitive personal information. The articles leave open how long the credential was exposed before the company reverted the commit.

stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge releases a Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis made with Claude
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, released a proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis on Friday, November 20, 2026. He created the proof with Claude, the company’s AI tool, and published it in the programming language Lean. The Riemann hypothesis describes how prime numbers are distributed and is widely assumed to be true. Many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, making the problem a holy grail of number theory.

The proof consists of 17 million lines of Lean code, and a written-out version would run more than 250,000 pages. On Saturday, the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. They confirmed the problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles. The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the hypothesis as unsolved. More than 200 people have been collaborating to verify the proof since its release.

Alpöge has not released a paper version, which he estimated at 250,000 pages and called a “travesty of slop.” On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said the 250,000 pages was a “joke” and that he finds big numbers extremely hilarious. Alpöge acknowledged the “extraordinary” situation of presenting a complete argument before mastering a massive neighborhood around its mathematics. He wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly.

Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, said knowing there is a proof is one thing, but understanding it would allow building new branches of mathematics. Saha reckons the community effort should simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. He said the proof draws on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. Saha said he does not think this kind of proof would ever come from a human, but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien. He has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters.

Alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday. He wrote that he just could not live if he waited even longer. Anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations. The pair also announced on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof. Platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof. The Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, complained that the announcement builds upon over a century of human work but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.

stories.Headline: Zimbabwe plans AI use to speed public services and social welfare
stories.Summary:
Zimbabwe is looking to use artificial intelligence to improve its public service delivery and reduce administrative delays for its citizens. Minister Edgar Moyo announced this goal at the United Nations Governance Innovation Summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, under a future-ready theme. The government wants to ensure that vulnerable communities receive timely social welfare assistance through the use of these new technologies. This initiative aims to make government services more responsive, efficient, and accessible, especially for those in disadvantaged communities. The plan was discussed recently to align national goals with global innovations in governance and institutional management.

The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for 2026 to 2030 was launched by President Mnangagwa in March 2026 to guide development. Cabinet approved the Zimbabwe National Artificial Intelligence Charter last week to protect citizens from fraud, exploitation, and other harmful activities. The 2025 Citizen Satisfaction Survey recorded a satisfaction index of 65.31 percent but identified several barriers for persons with disabilities. AI could be integrated into the Zimbabwe Case Management System to help officers manage cases involving vulnerable children more efficiently. This technology would summarize case notes, remind officers of overdue visits, and identify referrals that are currently awaiting action.

Minister Edgar Moyo stated that AI offers an opportunity for public institutions to analyze information and coordinate care more effectively. He said that technology-driven reforms must be guided by the needs of citizens to ensure innovation creates tangible life improvements. Moyo cautioned that faster systems have limited value if people without smartphones, formal documentation, or reliable connectivity are excluded. He argued that AI should complement professional judgment while safeguarding personal information and maintaining accessible channels for seeking assistance. The minister emphasized that success should be measured by shorter waiting times and the timely delivery of assistance to households.

Observers have commended the government for launching the strategy to establish a framework for responsible AI application in national development. The affected groups include public servants who need new skills and citizens who face unequal access to digital platforms. These observers noted that the strategy covers key sectors such as healthcare, education, agriculture, and general public administration. The plan seeks to protect the interests of citizens while promoting inclusive development across the entire country. It aims to address resource constraints and the digital divide that currently hinders the delivery of essential government services.

The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy provides the policy foundation for integrating emerging technologies into public administration to improve overall service delivery. The Zimbabwe National Artificial Intelligence Charter was developed with contributions from government, the private sector, academia, civil society, and the public. Finance Minister Professor Mthuli Ncube presented the Charter last Tuesday as Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on National Development. He stated that the initiative ensures AI deployment adheres to ethical principles, national values, and the Constitution of Zimbabwe. This framework operationalizes the pillars of the strategy to ensure that AI remains human-centric, transparent, and inclusive.

Government ministries must now collaborate with higher education institutions to develop training programmes, mentorship initiatives, and various practical projects. Minister Moyo identified four priority areas for capacity, including data literacy, role-specific training, defined responsibilities, and continuous inclusive learning. The government is pursuing devolution and decentralization to extend these modern services to communities in the remotest parts of Zimbabwe. Progress will be measured by demonstrated competence and tangible improvements, such as fewer errors and reduced administrative delays for citizens. The articles leave open how the government will specifically provide connectivity and devices to those currently excluded from digital platforms.

stories.Headline: China-linked hackers use autonomous AI agents to exploit medical software zero-day vulnerability
stories.Summary:
Amazon reports that suspected Chinese state-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to exploit a zero-day vulnerability in medical imaging software. This activity occurred between September 8 and September 10, 2026, targeting university servers located in East Asia outside mainland China. The AI agents operated with minimal human input to find and exploit the unknown flaw in the target systems. These agents were running on Cairn, which is an open-source AI penetration-testing framework that coordinates multiple AI agents. Amazon detected the campaign after the operators left their Cairn instance accessible on the internet without any required authentication.

The agents targeted MONAI Label versions 0.8.5 and earlier, an open-source application used for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. Hackers provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to Chinese Standard Time to obtain shell access. The agents found a path traversal vulnerability in a file upload function and wrote arbitrary files in eleven minutes. They later used this flaw to plant a Python reverse shell, which granted the attackers root-level system privileges. The operators then directed the AI agents to attack a second university that was running the same medical software.

Amazon Threat Intelligence reported the findings on November 20 and stated that agentic offensive operations are already happening now. They warned that defenders must prepare for the speed and persistence that these autonomous AI tools enable for attackers. Amazon assessed with high confidence that this was a zero-day because no prior fix existed in vulnerability databases. The company attributed the attack to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence based on language and time zones. They noted the agents operated beyond a simple instruction to gain root access on the East Asian server.

Senator Mark Warner said AI tools identify security weaknesses faster than companies can safely test and deploy necessary patches. He expressed fear that companies trying to patch quickly will lead to a period of various technology outages. The maintainers of MONAI Label published an advisory on November 18, rating the vulnerability as a critical bug. The FBI issued a separate FLASH advisory on November 13 regarding a different AI-driven testing framework called ARTEX. This FBI warning stated that state-aligned actors used ARTEX since August against defense, government, healthcare, and financial targets.

The agents were given a list of IP addresses and the specific goal to obtain shell access to servers. Many attempts by the AI agents failed, including a sixteen-hour effort that targeted a specific Redis server. The vulnerability in MONAI Label is exploitable over the network because authentication is turned off by default in the software. Amazon traced the activity through the exposed Cairn instance, which allowed them to see the agents mapping the API. The attackers targeted universities in East Asia because those institutions are of strategic interest to the Chinese state.

MONAI Label developers planned a fix for the next release to address the critical path traversal vulnerability in the software. The FBI claimed that the ARTEX framework can move from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Senator Warner noted that he saw no evidence that these AI cyberattacks caused recent technology outages during the month. The articles do not state if the unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor has been officially named or caught by authorities. It remains open whether other medical imaging applications contain similar zero-day vulnerabilities that AI agents could autonomously exploit.

stories.Headline: UK financial watchdog warns tech firms that AI agents offering financial services may need authorization
stories.Summary:
Britain's financial watchdog issued a warning to technology and social media companies on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, regarding AI agents. The regulator stated that firms offering financial services through these agents could face regulatory action if they operate without authorization. This warning coincided with the launch of the Muse AI agent into the United Kingdom by the company Meta. The watchdog urged companies considering the launch of agentic products in the UK to engage early with supervisors. The Financial Conduct Authority did not name any specific companies in its statement delivered on that Tuesday.

The Financial Conduct Authority says that calling a business a technology provider does not exempt it from regulation for regulated services. These regulated services include payment services, financial advice, and financial promotions, which may require the companies to obtain necessary licenses. Meta launched Muse in the UK to perform tasks like making online purchases, chasing refunds, and renewing car insurance. Muse cannot initially provide personalized financial guidance or access mortgage information, investment holdings, or bank account statements for UK users. This differs from the US version of Muse, which launched in September and reached over 10 million downloads.

The Financial Conduct Authority stated it is prepared to intervene against businesses that conduct regulated activities without the necessary authorization. The regulator noted that regulatory obligations depend on the activities a company performs rather than its classification as a technology business. The watchdog also acknowledged that AI adoption could lead to broader access to financial services, improved productivity, and greater competition. It advised consumers to understand what protections they have if things go wrong and whether sharing their information is safe. The regulator urged developers of autonomous AI products to determine if their operations require authorization and to consult authorities.

Banks have already called on the regulator to scrutinize the use of AI chatbots to deliver financial advice to consumers. The financial sector is concerned that AI agents could help technology companies expand into lucrative areas of the financial industry. Meta said it has engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so moving forward. A spokesperson for Meta added that the company wants to connect Muse to UK banking services only after obtaining licenses. Consumers are affected as they must now consider the risks of sharing personal data with these digital assistants.

The guidance comes as AI developers move from conventional chatbots toward digital assistants capable of executing transactions and managing financial affairs. The growing autonomy of these AI systems raises questions about financial liability, accountability, and the protection of sensitive personal information. Meta's Muse is described by the company as one of the fastest-growing apps on record since its US debut. The regulator is responding to the rapid expansion of the AI industry and the shift toward more autonomous agentic products. These tools are now capable of handling financial transactions, which brings them under the potential oversight of the watchdog.

Meta intends to connect Muse to banking services in the UK after speaking to regulators to ensure compliance with local laws. The Financial Conduct Authority will continue to monitor whether technology firms are offering regulated financial services through their AI agents. The watchdog has left open how it will specifically handle the transition of tech firms into the regulated financial sector. It remains to be seen which specific licenses Meta or other technology firms will need to acquire for their agents. The regulator has not specified the exact timeline for when it might take the regulatory action it warned about.

stories.Headline: Financial counselor Christensen advises keeping sign-in details private before linking a bank account to AI tools
stories.Summary:
Amanda H. Christensen, a Utah State University Extension professor and Accredited Financial Counselor, wrote guidance published in late November 2026 on four things to consider before connecting a bank account to artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT Finance. The guidance, dated November 24, 2026, responds to new tools that let people link accounts and let AI weigh in on budgets, credit, and savings and investment plans. As of November 2026, privacy and security experts urge caution about giving AI tools access to bank and financial accounts, and financial institutions advise keeping account numbers, passwords, and statements out of AI chats. Christensen cites Stanford Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, which says AI is advancing faster than the testing meant to keep it responsible, as one reason to be careful with money and information.

The four points ask readers to keep sign-in information private, since typing a password or logging in to an AI chat is discouraged and linking an account means trusting a third party with financial data under that company's privacy policy. Readers are told to stay in control of their accounts, because some AI tools can log in and take actions rather than just view information, and authorizing that may leave a person responsible for what happens. The guidance notes that AI tools are new and the rules are still catching up, so it is not always clear how companies can use financial data, including whether it can help train AI or target ads, and it advises reading the privacy policy and checking what can be opted out of before linking an account. It also warns that AI can get things wrong by misreading numbers or giving advice that does not fit a situation, and that some mistakes cannot be undone if a tool can take actions in an account, so anything important should be double-checked against the bank's own records.

As a pro tip, Christensen suggests trying an AI assistant built into a bank or credit union's own app first, since the user is already logged in and nothing new is shared. Budgeting apps like Monarch Money and Rocket Money also offer AI features, but they require information from the user to connect to accounts, so their privacy settings should be checked first. She says AI can be a helpful money tool but linking accounts is not required to get value from it, and she suggests sharing rounded numbers and broad categories, keeping sign-in details and account numbers private, and checking privacy settings. AI can help with planning, she says, but the bank should track what is really happening.

stories.Headline: 24 House Democrats question FAA over safety validation of its AI air traffic system before nationwide rollout
stories.Summary:
A group of 24 House Democrats sent a letter on Tuesday questioning the FAA's decision to expand its artificial intelligence-supported air traffic management system nationwide, according to AVweb. The letter was led by House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen, Democrat of Washington, and asked for documentation of the system's safety validation ahead of its nationwide deployment on Nov. 10. The lawmakers wrote that they had yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion. They also requested information on the data used to validate the system and on what safeguards are in place to keep air traffic control operations running should the software experience an outage.

The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART, was first introduced in the Washington, D.C., area on Sept. 21 and was expanded nationwide in November to cover airspace managed by all 22 U.S. air route traffic control centers. The system consolidates approximately 200 data streams to help FAA personnel identify potential congestion and develop scheduling recommendations. According to a Nov. 10 FAA statement, the system had helped reroute 180 flights since September, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. The lawmakers gave the FAA a Nov. 30 deadline to respond and also raised concerns about reports of possible retaliation against FAA employees who questioned the pace of the deployment.

The FAA has reported that SMART has already reduced flight times and saved fuel, while the lawmakers pointed to recent system disruptions, though the agency denied that SMART caused a Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop. The letter referenced that ground stop, which occurred three days after SMART's expansion, and the FAA has ruled out SMART as a contributor to the telecommunications failure, noting that the platform does not feed information directly into the air traffic control system. The lawmakers, who previously requested an audit of the technology in October, asked the FAA for a response by Nov. 30. The FAA has not yet responded to the letter, and the lawmakers are awaiting the documentation they requested.

stories.Headline: New York Assembly investigates AI impacts in K-12 classrooms ahead of Dec 1 hearing
stories.Summary:
The New York State Assembly is investigating the impacts artificial intelligence is having in K-12 classrooms, Spectrum News reported on Nov. 24, 2026. A hearing is set for Dec. 1, 2026, where lawmakers will hear testimony from educational leaders. The hearing is being held so lawmakers can seek a better understanding of how AI can impact students in the classroom, in libraries, and at home. The Assembly's Dec. 1 hearing is scheduled for 10 a.m. The New York State United Teachers Union is preparing to testify in front of the Assembly Standing Committees on Education, Libraries and Education Technology, and Science and Technology.

NYSUT has taken the position that children pre-K through second grade should not have access to AI. From the third through eighth grades, it believes students should learn AI literacy, and only in high school should students be allowed to use AI with adult supervision. NYSUT is also calling on tech companies to protect students' privacy and that any AI programs be tested before they're deployed in classrooms. Democratic Assemblymember Robert Carroll is chair of the Committee on Libraries and Education Technology. Carroll says New York state has 750 school districts, which means it is the Wild West, and sometimes schools in the same district do totally different things.

Melinda Person, president of the New York State United Teachers Union, said children only get one childhood and should not spend it participating in some experiment that Silicon Valley is running. Person said every decision about every product that goes onto a Chromebook in a school, or that kids get access to via their school technology, should be a really intentional conversation deliberated with educators and parents at the table. She said it should not be a decision being made by tech companies. Carroll said what New York should not have, and the state is rare in this, is that it too often allows for complete local control.

Carroll is hoping for a more mainstreamed approach when it comes to AI. Last legislative session, Carroll introduced a bill that prohibits the use of most artificial intelligence in classrooms prior to high school. It was referred to the Assembly Committee on Education, and he says he intends to reintroduce it this upcoming session. Carroll says the one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in New York City schools for grades K-8 is based on his proposal.

Student-facing generative AI refers to AI tools including chat and tutoring bots and writing assistants. Carroll said he sits on the AI task force in schools of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and in many ways the mayor's moratorium models his bill. Carroll said there is a basic moratorium for kids K-8, and then there are exemptions inside high school where they delineate specific programs that can be used. Carroll said New York state is rare in too often allowing complete local control.

Person said decisions should not be made by tech companies. NYSUT is calling for any AI programs to be tested before they are deployed in classrooms. The hearing will hear testimony from educational leaders. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenClaw launches ShellBench to test AI models on complex enterprise tasks
stories.Summary:
OpenClaw launched an AI performance benchmark called ShellBench on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. The organization worked with industry players including Hugging Face, Nvidia, Red Hat, Google, and Amazon. They also partnered with Parsewave and UC Berkeley to create this new testing tool. The benchmark compares various AI models to see how they handle complex queries. It aims to replicate complicated tasks that a typical enterprise would perform.

ShellBench tests 13 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, DeepSeek, MoonShot, and Nvidia. These models are tested across five harnesses named Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi. The benchmark uses 100 real world tasks involving emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, receipts, and PDFs. Roughly 20 tasks are public, while 80 tasks remain private to avoid benchmark contamination. The number of tracked models will double to 26 by next week.

Vincent Koc, the chief architect, said the focus was on everyday use for enterprises. He stated that most businesses cannot replicate the speed and scale of ShellBench. Louka Ewington-Pitsos said the division of public and private elements in the benchmark is complicated. He explained that private tasks prevent data leaks from the internet into model training data. OpenClaw argues that this benchmark is more realistic than other existing AI performance benchmarks.

Thomas Randall said ShellBench offers little direct use for organizations buying AI from large vendors. Brian Levine noted that reproducibility is essential and questioned if others can check the work. Ishraq Khan said the leaderboard will become outdated, but the evaluation methodology has longer life. Jason Andersen claimed the benchmark is interesting because it decouples the harness from the model. Frank Dickson said the researchers deserve credit for the high bar of rigor they set.

The benchmark tests models in messy environments rather than the clean settings of other benchmarks. It evaluates if agents can keep track of information while performing multi-step jobs across systems. The tool measures how agents fail, such as stalling or confidently doing the wrong thing. It looks at whether models are consistent when the same task is run three times. The system evaluates both open source and proprietary models and their corresponding agent harnesses.

The benchmark found a median gap of 45.7 points between the best and worst models. Top models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 hit only a 60 percent completion rate. The results show that 51 percent of failures were related to omitting important information. OpenClaw will soon expand the number of models it tracks to a total of 26. The articles leave open how useful the results will be for most enterprise buyers.

stories.Headline: California governor Newsom signs AB 1979 to protect clinical judgment and health chatbot privacy
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom signed California Assembly Bill 1979 on September 30, 2026, adding new guardrails for artificial intelligence in health care. The legislation addresses the displacement of licensed professionals' clinical judgment and the handling of medical information by consumer-facing health care chatbot businesses. AB 1979 establishes safeguards for AI deployment in healthcare settings and mandates that licensed professionals retain clinical judgment authority. The law also imposes strict confidentiality requirements on health care chatbot businesses. The bill was signed into law as chapter 854 of the 2026 California Statutes.

AB 1979 takes effect on January 1, 2027, and applies to health facilities, clinics, physicians' offices, and offices of a group practice. It requires these settings to take reasonable steps to preserve a licensed health care provider's ability to exercise independent professional judgment when patient care is informed by a clinical decision support system. A clinical decision support system is defined as an AI system producing a prediction, classification, recommendation, evaluation, or analysis that aids clinical decision making related to timing of care, diagnosis, or treatment. The definition excludes systems providing appointment management, such as booking, canceling, and rescheduling appointments, appointment reminders, patient education and pre-visit materials and preparation, and payment processing, to the extent that independently performing these activities does not require a professional license. The law prohibits these settings from using AI technology to independently perform clinical functions that must be performed by a licensed person under law, or to direct, guide, supervise, or instruct unlicensed personnel to perform those functions, though a trainee can use AI tools under a supervised course of study while working toward licensure. The law does not apply to automated decision systems for communications and documentation that do not involve professional judgment, and automated systems generating reminders to patients, informing patients of updates to their health records, or assisting patients with finding information at their request are permitted. AB 1979 amends California's Confidentiality of Medical Information Act to deem businesses that offer health care chatbots for consumers to manage their information, or for the diagnosis, treatment, or management of a medical condition, as health care providers subject to the CMIA's requirements, a designation that applies only for CMIA purposes. A health care chatbot is defined as a generative AI system with a natural language interface that provides adaptive, human-like responses to user inputs, is marketed as facilitating or supporting health services to a consumer, and uses health care chatbot information to facilitate or support health services to a consumer. Health care chatbot information includes information related to a consumer's physical or mental health or wellness that the consumer provides to the chatbot, directly or by allowing access, or that the chatbot collects, generates, or infers. The existing confidentiality standards and penalty provisions remain unchanged but now extend to the specific health care chatbot category.

A physician's violation of AB 1979 is subject to the jurisdiction of the Medical Board of California or the Osteopathic Medical Board of California, as applicable. The health care professional licensing board may pursue an injunction or restraining order to enforce the law to the extent that a violation constitutes the practice of a health care profession without a license. This authority does not preclude a health care professional licensing board or enforcement agency from pursuing any other legally authorized remedy. The articles attribute the analysis to Sheppard, with authors Carolyn Metnick, Alexandria Foster, Arushi Pandya, Mayah Gaines, and Carly Eisenberg Hoinacki. Mayah Gaines is identified as a law clerk in the firm's Washington, D.C. office.

The articles state that providers operating in California should review their use of AI to ensure that licensed professionals remain appropriately involved in clinical decision-making. The revisions to the CMIA may bring health care entities not previously subject to the CMIA within the Act's scope. Health care businesses that offer chatbots should assess whether the amended CMIA applies to their operations and prepare to comply with any applicable obligations. Health systems, physician practices, and digital health companies should examine how their AI tools affect clinical decisions and handle patient information. The articles state that the legislation creates a regulatory framework that balances technological innovation with patient safety and data protection, fundamentally reshaping how AI tools can be integrated into medical practice.

The articles cite AB 1979, 2026 Cal. Stat., ch. 854, approved September 30, 2026, sections 1 through 3, and California Constitution article IV, section 8(c)(1). They cite AB 1979 section 1, adding California Business and Professions Code section 22758.5(a) and (e)(4), and section 22758.5(b), (d), and (c). They cite AB 1979 sections 2 and 3, amending California Civil Code sections 56.05(i) and 56.06(f), and section 3 amending California Civil Code section 56.06(f) through (h). The bill is identified as Cal. Assemb. B. 1979, 2025, 2026 Reg. Sess. (2026), available at the California legislature's bill text page. The articles state the content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances.

The articles state that AB 1979 takes effect on January 1, 2027, and describe the compliance steps providers and chatbot businesses should take. The articles do not state what penalties the licensing boards have imposed or will impose under the new authority. The articles do not state whether any enforcement actions have been filed under AB 1979. The articles do not state how the CMIA's existing penalty provisions apply in specific cases. The articles do not state whether further legislation or regulatory guidance is expected.

stories.Headline: Malaysia proposes AI Governance Bill to mandate incident reporting for high-risk systems
stories.Summary:
Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo announced on November 24, 2026, that Malaysia is considering new regulations for artificial intelligence. The government plans to introduce the AI Governance Bill to create a formal incident reporting mechanism. This new system will allow the government to analyze emerging risks and strengthen existing safeguards. These measures are specifically designed to address high-risk applications that could cause emotional dependence in children. The proposed legislation requires mandatory crisis protocols and response mechanisms for high-risk AI companions and chatbots.

These measures will be determined by risk patterns that the government identifies through sectoral monitoring. Mental health issues will be handled through the Health Ministry’s HEAL 1555 helpline for those in need. Social protection matters will be referred to the Talian Kasih 15999 service to ensure proper support. Minister Gobind Singh Deo explained that the government is also developing the Malaysia AI Safety Institute under AI Malaysia.

This institute will focus on the research, testing, and assessment of AI risks to establish safety standards. He stated that responsibility for harmful AI content would depend on the roles of application developers and platform providers. Both parties could be held jointly liable for the harmful content generated by their systems. The Minister noted that platforms like TikTok and ChatGPT are already subject to regulation by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission.

This commission has the authority to investigate harmful content and can impose restrictions when necessary. Gobind provided these details while responding to questions in the Dewan Rakyat regarding legal liability for AI developers. The government aims to balance innovation with the protection of vulnerable users through these new laws. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta suspends Class C share issuance and $60b AI stock sale amid shareholder lawsuit
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms said it would suspend its planned Class C share issuance while it faces shareholder litigation challenging its proposed recapitalization, delaying a financing initiative intended to support artificial intelligence investments. The corporation agreed not to issue the shares during pretrial and trial procedures in Delaware's Court of Chancery. The suit targets Meta's proposal to issue a new class of nonvoting Class C common shares in January 2027. The plan would effectively be a two-for-one stock split, giving Meta more leeway to fund acquisitions and keep personnel while preserving CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting authority. The suspension also affects Meta's planned $60 billion at-the-market stock offering program, which was not slated to start until the Class C shares began trading.

The delay comes as Meta continues to make large investments in advanced semiconductor chips and data center infrastructure to compete with artificial intelligence startups like Open AI and Anthropic. The litigation creates uncertainty in the timing of Meta's anticipated equity fundraising and capital allocation strategy. The company has also been growing its consumer AI application business as competition heats up across the tech industry. Shareholders will be watching the shareholder lawsuit, with the trial due to begin April 19, 2027.

The articles do not name the shareholders who filed the suit or say what they are asking the court to do. The articles do not say what Meta or its executives said about the suspension beyond the agreement not to issue the shares during the proceedings. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the trial date. More to follow.
