stories.Headline: Google limits AI search in schools as students keep using AI tools at home
stories.Summary:
Google announced changes to how AI tools and Search behave on K-12 student accounts in early November 2026. These changes sparked fresh debates over what school districts should allow or block for their students. Some districts imposed strict limits or moratoriums while others tried to define where search ends and generative AI begins. These policies aim to restrict AI search inside school buildings and on school-issued devices or campus networks. However, these bans do not stop students from using AI tools at home on personal phones and laptops.

The changes affect K-12 student accounts and involve Google Search and AI tools used in classrooms. Some Google workers urged the company to let schools use search without AI features on November 20. Students can still access AI at home on family laptops, home tablets, and personal phones after the dismissal bell. This creates a split screen where students face filtered tools at school but use chatbots for summaries at home. These home tools can provide a three-bullet summary in two seconds for students to paste into worksheets.

Sebastian Chen says treating school policy like a force field around a teenager's brain is wishful thinking. He claims that prohibiting a tool at school does not teach skepticism and turns software into contraband. Chen argues that teachers lose visibility into how students use AI when the tools are banned on campus. He suggests that students will not admit to using inaccurate AI summaries if the tools are forbidden. He believes that wrestling with ideas is how students build mental muscles instead of using instant answer machines.

A letter to the editor claims that preventing AI use at school is doing something without accomplishing anything. This writer argues that students will still use AI at home and avoid engaging in true learning. Researchers Heather L. Schwartz and Melissa Kay Diliberti found rising AI homework use in a March 2026 report. Their RAND American Youth Panel report found that roughly 60 percent of surveyed youth expressed concern about AI. These students worry that using AI for school-related work can harm their own critical thinking skills.

A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Information Technology Education Research looked at AI and critical thinking. Researcher Storrøsæter and colleagues found potential upsides when tools act as support for youth and children. They warned that treating AI as a shortcut to ready-made answers increases the risk of shallower thinking. The researchers also pointed out major gaps in long-term evidence regarding the use of AI by youth. This background shows that AI search has become tightly tangled with AI assistants and summaries for students.

Next, parents can ask to see rough notes, outlines, or search history alongside any finished student assignment. They can also play spot-the-flaw by looking for missing nuance or mistakes in an AI summary together. Another suggestion is a first-try rule where students write three bullet points before they look anything up. Adults can talk openly about shortcuts and ask when AI helps learning versus just finishing faster. The articles leave open whether Google workers will successfully get the company to remove AI from search.

stories.Headline: Senator Chris Van Hollen endorses a bipartisan Senate select committee on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen endorsed a proposed bipartisan Senate select committee on artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026. This endorsement occurred as Congress weighs how to oversee the technology and as Democrats prepare to take control in January 2027. Van Hollen is competing with Senator Chuck Schumer for the Senate majority leader job following a Democratic midterm victory. He released a plan for tackling AI risks amid increased concerns about cybersecurity and the possibility of superintelligence. The senator argues that the American people should decide how AI is developed and governed rather than tech leaders.

The proposal is tracked as S. Res. 918, which was introduced by Senator Ruben Gallego on September 29, 2026. This resolution would establish the select committee and specify its investigative powers, including the potential for subpoena authority. A companion measure, the AI Systems Transparency Act, S. 5471, was introduced between September 23 and 24, 2026. This act would require disclosures about how AI models are structured and would be overseen by the new committee.

Van Hollen also suggests banning recursive self-improvement in AI systems to prevent agents from evading human controls. Senator Van Hollen said the Senate moves like a glacier compared to the rushing stream of AI risks. He believes the Senate needs to be equal to the AI age and mount an ambitious, sustained response. Van Hollen called for independent third-party evaluations of leading AI models and said companies should bear responsibility for harms. He also wants to re-establish the Congressional Office of Technology Assessment to operate independently of the executive branch.

His plan includes moving bipartisan legislation concerning AI safety, affordability, and national security through the Senate. Supporters argue a dedicated committee would provide sharper oversight, focused resources, and the power to compel testimony and documents. Senators John Hickenlooper, Ben Ray Luján, and Ruben Gallego have voiced support for the proposed select committee. Hickenlooper sent a letter advocating for AI oversight on November 19, 2026, which Van Hollen later posted on X. AI companies could be affected by mandatory outside testing and liability for the risks their products create.

Van Hollen also wants to protect workers from paying higher electric bills for data centers built by corporations. Congressional AI oversight has so far been spread across existing committees that have other priorities and different focuses. Senator Chuck Schumer has previously supported the CHIPS and Science Act and the 2024 AI roadmap from Insight Forums. Schumer has called on the administration to brief Senators on frontier AI testing and protecting against AI-enabled cyber threats.

Van Hollen has pushed the White House for tougher guardrails with China and demanded transparency from the Federal Aviation Administration. He also introduced the Ready to Work Act in September to provide job opportunities for long-term unemployed workers. The Senate is set to vote on the new majority leader on December 1, requiring a simple majority. It remains unresolved whether S. Res.

918 or the AI Systems Transparency Act will receive a vote before 2028. The new Senate majority must decide if it will embrace mandatory outside testing of leading AI models. These decisions will determine whether the resulting oversight of the AI sector becomes binding or remains merely advisory. The articles leave open whether Van Hollen or Schumer will ultimately secure the Senate majority leader position.

stories.Headline: North Carolina treasurer Brad Briner says state's $250 million Anthropic stake is now worth $950 million
stories.Summary:
North Carolina invested $250 million in the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, State Treasurer Brad Briner said, and that figure was worth $950 million after the company went public last week. Briner said the state found Anthropic's Series G round, raised in March of this year, extremely compelling when the company was worth $380 billion. The investment is emblematic of a broader shift of strategy since Briner took office in January 2025, which has seen a more aggressive approach in investing. Briner said North Carolina had long run a roughly 45% equity and 55% cash and debt portfolio. The state's investment grew to $950 million after Anthropic's public debut, the articles reported.

Briner said the average pension fund in the country runs 70% stocks and 30% bonds, so much higher risk than North Carolina's. He said the state has changed that fundamentally and is now roughly 65% stocks and equities and other things like that, 35% debt and cash. Briner said the state delivered a 13% rate of return in its first full fiscal year, which is double of what it is trying to do at 6.5 percent. Other notable investments include Andruil, Revolut, Databricks, and Bending Spoons. Briner said the state cannot sell its entire Anthropic position at once because there are 23 different expiration dates governing when shares can be sold.

Briner said the goal is very clear to get to 100% funding and to reinstate cost-of-living adjustments on a permanent basis for state employees. He said the state will get a little bit in a couple weeks and then unlock slowly thereafter. Briner said the state will begin selling that stock through its investment manager when it can, and it is a lot for the state in a single position. He said the state wants to take some of those profits in reinvestment of other things. Briner said the state's retirees haven't had a cost-of-living adjustment in nine years.

Wendell Powell, President of the State Employees Association of North Carolina, said if the state makes $700 million in gains, that will definitely go a long way toward helping retirees get a COLA and putting money into the benefit package so employees can get raises in the upcoming year. Powell is a Correctional Captain at Harnett Correctional Institution. Powell said stronger pension performance could also help the state attract workers by giving employees confidence that their retirement benefits will be available. He said people want to make sure there is money there so they say they want to come to North Carolina and get into its pension system and work for the state because they know they have a defined benefit waiting. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly, whose new session will begin in January, will utilize the additional funds.

Powell said the association is happy that the Treasurer is finding ways to enhance the pot, making the pot bigger so the legislature can have tools and revenue streams to pull from to take care of state workers. The performance is especially noteworthy to public sector employees and retirees. The articles said Anthropic's IPO made major headlines last week, and in the case of North Carolina, major money. The articles were reported by Michael Perchick and published Monday, November 23, 2026 at 11:11 PM. The articles were datelined Raleigh, N.C.

The state will take a piecemeal approach to selling its Anthropic shares, with a little bit coming in a couple weeks and unlocking slowly thereafter. Powell said he is hopeful the General Assembly will utilize the additional funds when its new session begins in January. The articles leave open how much the state will ultimately realize from the position and what the General Assembly will do with the funds. The articles leave open whether retirees will receive a cost-of-living adjustment and whether employees will get raises in the upcoming year. The articles leave open what the state will reinvest the profits in.

stories.Headline: FCA sets out agentic AI expectations for financial firms and their senior managers
stories.Summary:
On 24 November 2026 the Financial Conduct Authority published a new webpage, Our approach to Agentic AI, setting out more specific expectations for those looking to develop and deploy products in the financial services sector. The FCA said some of these products may require FCA regulation at launch or evolve in a way that makes regulation apply. The webpage follows a statement that the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum recently published setting out its views on firms developing and deploying personal AI agents. The FCA said firms across financial services are moving from experimentation to deployment of AI agents. The FCA said it is engaging with firms looking to offer personal AI agent products to UK consumers.

The FCA said it will provide regular updates on the webpage to support the development and roll out of agentic products at pace. The update for 24 November 2026 states that the FCA expects AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers, bolstered with effective operational safeguards. The FCA said that where a regulated firm develops or deploys agentic AI or relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with the firm and senior managers within the firm. The FCA said it expects firms to demonstrate that they understand the systems they use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations. The FCA said senior managers are responsible for any AI models deployed within the area of the business they are responsible for, whether developed in house or by a third party.

The FCA said senior managers need to take reasonable steps to understand the risks arising from AI, provide effective oversight, challenge deployment and make sure governance, controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks. The FCA said a technology provider or social media platform considering launching an agentic product in the UK needs to consider whether it is carrying out activities regulated by the FCA. The FCA said that just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean it does not need to be authorised by the FCA to provide financial services in the UK, and that this boundary is set by Parliament. The FCA said it has powers to intervene if it believes regulated financial services are being offered without its authorisation and will not hesitate to use them if necessary. The FCA said it intends to facilitate cross-industry engagement through the launch of a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers and tech providers to collaborate and unlock innovation in a safe and responsible way.

Matthew Gregory, partner at global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, said many financial services firms are now facing increased interaction with clients' agents as well as deploying AI systems themselves in connection with the provision of regulated products and services to clients. Gregory said the FCA has provided a timely reminder of its requirements with the publication of the new webpage. Gregory said the regulator notes that these products can blur the line between regulated and unregulated activity, and between the protections consumers receive for their finances and their data. Gregory said that under the Consumer Duty firms must avoid causing foreseeable harm, make sure consumers get the information they need and support customers in pursuing their financial objectives, which makes the conduct risks of autonomous agents a frontline concern for client outcomes. Gregory said governance is another key area, with responsibility for meeting regulatory obligations staying with the firm and its senior managers, including where a firm relies on a third-party provider.

Gregory said the FCA's October 2026 publication, AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement, reinforces this and calls for governance that covers the full AI lifecycle, ongoing monitoring, meaningful human oversight and a clear risk appetite. Gregory said firms should therefore avoid a piecemeal approach and adopt a coordinated, firm-wide strategy for agentic AI. The FCA said its AI Lab provides a range of services to support firms develop and test new agentic services and products. The FCA said it and other regulators welcome early engagement and provide services to support those looking to innovate so they are clear on what regulatory requirements may apply and to test products. The FCA said companies developing or deploying agentic AI products can engage with it through its innovation services and pre-application support service.

The FCA said AI is redefining financial services and that, deployed well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth. The FCA said AI agents can widen access to financial tools and information and be part of new products that offer significant consumer benefit and convenience. The FCA said these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data. The FCA said that as AI becomes capable of moving beyond providing information to initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions, all at speed and scale, firms must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply. The FCA said firms must be mindful of the operational resilience of their platforms and their commercial partners.

The FCA said it will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements. The FCA said firms should also consider how they will respond when customers use AI agents to interact with them, including how they establish that they are dealing with an agent, what consents are in place, what an AI agent is allowed to do, and how customers can get support if something goes wrong. The FCA said this also includes information provided to consumers through agentic chatbots or where agents are used to help resolve complaints. The FCA said firms should consider their systems and controls, any liabilities that may arise from accepting instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent, or from a digital wallet controlled by an AI agent. The FCA said consumers should make sure they understand how a tool works and what protections, if any, they might have if something goes wrong before using it and allowing it to make transactions for them.

stories.Headline: New York bans AI powered toys for five years to protect children
stories.Summary:
New York enacted a five year moratorium on AI powered toys on November 25, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the ban at a Harlem toy store called Grandma's Place. The ruling prohibits the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of these specific products. This action occurred just before the start of the holiday season. The state took this step to protect children from potential harms.

The ban lasts for five years and applies to the state of New York. Companies that violate these new rules could face fines of 15,000 dollars per day. The ruling targets toys that use artificial intelligence to operate. It specifically addresses products that may lack sufficient safety guardrails for young users. The measure aims to stop the sale of these devices immediately.

Governor Kathy Hochul stated that some toys available for purchase could be harmful to children. She warned parents that regulations must keep pace with technology to ensure safety. Hochul encouraged parents to engage with their children instead of using technology for entertainment. She noted that some toys request dangerous levels of access to microphones and cameras. The governor highlighted the risks of AI hallucinations and invasive data collection.

Muna Heaven of Mothers Against Media Addiction said parents expect toys to be safe. Dawn Harris-Martine said good toys should stretch a child's imagination. Harris-Martine warned against letting children play alone with tablets or strange talking bears. Child safety groups have asked Amazon and eBay to pause sales of AI toys. These groups want the products to be proven safe before they are sold.

Studies found AI toys to be highly data invasive and lacking safety guardrails. Some toys allegedly encouraged children to find dangerous objects like knives and matches. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has already banned AI in some New York schools. He has encouraged citizens to push back against the reckless adoption of AI. This technology has already caused issues with Google search use in education.

The state will now enforce fines against companies that sell these banned toys. Parents are encouraged to be present with their children during their playtime. The articles do not say when the five year moratorium will be reviewed. It is unclear if other states will follow the lead of New York. The text leaves open how the state will monitor all toy distributions.

stories.Headline: Scottish secondary pupils debate the use of AI facial recognition in policing
stories.Summary:
Seventy five secondary school pupils debated the rise of artificial intelligence during a pilot education scheme on Monday, November 23. The event took place at Glasgow Trades Hall and involved students from Glasgow, East Dunbartonshire, and South Lanarkshire. These S3 students came from Hamilton Grammar, Bishopbriggs Academy, and King’s Park Secondary to tackle a major societal debate. The project was led by the legal charity JUSTICE and the education charity Young Citizens as a hackathon. Pupils worked with one academic and four lawyers to analyze the use of AI driven live facial recognition.

The pupils examined whether Police Scotland should use this technology after a real case involving bias and mistaken identity. This event was the first of three UK pilots, with Manchester hosting a second on December 8. A third pilot event will take place in London in February to help students apply learning to civic challenges. The Big Challenges Programme is backed by the Attorney General’s Office and the law firm Mishcon de Reya LLP. It aims to build skills in teamwork, media literacy, advocacy, and oracy for entire classes or year groups.

Ashley Hodges, chief executive of Young Citizens, said the programme helps young people engage with issues facing democracy. She stated that students proved they could find practical and thoughtful solutions to one of the toughest questions today. Fiona Rutherford, chief executive of JUSTICE, said every child deserves a high quality education about the justice system. She claimed that AI raises big questions about democracy and privacy that will shape the future of this generation. Both leaders believe the programme gives students the tools to become informed and active citizens in a changing world.

One pupil from King’s Park Secondary School said the day was interesting and helped explore risks in more detail. This student noted that people do not currently know enough about AI and will discuss it with others. James Libson of Mishcon de Reya LLP said public legal education is fundamental to improving the access to justice. He claimed the programme gives young people the confidence to understand issues shaping their lives and participate in society. Volunteers acting as critical friends helped the affected students learn how to assess evidence and challenge various arguments.

Young Citizens is a national charity that helps young people develop skills to participate in democracy and shape communities. JUSTICE is a law reform charity that focuses on improving the UK justice system through practical and evidence based solutions. The Attorney General’s Office supported Young Citizens in developing this hands on approach to public legal education for students. The programme uses organisations and institutions that shape the world to make the rule of law relatable and engaging. It is designed to build an understanding of how institutions work while giving young people confidence to question them.

The programme will continue with the upcoming pilot events in Manchester and London to further engage secondary school students. These sessions will continue to use legal professionals and law students to help pupils reach balanced and informed conclusions. The articles leave open how the results of these three pilot events will influence future citizenship education in schools. It remains unclear if Police Scotland will change its approach to facial recognition based on these student led discussions. The text does not state if the Big Challenges Programme will become a permanent part of the national curriculum.

stories.Headline: Nestlé opens Swiss deep tech center to test AI and robotics across its food brands
stories.Summary:
Nestlé opened a deep tech center in Orbe, Switzerland last week, the company said, to develop, test and scale advanced technologies across its portfolio of frozen pizza, chocolate chips and coffee. The world’s largest food company said the center will help it develop and test ideas faster, maintain consistent quality and improve efficiency. Nestlé is leveraging artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics to boost growth across its sprawling portfolio, according to Food Dive. The Lean Cuisine and Hot Pockets manufacturer said it will use AI, sensors and rapid prototyping to develop and test ideas faster. Sensors and robotics will handle routine or physically demanding tasks and help maintain consistent product quality and improve efficiency, Nestlé said.

The center will handle consumer experiences, research and development and manufacturing, Nestlé said, and will help create more personalized experiences. Those experiences range from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition, according to the company. The center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations, according to the company. Nestlé said real internal growth, which measures volume, rose 1.8% in North America in its third quarter compared to a 0.6% decline in the prior three months. In the U.S., Nestlé’s biggest market, food and snacks delivered strong growth, led by an improvement in confectionery and in frozen brands like Stouffer’s and DiGiorno that resulted in market share gains, according to the company.

Philipp Navratil, Nestlé’s CEO, said in a statement that innovation at Nestlé starts with the consumer and that for the company technology is an enabler. Navratil said technology helps Nestlé understand consumers better, deliver superior quality, drive smart innovation and run more efficient operations. He said this ultimately supports the company’s growth. Navratil also said Nestlé is still struggling with Gerber and its nutrition unit, which he said underperformed. The company said the snacking giant’s brand is growing 2.5 times faster than the cookie category and is benefiting from consumer demand for high-end treats.

Food Dive reported that CPG companies have turned to advanced technology to help them improve efficiency and more quickly respond to changing consumer demand for healthier offerings. AI and other technologies have proven especially valuable as consumers cut back on spending due to inflation, putting pressure on food volumes, according to the report. International Supermarket News reported that Nestlé is stepping up its investment in advanced manufacturing technology as artificial intelligence, robotics and data-driven production become increasingly important to the global food industry. The publication reported that the initiative reflects a wider shift among major food producers towards factories that can respond more intelligently to changing ingredients, production requirements and consumer demand. The publication reported that the development comes as food manufacturers face pressure from higher operating costs, supply-chain uncertainty and changing consumer expectations.

International Supermarket News reported that one of the biggest challenges in food manufacturing is managing natural variations in raw materials, because milk, coffee, cocoa and other agricultural ingredients do not always behave in exactly the same way. Temperature, quality and composition can influence production, creating challenges for consistency and efficiency, the publication reported. Nestlé’s research is exploring how artificial intelligence, sensors and robotics could help manufacturing systems respond to these variations, according to the publication. Instead of relying entirely on fixed production settings, intelligent systems could use real-time information to adjust processes and improve operational control, the publication reported. The publication reported that better monitoring and more responsive production could help reduce waste, improve quality management and make factories more adaptable.

International Supermarket News reported that moving from research to large-scale industrial application will require substantial investment, and that manufacturers must demonstrate that advanced systems can deliver reliable results, integrate with existing equipment and generate measurable financial returns. The publication reported that for retailers the implications could eventually reach beyond the factory gates, and that more flexible production may help suppliers respond faster to changing demand, improve product availability and manage manufacturing costs. The publication reported that Nestlé’s initiative highlights an important question for the industry about whether the next generation of food manufacturing will be defined as much by artificial intelligence and robotics as by traditional production expertise. Food Dive reported that the center will help Nestlé draw on consumer insights, accelerate innovation, maintain quality and run more efficient operations. The company said the center will help create more personalized experiences, from customized coffee menus to insights that help pet owners support their pets’ health and nutrition.

stories.Headline: Nvidia uses parallel processing and CUDA software to dominate the AI chip market
stories.Summary:
Nvidia created graphics processing units that placed the company at the center of the current artificial intelligence boom. These chips evolved from simple add-on cards for video games into powerful tools for generative artificial intelligence. The company dominated the graphics chip market during the late 1990s and the 2000s. A research breakthrough and a global race to build larger models helped Nvidia become a dominant supplier. These developments occurred as the US and China competed for leadership in the field of artificial intelligence.

The chips use a parallel execution model to perform over a quadrillion mathematical operations every single second. In 2007, Nvidia released Compute Unified Device Architecture, known as CUDA, based on tools from Stanford University. The AlexNet neural network used two Nvidia GPUs to win the ImageNet challenge in 2012. Google researchers introduced the transformer design in 2017, which became the foundation for many generative AI systems. These chips are fabricated largely by the Taiwanese company Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which is called TSMC.

Jeffrey Young, a principal research scientist at Georgia Institute of Technology, explains why these GPUs are so important. He states that GPUs are ideal for AI because training neural networks requires multiplying enormous grids of numbers. Young notes that software made GPUs useful beyond graphics, allowing scientists to run general purpose programs. He explains that Nvidia was positioned to benefit because it spent years building the CUDA software environment. The author describes how the company now earns record profits by selling chips and software to others.

Companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and xAI are building large data centers using these high-end GPUs. Chinese firms including DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Baidu are also focused on training next-generation foundation models with this hardware. These models, such as Gemini, Claude Fable, and GPT Astra, can reason and write software code. Competitors like AMD and Google, which makes tensor processing units, have built strong alternatives to Nvidia chips. The US government has debated restricting advanced chip sales to China following a scandal involving Jensen Huang.

GPUs began as modestly priced cards for video rendering and were sidekicks to central processing units, or CPUs. While CPUs handle a few complicated tasks, GPUs perform many simpler mathematical operations in parallel. Nvidia redesigned its hardware to include specialized matrix multiplication math and larger amounts of fast memory. The Trump administration tightened export controls for advanced GPUs after Huang was linked to an alleged Chinese spy. This boom relies on the ability of neural networks to identify objects and translate between languages.

Leading AI companies continue to compete to build more capable models, which will likely keep chip demand growing. However, the boom faces limits because AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity for their operations. Memory chip shortages have also strained supplies, affecting everything from smartphones to gaming graphics cards. Startups and cloud companies are promising to run artificial intelligence more cheaply and with less power. It remains an open question if Nvidia's hardware and software advantages can hold off these various challengers.

stories.Headline: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sue SpaceX over Grok generating sexualized images
stories.Summary:
Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones filed a lawsuit Monday against SpaceX and its related companies over safety concerns about the platform X and its AI tool Grok, according to SuperTalk 92.9. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a separate lawsuit this week in Multnomah County Circuit Court against various affiliates of SpaceX, according to the Oregon Capital Chronicle. The Oregon suit targets the creation and “material defects” of Grok AI, a chatbot feature on X launched in 2022. The legal challenges allege that Grok’s “spicy mode” enabled the generation of non-consensual sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images appearing to depict children over an 11-day period. The Oregon suit coincides with the separate Virginia lawsuit filed by Jones against SpaceX over similar concerns.

The Oregon lawsuit hinges on Oregon’s Unlawful Trade Practices Act, alleging the company misrepresented the nature of its product, failed to disclose its shortcomings and relied on “unconscionable tactics” to sell and distribute the chatbot on X. The suit asks for a jury trial, a judgement that the company violated Oregon law and an order for it to give up any profits made from those practices. Oregon attorneys cite a review from the nonprofit internet safety group Center for Countering Digital Harm from Dec. 29, 2025 to Jan. 8, 2026, finding approximately 23,000 sexualized images involving minors posted on X by Grok. The lawsuit argues that most of the 135,000 reports xAI submitted since 2025 to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children lacked the location and user information necessary for law enforcement to investigate. The lawsuit alleges hundreds of thousands of Oregonians have X accounts and therefore access to Grok, and that a mobile Grok app for Android and Apple users has been downloaded hundreds of thousands of times by people in the state.

Rayfield told reporters Monday that the company purposefully made it easy for users to create explicit images of individuals without their consent, including minors. He pointed to a “spicy mode” feature introduced in summer 2025 allowing Grok users to generate sexualized content. “They created a product intentionally designed to create sexualized images of nonconsenting adults and children,” Rayfield said. He said AI companies are in a race to become relevant and “the reason they’re doing this is for a simple reason: It’s called profit.” Rayfield said he expects conversations with SpaceX and Grok AI about whether they can put in acceptable safeguards, adding, “I hope that they absolutely can, but if they can’t, we’ll find ourselves in a Multnomah County courthouse.”

A spokesperson for SpaceX pointed to a Monday social media post from X’s safety team that didn’t directly acknowledge the lawsuits. The team wrote that creation of sexual content involving minors or individuals without their consent runs contrary to terms of service for the app and Grok. The post said that when “some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year,” the company acted promptly to tighten protections designed to refuse requests to generate explicit images of minors or real people. The post said the company keeps testing and adjusting those protections as abusers change tactics, calling the conduct “disgusting and indefensible.” Rayfield and state attorneys say Musk’s company, which has sued users for creating explicit deepfakes, has not taken enough action to ensure law enforcement can do their jobs.

The feature often results in images using a real person’s face or image while making them say or do something that did not actually happen, such as by removing their clothing, the lawsuit alleges. X in January restricted access to the mode to paid users following intense backlash over a rise in sexual content involving minors and nonconsenting adults on the platform. Since its 2022 launch, the tool has evolved to generate new images or videos in response to prompts that users can then post on X. The chatbot is also available through a separate, standalone website. Musk stated later that month that he was not aware of “any naked underage images” generated by Grok.

Rayfield said he expects conversations with SpaceX and Grok AI to see whether they can put in appropriate safeguards he considers acceptable. He said he hopes they can, but if they cannot, the matter will end up in a Multnomah County courthouse. The Oregon lawsuit asks for a jury trial and a judgement that the company violated Oregon law. The articles do not state what the Virginia lawsuit seeks or what penalties it requests. The articles do not state when the Virginia lawsuit was filed beyond Monday, nor do they give the outcome of either case.

stories.Headline: Indian AI companies raise 1.6 billion dollars in first nine months of 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian AI companies raised 1.6 billion dollars in equity funding during the first nine months of 2026. This total represents a 96 percent increase compared to the same period in 2025. The funding occurred between January and September of 2026. Data intelligence platform Tracxn provided these figures in a recent report. This amount is the highest nine-month total recorded by the report since 2019.

The funding total was 1.6 billion dollars, which is 162 percent above the 616 million dollars raised in 2024. Mumbai became the largest recipient of AI funding, raising 765 million dollars for a 48 percent share. Bengaluru raised 711 million dollars, which was a 44 percent share of the total. Neysa in Mumbai raised 600 million dollars in February, while Sarvam in Bengaluru raised 255 million dollars in June. Sarvam raised another 90.4 million dollars in August, and Yotta raised 150 million dollars in July.

Tracxn reported that a small number of large deals drove the surge in funding. The platform stated that around 90 percent of the total capital was raised in just 10 rounds. Tracxn noted that the number of deals fell from 149 in 2025 to 87 in 2026. The report indicated that the average deal size more than tripled to 18.5 million dollars. This increase was up from an average of 5.5 million dollars a year earlier.

Fortune India noted that a handful of deals drove the surge, showing a concentration of capital. Seed-stage founders are affected as they compete for a thinner slice of investor attention. Early-stage and late-stage funding rose by 191 percent and 4 percent, but seed-stage funding fell by 42 percent. This suggests investors favor companies with more mature technology and business models. India accounted for 0.4 percent of global AI money, trailing countries like the US, China, and the UK.

The 2024 base of 616 million dollars was the lowest of the three periods in the report. Funding in the first nine months of 2025 was 822 million dollars. Mumbai's funding was only 15.7 million dollars, a 2 percent share, in the first nine months of 2025. The report tracks equity funding only, excluding debt, grants, and compute credits. India is ranked ninth among countries in terms of AI funding raised during this period.

The reports leave open how much funding went to applications versus infrastructure. They do not disclose the specific investors or individual deal sizes for all rounds. It remains unclear if the funding is driven by infrastructure, enterprise traction, or scarcity. Future durability depends on whether customers renew contracts or compute demand continues. The data does not specify which firms drove the jump beyond the largest named rounds.

stories.Headline: Tampa Bay professors split on whether AI harms the arts as some teach AI tools
stories.Summary:
The Tampa Bay Times reported on November 25, 2026, that Tampa Bay professors are mixed on whether AI is destroying the arts. The article was written by reporter Lucy Marques. It was published in the Times’ Education Gradebook section. Govtech.com republished the story on November 24, 2026, credited to Lucy Marques of the Tampa Bay Times. The articles talked with five Tampa Bay professors who teach English, music, film and art history.

The articles name five professors. Santiago Echeverry, 56, teaches film at the University of Tampa. Tom Hallock has worked three decades at the University of South Florida. Steven Lewis, 37, is a USF music professor. Sheila Levi-Aland, 46, is a professor at St. Petersburg College.

Anuj Gupta, 34, is a USF English professor. Echeverry pitched a class called AI: Imaging the Future to the university’s trustees last year. Lewis teaches Artificial Intelligence in Music. Gupta teaches Writing with AI. Echeverry requires students to turn in chat logs that can stretch to over 100 pages.

Levi-Aland noticed in 2022 that one of her students had used generative AI to complete a project. Hallock offers extra credit if students draft with typewriters. Echeverry said filmmakers should use whatever tools they have to keep up. He said he cried when he first saw a student’s AI-made song and video about a college graduate. He said he wonders if more artists will find their purpose dancing, making sculptures and painting.

Hallock said it feels like a broken trust to have to read auto-generated writing. He said he feels more like a cop than a teacher when grading papers. Hallock said AI is really only a tool and cited Henry David Thoreau. Lewis said what one person finds value in is going to be completely dismissed by someone else. Lewis said a class on AI in music introduces a completely different way of thinking about music.

Levi-Aland said the biggest reason she keeps doing this is because you need to learn to experiment and enjoy. She said getting your hands dirty is really the way. Gupta said students are overwhelmed with AI tools and hear conflicting narratives. Gupta said he predicts more people will be able to access writing and learn to write because of AI. The articles said many artists and writers were quick to call generated content “slop” that at best lacks creativity and humanity.

The articles said some humanities professors say their students are vehemently against using AI. The articles said most of the five professors have mixed feelings about AI. The articles said some are diving in by teaching classes on how AI tools can support artists and writers. The articles said others are staying away from it and returning to traditional assignments like annotating physical books. The articles said Florida colleges are preparing students for an AI-era workforce.

The articles said many professors believe artificial intelligence can benefit industries like healthcare, technology and manufacturing. The articles said there is more skepticism in the arts and humanities. The articles said AI chatbots came on the scene four years ago. Levi-Aland said she was livid that a student literally put a project in AI and didn’t do a single thing. She said a student once challenged her on the date of a historical event, and a chatbot gave the student’s answer, pulling from an old and outdated website.

She said it is worrying that students rely on AI for the truth. She said AI can be a helpful tool for artists to market their work. Gupta said he teaches the differences between cognitive offloading and uploading. He said cognitive offloading is when technology handles mental labor, like having our phone store numbers or using Google Maps. He said cognitive uploading is when technology builds on our opportunities to think.

He said if we offload for a lot of meaningful tasks like writing, we lose out on opportunities to build our critical thinking. He said he is guessing that in the next few years we will reach some sort of equilibrium as these tools become a regular part of our lives. Echeverry said that in the next few years filmmakers will reckon with AI tools that can create more efficiently than they can. He said the discussion comes up often in class because everyone’s future jobs are at stake. He said anything that is going to be electronically based is going to be controlled by AI.

Lewis said he understands why some students are apprehensive to discuss or use AI tools, especially because there is now software that uncannily reproduces their work. He said if we are worried about AI-generated music being able to reproduce what we can already do, perhaps this is a catalyst to recognize or create completely new ways of musicking. Hallock said he does not want to be paranoid about the change AI brings. Gupta said he thinks we are currently in a phase where there is a lot of criticism and a lot of issues coming up.

stories.Headline: Mike Lynch predicts a 2027 AI agent loss from missing controls
stories.Summary:
Mike Lynch, Principal and Chief Evangelist for AI Strategy at Auditoria.AI, predicted that 2027 could bring the first major financial restatement or material loss attributed to an AI agent acting without proper governance and controls. He made this prediction in an article published on 25 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. Lynch said he hopes the prediction does not come true, but businesses are giving AI agents greater responsibility for financial and operational processes. He suggested a high-profile incident would expose the consequences of giving agents too much authority without matching controls. The article did not name any specific company or agent involved in such an incident.

Lynch predicted that internal and external auditors will start auditing AI agents as part of their normal audit scope in 2027. Auditors will want evidence that appropriate controls are in place and working as agents become more involved in finance operations. Businesses will need to show which agents have access to particular systems, what they are authorized to do, and how their activities are monitored. Lynch said companies should treat agents as non-human employees within existing policies and control frameworks. The same principles around segregation of duties, access certification, delegation of authority, supervision, and audit trails should apply to agents.

Lynch said organizations will need reliable ways to verify an agent's identity, manage its credentials, and control its permissions in 2027. He stated that whoever owns agent identity will ultimately own the control plane for enterprise AI. Companies also need to establish clear decision rights, including what agents can do independently and when they must escalate a decision. Financial thresholds, timing considerations, and approval requirements all need to be accounted for. Lynch also predicted a token revolt as organizations begin challenging how they pay for agentic AI.

Lynch said businesses will become much more interested in paying for the outcomes agents deliver as they move from experimentation into production. Finance is likely to be one of the first areas where outcome-based pricing becomes more established because many finance activities can be counted and measured. An organization can measure how many transactions an agent processes, how many reconciliations it completes, or how much work it handles within a particular process. That creates an opportunity to connect pricing more directly to completed work instead of relying primarily on consumption-based models. Lynch also said it is time to kill AI pilot purgatory.

Lynch said every AI initiative should be tied to profit and loss visible outcomes within two quarters. If an initiative cannot demonstrate meaningful progress toward those outcomes, businesses need to be prepared to stop investing in it. The finance function is particularly well placed to enforce that discipline because it must understand how investments affect the business's financial performance. Lynch also expected 2027 to bring advances in probabilistic accounting, where agents support estimates with confidence intervals and evidence rather than simply producing a number. He said that makes governance and auditability essential, as organizations need to trace the evidence behind an agent's calculations.

Lynch drew attention to the SAP ECC support deadline at the end of 2027, saying many organizations are still managing complex migrations. Those that have not completed them in time may have to operate without standard support, pay a premium for extended maintenance, or turn to third-party providers. Lynch said he expects 2027 to bring much greater accountability for AI investment, with businesses wanting evidence that agents are properly governed and deliver measurable financial value. He said painful lessons lie ahead for those that have given agents too much authority without the right controls. stories.Headline: YYForce deploys a trained humanoid concierge robot at Novotel Singapore on Stevens
stories.Summary:
YYForce Inc., which trades on the NASDAQ as YFOR, announced the launch of a proprietary trained humanoid robot on November 24, 2026. This new robot is specifically built for live hospitality concierge operations to assist guests within a professional hotel environment. The company developed this technology to transition commercial embodied AI from training environments into real world, guest facing hotel services. This humanoid robot will be deployed at the Novotel Singapore on Stevens to handle various guest interactions in the lobby. The hotel team gave the robot the name Six Seven, which is also referred to as 67 in documentation.

The robot utilizes NVIDIA Jetson edge AI computing and NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulation workflows to achieve reliable performance in dynamic public spaces. It is integrated into the Workforce OS architecture to combine natural conversational intelligence with real time property and local knowledge. Six Seven provides immediate answers regarding on site restaurants, venue locations, operating hours, dining menus, and daily hotel events. It assists visitors with neighborhood navigation, nearby attractions, transportation options, and curated tourism recommendations across the city of Singapore. The robot also engages visitors and families with interactive storytelling to create a memorable arrival experience for all hotel guests.

Mike Fu serves as the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of YYForce and is responsible for the company's strategic direction. He stated that the deployment at Novotel Singapore on Stevens will show that humanoid robotics deliver warmth, accuracy, and operational value. Fu claimed that using NVIDIA Jetson and Isaac Sim within the Workforce OS platform accelerates the commercial rollout of embodied AI. He believes this technology empowers hospitality partners to elevate guest experiences while addressing persistent staffing challenges on the hotel front line. The company aims to bring together people, intelligent software, and commercial robotics into one connected ecosystem for its clients.

The deployment of the robot is intended to help hospitality partners who are currently facing persistent frontline staffing challenges in their operations. Guests at the Novotel Singapore on Stevens are the primary people affected by the introduction of this humanoid concierge service. The robot is designed to respond naturally to open ended guest inquiries to improve the overall arrival experience for visitors. By providing immediate answers and travel guidance, the robot aims to enhance the everyday experiences of people visiting the hotel. This technology is meant to provide a more efficient way for guests to receive information about the local area.

YYForce is an AI enabled workforce solutions and integrated facility management provider that operates across Asia and other global regions. The company has conducted dedicated robotics training and data collection initiatives in both Singapore and Malaysia to support this launch. Its broader portfolio includes intelligent workforce matching through YY Circle and Yolara AI, as well as digital estate management via 24iFM. The company provides service robot deployment, leasing, and maintenance for hospitality, retail, logistics, and other frontline driven industries in its market. This specific project builds upon those previous regional initiatives to advance the company's strategy for scaling commercial service robots.

YYForce plans to scale commercial service robots across hospitality, retail, and integrated facility management environments as part of its growth strategy. The company will continue to use its Workforce OS platform to deploy embodied AI for various partners in the future. The articles leave open whether the robot will be deployed to other hotels beyond the Novotel Singapore on Stevens location. There is no information regarding the specific timeline for expanding these humanoid robots into the retail or logistics sectors mentioned. stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang cites Anthropic proof of Riemann Hypothesis to argue superintelligence is near
stories.Summary:
Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, warned on Sunday that superintelligence is arriving, and he built his case on a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number problem. The proof was produced at rival Anthropic, and Wang's essay asks the AI industry to change course. Wang runs Meta's own superintelligence lab, and Meta shareholders are funding that push with up to $145 billion in capital spending this year. The essay never names the proof or its author. The claim arrived one day after Anthropic's $1.5 trillion debut on Nasdaq.

On November 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he found the proof while working with Claude, the company's AI model. The Lean and Mathlib communities, which maintain software that machine-checks proofs, certified the result on November 21. Wang says the proof came with help from an "alien mind" humans do not understand. Wang also calls the problem perhaps the hardest humanity has devised. The essay does not spell out what Meta would do differently from the "default path" it criticizes.

Wang argues the scientific problems behind AI capability gains are now likely solved, and he expects models to automate AI research itself. Even so, he rejects the view that artificial superintelligence is simply inevitable, writing that society should resist ceding control. Wang said he notices "a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry," which holds that ASI is inevitable and the only problem is how to do it safely. He said there is much more at stake and that we should not be okay with a "handover" of society to AI. His employer, however, is spending at full speed on that same race.

Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, credited Alpöge instead of an alien mind. Saha said others with similar access to frontier AI models and computing resources were not able to come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. Meta's third-quarter report showed $34.91 billion in capital expenditures over three months, pushing free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion. That money is building the data center capacity Meta uses to train AI models and run its core business. The company expects full-year 2026 capital spending of $135 billion to $145 billion.

Meta also plans to cut Reality Labs losses next year by shifting investment toward AI. It is creating a new class of stock, partly to raise capital for that buildout. Mark Zuckerberg framed those results as progress toward personal superintelligence for everyone. The question of what Meta would do differently now sits with Meta shareholders funding the same race their AI chief wants rerouted. stories.Headline: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo to block Linux exploits before patches arrive
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Cisco released an open-source approach called Shirudo on November 24, 2026, to block exploits before patches are ready. This new tool creates shields to protect vulnerable systems while security teams work on developing and rolling out longer-term fixes. The two companies developed this technology to widen the timeframe organizations have to address security holes found by artificial intelligence. These AI-powered shields aim to protect systems from being compromised during the days or weeks it takes to deploy patches. The project is designed to help defenders maintain system uptime while they build the necessary code to fix critical bugs.

Shirudo, which means shield in Japanese, currently runs on Linux systems and is licensed under the BSD 2-Clause open-source license. It uses extended Berkeley Packet Filter, or eBPF, to run many of these shields inside the core of the operating system. The system allows security teams to block behaviors that expose vulnerabilities while still allowing legitimate requests to pass through the system. An agent writes a temporary block in front of vulnerable code to prevent the malicious input that an exploit depends on. This process allows teams to test if a patch works without bringing the entire system down during the deployment phase.

Greg Brockman, the president and co-founder of OpenAI, stated in a blog post that finding a bug does not mean patching. He explained that OpenAI is partnering with Cisco to help teams protect systems they need to keep running while building fixes. Brockman noted that it makes sense to build these tools in the open because so many teams rely on the same software. The companies invited infrastructure operators, security researchers, and other developers to contribute to and iterate on the work for Shirudo. They claimed that AI-powered platforms like this are the first step toward building infrastructure that adapts quickly to emerging threats.

Security teams are the primary group affected because they are already overwhelmed by the growing number of vulnerabilities found by AI. These teams are being encouraged to use AI agents to find and patch issues, though testing still takes significant time. Other affected parties include developers and infrastructure operators who are invited to help improve the open-source shields for the wider community. The tool specifically helps those using Linux, as the agent decides where to intercept attacks and place the written shields. These shields prevent malicious attempts to access the kernel while the agent generates and tests the actual patch code.

The articles state that cyber-capable AI models, such as Anthropic's Mythos 5 or OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, have surfaced unknown vulnerabilities. This trend has given organizations a shorter timeframe to send out patches, even when they use agents to plug holes. OpenAI tested Shirudo using Codex agents on the Java4Shell vulnerability, which was originally found by a research firm called Calif. The team used the Elasticsearch platform, which runs on the Java language, to test if the shield blocked malicious input. The test showed that the shield rejected the attack while the Elasticsearch platform continued running without any system interruptions.

The next step involves making tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures while the open-source community continues to build out the patches. OpenAI wants to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at a larger scale for more users. This goal includes limiting workload permissions, hardening core services, and hardening the kernel to make recovery and updates much safer. The articles leave open how other operating systems besides Linux will be supported by the Shirudo open-source shielding approach. It remains unclear which specific developers or researchers have already begun contributing to the iteration of the Shirudo project code.

stories.Headline: National Taiwan University researchers create energy-efficient chips for on-device generative AI
stories.Summary:
A research team from National Taiwan University developed two generations of energy-efficient chips for generative artificial intelligence. The National Science and Technology Council announced this development on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Professor Yang Chia-hsiang of the electrical engineering department led the team during this project. They created transformer learning processors that integrate AI algorithms, hardware architecture, and chip design. These processors simplify AI processing and reduce unnecessary computations to improve overall device efficiency.

The first chip used a 40-nanometer process and reached a peak energy efficiency of 99.2 TOPS/W. The second chip reached 157 TOPS/W and reduced both memory requirements and computational needs for training. The first chip was reported as the first learning processor to accelerate transformer inference and training. The second chip is 1.6 to 7.6 times more efficient than advanced transformer learning processors. The first chip was 2.6 to 162 times more efficient than advanced processors designed for inference.

Professor Yang Chia-hsiang stated that on-device generative AI requires energy efficient computations and reduced data transfer energy. He explained that the team goal is to move less data and compute only what is necessary. The National Science and Technology Council said the chips enable devices to analyze real-time data. They stated that the chips allow devices to interpret surroundings and make informed decisions more autonomously. The council noted that these chips reduce the reliance on cloud computing and network connectivity.

The council said that smartphones, robots, industrial equipment, and uncrewed vehicles are affected by this new technology. These devices can gain advantages in applications that require reliable connectivity, strong data privacy, or rapid responses. The council noted that relying on cloud data centers can increase energy consumption due to data transfers. Such cloud reliance can also introduce network constraints and transmission delays for the users of these devices. The first chip allows AI applications to run on devices that have limited computing resources.

The council likened the first chip approach to reading an article by identifying keywords and main points first. The research was conducted under the Taiwan Chip-based Industrial Innovation Program of the National Science and Technology Council. This program supports critical semiconductor technologies and the research and development of advanced AI chips in Taiwan. The program aims to use semiconductor expertise to advance high-performance, low-power AI chips and on-device generative AI. The team presented their findings at the IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits in 2024 and 2025.

The team is developing a next-generation chip to address memory bandwidth limitations during the process of AI inference. This new design incorporates data compression and optimizes the management and transfer of external memory for efficiency. The team fabricated this new chip in October 2026 using a 16-nanometer process for better performance. The articles do not state when this next-generation chip will be fully completed or released for use. They also leave open the specific date for the next presentation of these new research findings.

stories.Headline: Judge grants former OpenAI engineer Alfozan $1 million bail with ankle monitor
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in San Francisco granted bail to former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan on Tuesday. Alfozan is a Saudi national who was arrested in October for allegedly bugging an office conference room. He is accused of placing a concealed recording device behind a television to capture confidential company discussions. The judge decided to release the defendant from jail on a bond of one million dollars. His release is expected to take place on Wednesday under specific court ordered conditions.

The release requires Alfozan to use an ankle monitor while he awaits his upcoming criminal trial. He is a thirty five year old US green card holder who worked at OpenAI since July 2025. He was fired on the day of his arrest after staff discovered the sophisticated recording device. Prosecutors found hundreds of audio files and AI transcripts on his personal computer from September 2026. They also found a confidential strategic partnership term sheet photo on his mobile phone.

Magistrate Judge Alex Tse presided over the hearing where the decision for pre trial release was made. Attorney David Rizk said he was grateful the court made the right decision to release his client. Rizk described Alfozan as an overly curious tinkerer who has been forthcoming with the federal investigators. He argued that most of the recordings on the computer contain only random noise and silence. The defense claims prosecutors found no evidence of trade secret theft or unregistered foreign agency.

The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the release and claimed Alfozan remains a significant flight risk. Prosecutors cited his considerable resources and strong connections to Saudi Arabia as reasons for their concerns. They stated that the legal team blithely dismisses the seriousness of the illegal eavesdropping charge. OpenAI executives are affected as the recordings may involve trade secrets and attorney client privileged material. Some recordings reportedly captured meetings between the company and representatives of a foreign government.

Alfozan is charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations and has pleaded not guilty to this. He allegedly uploaded some of the meticulously categorized recordings to the cloud based platform known as Dropbox. Prosecutors noted he was in frequent communication with various people affiliated with the Saudi government. The government previously told a judge they were not aware of evidence that he committed espionage. They have not stated whether the defendant shared any of the recorded information with other people.

The investigation into the activities of Abdulrahman Alfozan is ongoing as the legal case proceeds forward. David Rizk stated that the legal team now looks forward to defending the case in court. It remains unknown what specific information was recorded or if sensitive data was shared outside OpenAI. The government is still investigating what the defendant intended to do with the stored audio files. The articles leave open whether more serious criminal charges will be filed against the former engineer.

stories.Summary:
B.Grimm announced on November 24, 2026 that B.Grimm Power had signed a memorandum of understanding with NTT Global Data Center to pursue a 400 MW data center opportunity in Thailand. The memorandum covers digital infrastructure, an AI ecosystem and energy infrastructure, with an investment value of approximately THB 113 billion. The memorandum is an agreement to pursue the opportunity, not a confirmation that construction has started. Nopadej Karnasuta, B.Grimm Power’s president for Thailand, Malaysia and Energy & Industrial Solutions Business, joined the Japan visit during which it was signed. B.Grimm dates the visit, led by Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas, to November 17, 21, 2026.

Amata B.Grimm Power, a subsidiary of B.Grimm Power (SET: BGRIM), signed the memorandum with NTT Global Data Centers (Thailand), part of NTT DATA, to jointly carry out a feasibility study for a 400MW hyperscale data center campus at Amata City Chonburi Industrial Estate. Investment in the project is estimated to exceed THB 113 billion, and it is expected to create more than 2,500 jobs. The memorandum was signed on Nov. 19 in Tokyo at the Thailand-Japan Investment and Business Dialogue 2026, organized by the Thailand Board of Investment and Japan's Keidanren business federation, with Ekniti presiding. A November 23, 2026 release from Thailand’s Board of Investment dates the Tokyo delegation to November 17, 20, 2026. The BOI, Keidanren dialogue drew 64 Japanese private-sector executives from 38 companies across nine industries.

Under the memorandum, Amata B.Grimm Power would develop the energy and utility infrastructure for the campus, while NTT GDC would bring its experience in data center design, construction and operation. The partners named cloud service providers, AI platform developers and global companies, including clients from Japan, the US and Europe, as target customers. Nopadej Karnasuta said the collaboration reflects a shared vision to develop stable and sustainable energy and digital infrastructure. B.Grimm Power’s company profile reports 5,180 MW of installed capacity and energy delivery through its own distribution networks to more than 400 industrial users. B.Grimm Power states a goal of secured power purchase agreements totaling 10,000 MW by 2030.

The delegation also visited NTT Data Mitaka EAST Data Center to study security, system continuity and energy efficiency in infrastructure supporting AI. B.Grimm’s account says Ekniti highlighted NTT’s Japanese facilities as efficient, quiet, environmentally considerate and able to coexist with local communities. Discussions at the dialogue covered three supply chains: modern vehicles; AI infrastructure and advanced electronics; and modern power grids. NTT DATA appointed Yasuhiro Kajiki on September 10, 2026, as managing director, Japan and APAC, for NTT Global Data Centers, responsible for regional operations and growth strategy. The company linked the expanded leadership role to growing customer demand for AI-ready digital infrastructure across APAC.

A separate agreement with Bloom Energy, announced on November 5, 2026, calls for NTT to deploy 900 MW of onsite power across multiple data center projects globally, with initial shipments planned for 2027. Doug Adams, CEO of NTT Global Data Centers, said clients are building AI capabilities at a pace the grid alone cannot always match, and that speed to power has become one of the defining factors in delivering capacity when and where it’s needed. In January, Amata B.Grimm Power signed a 100MW power purchase agreement with NTT Global Data Centers to supply NTT's fourth data center at Amata City Chonburi, scheduled to start commercial operation in June 2027. Amata B.Grimm Power also supplies electricity to NTT's second and third data centers in Thailand. On June 18, 2026, subsidiary B.Grimm BeyondBridge and INET established B.Grimm INET to develop and operate platforms in Thailand covering energy management, environmental and smart utility systems, greenhouse-gas monitoring and management, cloud security and AI technologies.

No final investment decision, construction start or completion date has been announced. The open question the articles raise is execution: whether the partners can combine NTT’s data center expansion with B.Grimm’s power operations and digital-infrastructure experience. B.Grimm Power also aims to uphold the practices highlighted during the Japan visit while sharing knowledge and technology with Thai people over the long term. NTT DATA expects Bloom’s modular fuel-cell systems to bring power online alongside construction and expand with increasingly power-dense AI workloads. The articles state that turning the investment-mission memorandum into operating AI infrastructure would require delivering the efficiency, quiet operation and community coexistence highlighted during the Japan visit.

stories.Headline: Nscale engineer explains how data center networks shape multi-node AI workload performance
stories.Summary:
Oscar Savolainen, Lead AI Engineer at Nscale, published an engineering blog on November 19, 2026, titled "How the data center shapes the AI workload." In it he argued that once an AI job spans more than one node in a GPU cluster, the data center itself starts making performance decisions. He drew on his lightning talk at Ray Summit 2026, where he walked through what that means in practice. He said he thinks about multi-node optimization the same way he thinks about GPU optimization, as the same problem at a bigger scale. He wrote that two questions decide performance either way: how does the data move, and where does the compute happen.

He said every compute tray already has CPUs, which schedule work onto the GPUs and in inference setups may run the web server and hand heavy matrix math to accelerators. He said agentic reinforcement learning loops may need a CPU to run a VM sandbox for the agent, which usually means standalone CPU nodes. He said teams should colocate CPU nodes when they are on the hot path, because any delay between CPU and GPU shows up directly in the workload. He said teams should colocate to keep traffic east-west, since training data that stays inside the data center avoids north-south trips over the internet, helping performance and security. He said teams can skip colocation when GPU-to-CPU latency isn't critical and there is no strong networking requirement, citing pre-tokenizing a dataset as a good example.

He said a data center has several physically separate networks, and that management and sensor networks rarely touch an AI job. He said the front-end network, usually Ethernet, carries SSH access, code uploads, dependency downloads, the initial TCP handshake before RDMA takes over, and storage traffic to standalone storage racks holding model weights, training data and offloaded KV cache. He said a workload that leans heavily on the front-end network can congest it, slowing weight loading, training data, KV cache, checkpointing and node access. He said the back-end network does peer-to-peer RDMA between GPUs and turns many individual GPUs into one supercomputer. He said a back-end network typically runs on NVIDIA InfiniBand or RoCE with NVLink alongside, so most clusters are RoCE plus NVLink or InfiniBand plus NVLink.

He said RoCE scales to very large deployments, and a multi-plane topology of distinct networks that don't share a spine lets it reach cluster sizes awkward on a single-plane fabric. He said Mellanox, now part of NVIDIA, drove much of InfiniBand's adoption, and the fabric has since added AI-optimized features such as SHARP. He said that in NVIDIA's reference architecture GPUs in the same scale unit talk through the nearest switch while GPUs in different scale units take an extra hop over the spine, so communication within a scale unit is slightly faster. He said NVLink is the highest-bandwidth peer-to-peer link between NVIDIA GPUs and has shaped workload layout, with teams traditionally keeping communication-heavy work such as tensor and expert parallelism inside a single node. He said lighter traffic such as pipeline and data parallelism crossed the node boundary over InfiniBand or RoCE.

He said the one-to-one relationship between a node and an NVLink domain has gone away in the latest NVIDIA systems, and that NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems connect 18 compute trays per rack, four Blackwell or Blackwell Ultra GPUs per tray, and an NVSwitch fabric into one NVLink domain of 72 GPUs. He said he is seeing three effects: bigger models, because tensor and expert parallelism no longer have to fit inside one node or cross InfiniBand or RoCE; faster foundation model training wherever communication inside the rack has been the bottleneck; and faster RL weight transfer. He said RL at scale moves model weights between training and inference instances, and communication between nodes is often a bottleneck that teams work around with off-policy training, which can introduce instability the further off-policy it goes. He said faster weight transfer gives a choice to grow the model or stay closer to on-policy at the same size for greater training stability. He said that with SHARP on InfiniBand and NVSwitch the aggregation in an all-reduce happens inside the switches, reducing network hops and latency, analogous to kernel fusion in GPU programming.

He listed questions to ask a GPU cloud provider: whether nodes are in the same InfiniBand scale unit, whether SHARP is enabled on the switches, whether the customer gets a full NVLink domain and how large it is, and whether CPU nodes can be colocated with the GPUs. He said that for the past year he has been building Control Center, part of Nscale Fleet Operations, the control panel used to manage the GPU fleet from inventory management to proactive health checks and automated remediation. He said commissioning a new data center means testing every layer, with GPUs running multi-day stress workloads to find stragglers, XID errors and memory-remapping issues, and GPU and CPU nodes stress-tested. He said front-end, back-end and management networks are tested down to flapping ports and cables that aren't plugged in correctly, and storage is validated. He said Nscale also runs real end-to-end workloads, which proves the whole system works together and finds tuning that default settings miss on new hardware such as GB300 NVL72 today and NVIDIA Vera Rubin next, and that NVIDIA validated Nscale can train a range of LLM workloads at top performance, which earned NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud status.
