stories.Headline: AmCham and Korea AI policy chief discuss US-Korea AI cooperation in Seoul
stories.Summary:
The American Chamber of Commerce in Korea held a roundtable meeting on Wednesday to discuss strengthening artificial intelligence cooperation between the United States and Korea. Ha Jung-woo, the vice chair of the Presidential Council on National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, met with the chamber and member companies in Seoul. The participants focused on ways to advance the ambition of Korea to become one of the world's top three AI powers. This closed-door event took place at the chamber's office located in Yeouido, which is in the western part of the city of Seoul. The meeting brought together government policymakers and executives from several global technology companies to share industry perspectives and discuss national AI strategy.

The discussions required expanding infrastructure like data centers and making advances in semiconductors, AI models, and software to strengthen the national AI ecosystem. Ha Jung-woo outlined three government megaprojects focusing on semiconductors, AI data centers, and physical AI to accelerate transformation across industries and public services. The meeting included representatives from Apple, Amazon Web Services, Corning, Palo Alto Networks, PTC, Qualcomm, and the safety testing provider UL Solutions. Participants explored how to leverage complementary strengths in digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing while cooperating on cybersecurity, AI safety, and international standards. These efforts aim to foster a sustainable and inclusive global AI ecosystem through international cooperation in energy, infrastructure, and cybersecurity.

Ha Jung-woo stated that the three major megaprojects are central to efforts to accelerate AI transformation in everyday life and public services. He said that Korea would continue expanding international cooperation in energy and AI safety to help foster a sustainable global AI ecosystem. James Kim, the Chairman and CEO of AMCHAM, said that the chamber strongly supports the ambition of Korea to be a leader. Kim noted that the complementary strengths of both nations in semiconductors and AI technology present tremendous opportunities for bilateral cooperation and growth. He described artificial intelligence as one of the most promising areas for the next phase of the bilateral economic partnership between countries.

Representatives from global firms like Apple and Qualcomm discussed how US companies could help expand infrastructure and speed up AI adoption in manufacturing. The participants explored the role of public-private partnerships in enhancing the competitiveness of Korea and accelerating transformation across various key industrial sectors. The meeting affected executives from across the AI value chain who sought to share their business perspectives with the Korean government policymakers. These industry leaders discussed how government and industry could work together to expand computing infrastructure and advance the development of AI software. The discussions highlighted the importance of building a trusted AI ecosystem through the establishment of international standards and improved cybersecurity measures.

The AMCHAM AI Leadership Council was launched in July to bring together executives from across the AI value chain to share perspectives. This council serves as a bridge to promote closer public-private cooperation on policies related to artificial intelligence and overall industry innovation. The background of the meeting involves Korea's strategic push to integrate AI into manufacturing and other key industries to increase global competitiveness. The government's national AI strategy prioritizes the development of physical AI and the expansion of data centers to support its technological goals. These initiatives are part of a broader effort to ensure that AI transformation reaches public services and the daily lives of citizens.

The AMCHAM AI Leadership Council will continue working with the Korean government to promote a predictable and business-friendly policy environment for AI. James Kim pledged that the chamber would continue talks with the government to encourage further AI investment and innovation in Korea. The participants will look for ways to build on the complementary strengths of the United States and Korea in advanced manufacturing. The articles leave open the specific details of how the three megaprojects will be funded or the exact timeline for implementation. It remains unspecified how the mentioned global companies will specifically contribute to the expansion of the Korean AI infrastructure and manufacturing.
Orgs: presidential council on national artificial intelligence strategy

stories.Headline: Pinterest lets parents limit AI-generated content teens see
stories.Summary:
Pinterest announced this week that it is adding new parental controls for AI-generated content. The company introduced these updates on November 24, 2026, to help parents manage teen accounts. These changes allow parents to adjust the amount of AI-generated content in recommendations. The platform is expanding its existing tools to give parents more control over the experience. This update focuses specifically on the content that teenagers see while using the app.

Parents can now use an updated Parental Controls page to manage various settings for their children. They can tweak if videos autoplay and adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The redesigned page also allows parents to configure settings related to personalized ads for their teens. These tools are available on the Pinterest platform to help parents dictate the user experience. The update includes these standard options alongside the new AI-generated content limit settings.

Pinterest is responsible for these changes and claims to be one of the first major platforms to do this. The company says these tools allow users to dictate the type of experience they want on the app. They are providing these settings as part of an overall expansion of their parental control features. The company is putting these specific tools into the hands of parents to manage AI exposure. This move follows the company's own efforts to fight AI content within its user feeds.

Parents have said that the lack of AI controls is harming children's well-being in favor of profits. The children's advocacy group Fairplay expressed similar concerns in a letter sent in April to other tech leaders. Over 200 organizations and experts signed that letter to demand the removal of AI content for minors. Teens are the primary group affected by these new settings and the general presence of AI content. Other platforms like Snap and Meta have also implemented different limits for their younger users.

Pinterest introduced settings to restrict AI-modified content in 2025, but some AI content still appeared in feeds. Other platforms have focused on limiting access to AI chatbots or pausing access to AI characters. WhatsApp allows parents to adjust how teens use Meta AI to create content or ask questions. Most social media platforms generally provide few controls for AI-generated content filling user feeds and recommendations. These new Pinterest tools build upon the company's previous attempts to manage AI-generated material.

The new parental controls are now available for parents to use on the updated settings page. Parents can now limit the AI-generated content that appears in the recommendations for their teen children. The articles do not state when further updates to these parental controls will be released. It remains open whether these tools will fully stop AI content from appearing in teen feeds. The text does not mention if other social platforms will follow this specific model of control.

stories.Headline: Google launches Momentum to give Indian startups AI and cloud support
stories.Summary:
Google launched an initiative called Momentum on 24 November 2026 to deepen its support for Indian startups by giving them access to AI technologies, cloud infrastructure, engineering expertise and global platforms. The company said the initiative builds on a decade of its Google for Startups Accelerator programmes in India and is meant to help founders develop products, deploy AI solutions and expand into new markets. Google also said Momentum would bring together its technology, research and global networks to support Indian founders. The programme is designed to help startups move beyond product development into areas such as trusted AI deployment, customer acquisition, commercial readiness and expansion into new markets. In July, when it marked ten years of its accelerator programmes in India, Google said it had supported 277 Indian startups, with 94 per cent of its alumni continuing to build and scale their businesses.

As part of Momentum, Google cited several Indian startups using its technologies, including the healthcare startup AiSteth, which it said has screened more than 160,000 patients across over 20 Indian states using Gemini, MedGemma and Gemma for clinical summaries and medical training. Google said the legal tech company SpotDraft integrated Gemini with on-device capabilities through Chrome for its contract workflows, reducing latency by 70 per cent and processing costs by 80 per cent. Google also said VideoSDK built real-time conversational AI agents using the Gemini Live API and reported a 25 per cent improvement in response quality and a roughly 40 per cent reduction in infrastructure costs after moving to Google Cloud. Google highlighted startups developing AI models for Indian languages, including Shunya Labs, which supports more than 200 languages and dialects and has used Gemma models and Project Vaani speech data to develop specialised models such as an offline Hindi speech recognition model. Bengaluru-based ZenteiQ, a spinout from IISc, is developing small AI models for edge devices and increased its inference throughput fourfold using Google Cloud TPUs and Google Kubernetes Engine, according to Google.

Google said ZenteiQ has also been selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop foundation models covering English and 10 Indian languages. Google also cited Phot.ai, an AI-powered creative platform that uses Google Cloud to scale its infrastructure and Google Ads to improve customer acquisition. Google said its support extends beyond technology to infrastructure costs, customer acquisition, security and market expansion, and that security, privacy and responsible AI development will remain central to its work with Indian startups as they move towards wider adoption and deployment. The company also said it supports startups addressing scientific and environmental challenges through the AI for the Planet Accelerator, an initiative by Google DeepMind that provides access to frontier AI technology and technical expertise for climate, agriculture and environmental resilience applications. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch of the initiative and the support Google has described.

stories.Headline: Google books Blue Origin New Glenn to launch AI computing satellites in 2029
stories.Summary:
Google has booked a Blue Origin New Glenn launch for the first quarter of 2029 to advance Project Suncatcher, a test of solar-powered computing satellites. The companies announced the agreement on Nov. 19, outlining a dedicated heavy-lift mission to place satellites equipped with Google's Tensor Processing Units into sun-synchronous orbit. Blue Origin said on Thursday that Alphabet's Google had selected its New Glenn rocket to launch satellites for Project Suncatcher. The launch will be Google's first heavy-lift flight dedicated to Project Suncatcher and will carry several computing satellites aboard New Glenn. Google and Planet Labs launched the first Project Suncatcher prototype aboard a SpaceX rocket in October and said the satellite was operating as expected after establishing contact.

The mission is designed to evaluate whether space-based infrastructure can support AI workloads at roughly the scale of individual data center racks. Each satellite will carry Google's tensor processing units, with computing capacity roughly equal to a rack of servers in a conventional data center. The satellites will enter an orbit that provides near-continuous sunlight, allowing Google to examine whether solar energy can support intensive computing in space. The first prototype mission is testing whether the chips can withstand launch forces, radiation and extreme temperatures, while engineers study how to cool them without the airflow available on Earth. Google has described the project as a long-term effort to expand AI infrastructure by tapping solar energy in space.

Dave McCarthy, IDC's group vice president for cloud and datacenters, enterprise infrastructure, said successful deployments will need to demonstrate sustained uptime, autonomous fault recovery, and optical communications capable of keeping pace with the processors. He said a server rack in orbit has to prove it can run for long periods because you cannot send a technician to swap a failed GPU at 500 kilometers. McCarthy said falling launch prices will need to coincide with hardware that can survive at least five years, roughly matching standard data center depreciation cycles. He said abundant solar power in orbit does not automatically offset a steep launch bill, and that if radiation or thermal wear forces operators to replace satellites every two or three years, the unit economics will not work. Rob DeMillo, CEO and cofounder of orbital computing company Sophia Space, said the demonstrations must also show that multiple nodes can compute together and run useful customer workloads.

DeMillo said an operator does not necessarily need a demonstration to be large, but needs it to demonstrate that the underlying architecture works and can scale. He said there is a significant difference between putting a computer in space and building computing infrastructure in space. Bill Ray, distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said heat is the primary barrier but not the only one, and that micrometeorite shielding will be essential, along with redundancy to provide radiation resistance. DeMillo said designs that simply replicate enclosed terrestrial server racks could create substantial cooling burdens, including the need for pumps and fluid loops. DeMillo identified wildfire detection, disaster response, weather analysis, and maritime tracking as potential uses for orbital image processing.

Ray said radiation protection, micrometeorite shielding, and maneuvering capability to avoid debris in the heavily used sun-synchronous orbital environment are also critical. DeMillo said radiation is also a system-level engineering problem, and that shielding is part of the answer, but so are hardware error correction, fault detection and software that can recover or redistribute workloads. McCarthy pointed to asynchronous model training and synthetic data generation as possible use cases where computing demand is high but data movement is relatively limited. Ray said he expects orbital edge computing to focus on tasks such as screening imagery before transmission and providing security services. The constraints also surfaced in orbital infrastructure discussions at September's AI Infra Summit, where executives highlighted the tradeoffs among radiator size, weight, and launch requirements.

Companies including Elon Musk's SpaceX and startup Starcloud are exploring data centers in orbit as growing AI use drives demand for computing capacity and strains infrastructure supporting facilities on the ground. The planned mission advances efforts to move power-hungry AI computing beyond Earth, using sunlight in orbit to ease pressure on electricity grids, land and cooling systems. Thursday's agreement gives Blue Origin a major future mission for New Glenn as the company seeks to expand its launch business following delays and a launchpad explosion in May. Experts have also noted that high launch costs, engineering hurdles and limited satellite production can put data centers in orbit years away from commercial use. Because space has no atmosphere to carry heat away, operators must rely on radiators, which add weight and complexity and compete with processors and other components for launch capacity.

The long development timeline for space-based data centers leaves operators balancing potential energy advantages against launch, communications, and maintenance costs. Radiation damage and thermal wear could shorten satellite lifespan, increasing the frequency with which operators would need to launch replacement capacity. If more advanced AI workloads move into orbit, ground-to-space communications capacity will become even more important. Earth observation satellites can collect enormous amounts of imagery, and processing that information in orbit and sending down the answer rather than all of the raw data saves bandwidth and, in many cases, time. The articles leave open how much useful computing the satellites can sustain, how they recover from failures, and whether their operating lives can justify launch and replacement costs.

stories.Headline: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO to spark AI trade rally
stories.Summary:
United States stocks surged on Monday, November 23, 2026, after the board of Nvidia unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO. This immediate leadership change reignited the artificial intelligence trade and pushed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite to their largest single day gains since April 9, 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,447.98 points, or 3.01 percent, to 49,595.31. The S&P 500 added 326.78 points, or 4.73 percent, to 7,237.17. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 1,471.83 points, or 6.51 percent, to 24,089.56.

Nvidia shares surged 31.48 percent, which the company claims was the largest single day increase in market capitalization on record. The chipmaker added nearly 1 trillion dollars to its valuation, bringing the total close to 4 trillion dollars. Other chip stocks rallied, including Micron Technology at 19 percent, Marvell Technology at 18.37 percent, Intel at 16.34 percent, and Advanced Micro Devices at 6.85 percent. Dell Technologies rose over 20 percent, CoreWeave popped 22.32 percent, and Oracle jumped 12.34 percent. Technology led the S&P 500 sectors by adding 9.03 percent, while Tesla surged 11.46 percent and Alphabet and Meta Platforms each jumped over 6 percent.

Glen Smith, the chief investment officer at GDS Wealth Management, was responsible for analyzing the market reaction. He stated that the surprising decision to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO helped eliminate a major source of uncertainty for the AI trade. This trade had been struggling in the weeks leading up to the announcement. Following the news, the Cboe Volatility Index, which serves as the fear gauge for Wall Street, fell nearly 26 percent to 26.62.

Investors are now monitoring the October personal consumption expenditures price index, which is scheduled for release this Wednesday. This data will help them evaluate the possibility of a quarter point interest rate hike during the Federal Reserve meeting in December. Meanwhile, S&P Global reported that United States business activity growth slowed to a four month low in November. The composite index fell to 54.6 from 55.9 in October, while the services and manufacturing indices slipped to 54.7 and 54.5 respectively.

stories.Headline: Maine report finds office and administrative jobs most exposed to AI
stories.Summary:
A recent report from Maine’s Center for Workforce Research and Information categorized careers by how much work could be done by AI, and the Bangor Daily News and Portland Press Herald reported on it on Nov. 24, 2026. The report found that jobs in office and administrative support, business and financial operations, sales and related occupations, and computers and mathematics are most exposed to AI. More than 171,000 jobs in Maine fall into those categories, based on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. The affected positions include jobs at banks, call centers, schools, libraries, hospitals, engineering companies and graphic design firms. The topic comes up in everyday conversations, and a graphic designer client told South Portland salon owner Thomas Leighton last week that their job is going to be toast.

The report says 25% of employed Mainers use AI at work multiple times weekly and 13% use it daily. Among AI users, 55% reported higher productivity and 41% reported no difference. AI exposure is higher in Cumberland, Androscoggin and Kennebec counties, according to an October report from the Maine Center for Economic Policy. Maine’s unemployment rate has been around 3% for two years and below 4% for over four years, according to the state’s center for workforce research. In July, the University of Maine System entered a two-year, $1.4 million contract to provide access to ChatGPT across all campuses.

Mark McInerney, director of the Center for Workforce Research and Information, said at an October meeting of the state’s Consensus Economic Forecasting Commission that high AI exposure does not necessarily equate to job losses. He said there is a lot of nuance among occupations that rate very highly, with a mix of displacement, productivity gains and lots in between. Chancellor Dannel Malloy said the ChatGPT contract was a strategic investment that will help strengthen teaching and research, modernize operations and improve efficiency for Maine taxpayers. A BIW spokesperson said via email that the shipyard is committed to being transparent with all its employees about future AI and new technology initiatives. Patrick Woodcock, CEO of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce, said via email that increasing productivity can allow the economy to expand growth in a constrained labor force.

Devin Ragnar, spokesman for Local S6 of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, said the hardware is catching up to the software very quickly and the union wanted contract language that protected its people and interests. Andy O’Brien, spokesman for the Maine AFL-CIO, said AI is just taking over and called it the de-skilling of an industry, but said he still thinks people want to see quality animation produced by humans. Leighton said he would never not have his bookkeeper and accountant and does not think he would trust that to AI. The Maine Center for Economic Policy found no evidence of broad AI-driven unemployment or wage decline but saw significant risk that AI may increase workplace inequalities. Workers at General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, which employs over 6,800 people, have no illusions that hands-on skills will be enough to preserve jobs, Ragnar said.

Last spring, Lewiston-based Central Maine Healthcare, which employs about 2,748 people, laid off 50 IT workers while transitioning to Epic, a cloud-based health records system with AI features. In July, Portland-based MaineHealth, which has about 25,000 employees and also uses Epic, announced it would cut 83 IT and analytics positions. At the University of Maine in Orono, staff and students are challenging the administration’s plan to eliminate hundreds of positions to address an expected $19 million budget shortfall. Last year, BIW introduced a programmable robotic welding arm, a collaborative robot or cobot, capable of executing thousands of repetitive tasks alongside people, according to a company newsletter. In early August, Virginia-based Huntington Ingalls Industries, a BIW competitor, announced it will outsource $900 million in AI-guided work to two robotics companies over the next seven years.

Soon after that announcement, Local S6 ratified a five-year contract that requires BIW to inform the union of any proposed changes or additions in technology, equipment or processes, including AI and robotics, Ragnar said. The union has filed a grievance over the cobot that has yet to be resolved. The Animation Guild, a California-based union, began studying the impact of AI in 2023 and predicted that more than 21%, or 118,000, represented jobs would be consolidated, replaced or eliminated by the end of 2026. SHL, a global workforce consultant, found in a recent survey of over 2,000 employed adults in the U.S. and the U.K. that 52% had encountered AI rebounding, either directly or through someone they knew. McInerney said it remains to be seen who ultimately benefits and that growth alone might not tell how gains will be distributed between labor and capital going forward.

stories.Summary:
A landmark report on artificial intelligence has recommended that companies be required to report serious AI incidents to regulators and that safeguards be put in place around the technology, according to SmartCompany, which published the story on 25 November 2026. stories.Headline: Stratum and Ocean Power Technologies sign first-phase agreement to assess renewable-powered offshore AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Stratum Holdings Corp. and Ocean Power Technologies, Inc. announced on November 24, 2026 that they signed an agreement to begin the first phase of their strategic collaboration. The agreement moves the companies from a non-binding letter of intent announced on October 26, 2026 into defined work on evaluating offshore data center assets. Those assets would be powered by renewable wave, wind and solar energy. The agreement pairs OPT's patented PowerBuoy technology with Stratum's high-performance GPU infrastructure. That infrastructure includes Stratum's latest-generation NVIDIA B300 GPUs, to support edge AI inference and related computing applications.

The initial agreement covers feasibility and planning only and does not include equipment fabrication, GPU integration, offshore deployment or at-sea testing. Those steps would require a separate agreement. The companies intend to negotiate a separate demonstration program agreement providing a non-exclusive, non-transferable U.S. license to OPT's PowerBuoy technology for demonstration activities. That license would also cover potential commercial use, subject to agreed success criteria and commercial terms. The announcement was datelined Celebration, Florida, and carried by GlobeNewswire.

Nicholas H. Adler, Chief Executive Officer of Stratum Holdings, said the agreement takes the collaboration with OPT from a letter of intent to defined work, with a path toward a demonstration at sea. Adler said demand for AI computing is growing faster than the power and cooling available on land, and that the industry is beginning to look offshore. He said pairing Stratum's NVIDIA B300 GPUs with OPT's PowerBuoy platform, which generates its own renewable power in a natural cooling environment, could give Stratum a differentiated position in this emerging market. He said the feasibility assessment is designed to give the companies the technical and commercial roadmap to pursue it. Tracy Pagliara, Acting President and Chief Executive Officer of Ocean Power Technologies, said advancing into this initial phase allows a more detailed look at the technical and commercial requirements for combining PowerBuoy technology with Stratum's GPU infrastructure.

Pagliara said the focus will be on evaluating the power, thermal management and communications capabilities necessary to support offshore AI computing and on establishing a foundation for a potential demonstration program. The companies believe a key area of evaluation will be the potential to leverage the marine environment for cooling, which could reduce the energy required for thermal management compared to conventional land-based data centers. The companies believe their combined technologies could provide a differentiated approach to renewable-powered AI computing. The collaboration comes amid growing industry interest in offshore data centers as companies explore alternatives to traditional land-based infrastructure to address rising AI computing demand, power constraints and cooling requirements. The companies will also assess the technical requirements for supporting AI inference workloads in remote offshore environments.

The feasibility assessment is structured around several objectives. On AI compute requirements, the companies will define GPU configurations, AI workloads, power consumption, thermal requirements and operational performance criteria. On renewable energy integration, the work will evaluate wave, wind and solar generation capabilities, together with energy storage solutions, to support offshore computing operations. On thermal management, the assessment will evaluate cooling solutions that leverage the surrounding marine environment. Communications infrastructure will also be examined, including data connectivity, bandwidth requirements and the communications systems necessary to support remote AI workloads.

Platform and deployment planning will address PowerBuoy platform configurations, equipment integration, mooring requirements and potential offshore deployment locations. The commercial feasibility and demonstration roadmap component will develop preliminary cost estimates, project milestones and performance criteria for a potential subsequent demonstration program. Stratum Holdings Corp. is an AI infrastructure company focused on GPU leasing and high-performance compute capacity, and is transitioning from legacy real estate operations to provide scalable compute solutions supporting artificial intelligence workloads. Ocean Power Technologies provides intelligent maritime systems and services for defense and security, offshore energy, science and research, and offshore wind, and its PowerBuoy platforms deliver clean, renewable power and real-time data communications for remote maritime and subsea applications. The company also offers the WAM-V autonomous surface vehicle and Merrows software for multi-domain awareness.

Following completion of the feasibility assessment, the companies intend to evaluate the findings and negotiate a separate agreement governing a potential demonstration program. The collaboration reflects Stratum's broader strategy to expand its AI infrastructure business by exploring innovative deployment models for high-performance computing. That includes opportunities to support distributed AI inference in environments where traditional data center infrastructure may be impractical or cost-prohibitive. The articles do not state when the feasibility assessment will be completed or what its cost will be. The articles also do not state where any offshore deployment might occur.

stories.Headline: UK cyber center reports rise in AI-driven attacks exploiting weak security foundations
stories.Summary:
The National Cybersecurity Center, which is the cybersecurity unit for the United Kingdom government, has observed a marked rise in cyberattacks driven by artificial intelligence. These incidents have occurred in recent months, with several specific cases involving autonomous hacking tools reported since September. Hackers are increasingly using these agentic tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to breach various networks and systems. These attacks have caused significant intrusions and resulted in operational downtime for the affected organizations.

The current threat landscape requires a renewed focus on basic cybersecurity defenses and the implementation of established best practices. These AI tools often target internet-facing systems to rapidly test easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints used by developers. The rise in these attacks coincides with the release of open-source autonomous penetration testing tools, specifically naming Artex and Cairn. These tools allow malicious actors to find vulnerabilities in minutes that may have gone unnoticed for years.

The National Cybersecurity Center stated in a blog post that the exploited issues are not novel memory corruption flaws or unpatched vulnerabilities. Instead, the unit explained that these are unmitigated weaknesses resulting from years of accumulated technical debt within organizations. The NCSC noted that while AI makes it easier to find and exploit flaws, it does not make established security controls obsolete. They emphasized that building strong foundational cybersecurity has never mattered more than it does now.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has also issued a warning regarding the unprecedented speeds at which these AI-powered attacks are carried out. This suggests a broader trend where autonomous tools enable faster exploitation of known weaknesses across different regions. The UK government maintains that many of these intrusions are preventable if organizations address their underlying security foundations. No further future actions were specified beyond the urgent need for stronger foundational defenses.

stories.Headline: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic use AI to design custom chips
stories.Summary:
OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are using artificial intelligence to design their own custom chips, according to a report by Business Insider, in a move that could weaken Nvidia's hold on AI computing. OpenAI began using AI to develop a custom chip called Jalapeño in early 2025, and its models reduced the space required for two important chip parts by 10 per cent and 13 per cent. In one instance, the AI redesigned a circuit to use about 15 per cent less space while halving the calculation time, the report said. OpenAI also worked with Nvidia competitor AMD to improve existing chips, reaching gains of up to 14 per cent on some performance and efficiency metrics, and AMD has integrated those improvements into its manufacturing designs.

Google's DeepMind research division introduced AlphaChip in 2024, an AI system that arranges processor components and can complete work in hours that previously took engineers weeks or months. Google has used this technology for every generation of its AI chips, known as TPUs, since 2020. Anthropic is building an in-house chip design team and attracting engineers from OpenAI and Google, and it said its most advanced AI model showed significant improvements in designing electronic circuits. Custom chips let companies like OpenAI and Anthropic tailor hardware to their exact AI workloads, which can cut costs by eliminating unnecessary features found in general-purpose chips like Nvidia's.

AI is also simplifying the creation of software needed to run AI models, which could eventually reduce dependence on Nvidia's CUDA framework, the report said. CUDA has traditionally locked developers into Nvidia's ecosystem, according to the report. The articles do not say who at the three companies is responsible for the chip design efforts or what those people said about them. stories.Headline: GreyNoise Threat 13 uses AI tools to target Check Point servers globally
stories.Summary:
A threat actor known as GreyNoise Threat 13 used AI enabled tools to target Check Point Security Management servers globally. This campaign involved scanning, exploitation, and control activities that the threat intelligence firm GreyNoise began tracking in early October. The actor used 99 IP addresses, many of which were associated with disposable network infrastructure or ExpressVPN egresses. Activity was confirmed between October 17 and November 2, although the actor likely maintains persistent access to the servers. The campaign targeted multiple geographies and industries using a combination of automated operations and hands on keyboard activity.

The actor targeted 22 organisations in the US, UK, Australia, Austria, China, France, Germany, Hong Kong, the Netherlands, and South Korea. These victims were in the energy, engineering, financial services, government, manufacturing, mining, and transportation sectors across these various global locations. The attacker used 99 IP addresses to conduct over 1400 network sessions and create or download more than 1200 files. Between October 20 and 26, the actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 servers across the 22 organisations. On October 2, the actor forged a signed admin session cookie to gain administrative SSH access to an HFS server.

GreyNoise reported that the actor used agentic harnesses and systems to weaponise vulnerabilities and automatically exploit vulnerable assets. The firm stated they witnessed the actor use compromised victim Check Point devices as egresses for their malicious network activity. They noted that the actor had access to the Check Point servers before the compromise of the HFS server. GreyNoise explained that the actor used a relay server to collect responses containing victim IP addresses in incrementing order. The firm believes some timeline foibles reflect agentic offensive operations used to gather systems for operational relays or targets.

The campaign affected at least 22 organisations across several sectors, including government, financial services, and transportation, in ten different countries. One victim server was used as a hop to save data exfiltrated from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attacker deployed tools including Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, and Paramiko for reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation. Python utilities and scripts were also used to perform these tasks within the compromised environments of the targeted organisations. The bulk certificate management task failed, but the actor still collected victim IP addresses in text files on a relay.

The actor exploited vulnerabilities including CVE 2026 61500 in Rejetto HFS and CVE 2026 16232 in Check Point SmartConsole. Other targeted flaws included CVE 2023 4966 and CVE 2025 5777 in Citrix NetScaler, and CVE 2024 21893 in Ivanti systems. The actor also targeted CVE 2020 1472 and CVE 2026 41089 in Windows NetLogon, and CVE 2021 26855 and CVE 2021 34473 in Microsoft Exchange. Additionally, the activity involved CVE 2026 98432 in Linux IPv4 UAF and CVE 2021 21972 and CVE 2023 34048 in VMware vCenter. These vulnerabilities were used to gain access, scan environments, and exfiltrate data from the targeted global organisations.

GreyNoise believes the campaign is still ongoing because the threat actor maintained persistent access to the compromised Check Point servers. The actor likely continues to use separate agentic harnesses to scan for and automatically exploit new sets of vulnerable assets. The articles do not state when the actor first gained access to the Check Point Security Management servers. It remains unknown exactly how the attacker initially gained access to those specific Check Point assets before the HFS compromise. The reports leave open whether any further bulk actions were attempted after the failed certificate management task in October.

stories.Headline: Google engineer urges scoped credentials and containment policies for AI agents
stories.Summary:
Amanda Walker, Google's senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security, gave a session at QCon San Francisco 2026 on securing AI agents in production, InfoQ reported on November 23, 2026. The session addressed teams whose agents had been adopted organically and were running ahead of their security and observability frameworks. Walker argued that a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider, one that acts with superhuman speed and persistence. She covered identity and credentials, boundary defence, subagent orchestration and policy-based containment. TechGig reported the talk on November 24, 2026, saying she framed AI agents as an insider-risk problem operating at machine speed.

Walker recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone. She described giving an agent raw human credentials as the fastest path to production failure, because the agent inherits the user's authority and a prompt injection in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes. Scoped OAuth tokens limit an agent's access in time and scope but are immutable once issued, while credential attenuation lets an orchestrator mint narrower tokens for its subagents, such as read-only access to logs or read-only access to a repository between two commits when bisecting a broken build. She pointed to Eclipse Biscuit, a token format whose holders can append restrictions but cannot remove existing ones without invalidating its signature. For API keys, she said a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real one as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration.

Walker cautioned that a virtual machine protects the host, not the resources an agent can reach, since an agent with network access can still delete a database. She said container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies such as Envoy give finer control over file system and network access, but a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful, so teams need policies that constrain what agents do with the services they call. She highlighted poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets, citing Snyk research that found more than a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw. She described an agent that read internal SRE documentation and invoked a break-glass process intended for emergencies, having decided it was the most expedient route, and said monitoring caught it. She described computer-use agents, which drive a mouse and keyboard, as in essence impersonation, while acknowledging they solve problems that machine protocols such as MCP cannot.

Asked in the question-and-answer session about tagging identities as agents, Walker said the biggest thing it gave was auditability about some of these risk decisions. She said the distinction supports human-only rules such as emergency access and can help with agent-only rules such as signed releases in regulated environments, although an agent flag alone is not enough for those. In the Q&A she advised security teams not to simply say no, which pushes colleagues to work around controls, but to allow experimentation where mistakes are reversible and keep human review for irreversible actions such as wire transfers. She said organisations must distinguish agents from the people they work for, because some processes depend on a human accepting risk.

She said controls need to work at machine speed rather than relying on someone reviewing logs the next morning. The session took place at QCon San Francisco, held November 16 to 20, 2026, in San Francisco. The talk was published by InfoQ on November 23, 2026, in a three-minute read by Mark Silvester, and TechGig published its report on November 24, 2026. InfoQ listed the content under its DevOps topic and tagged it with AI Security, Eclipse, Digital Identity, QCon San Francisco 2026 and Agents.

Walker's session was aimed at teams whose agents were running ahead of their security and observability frameworks. TechGig's report carried the headline that Google discussed securing AI agents in production. Walker said it takes more work than reusing human authentication infrastructure, but suits services where teams control both ends. She said an agent flag alone is not enough for agent-only rules such as signed releases in regulated environments.

The articles do not say what QCon San Francisco 2026 attendees or Google plan to do next with the patterns Walker described. The articles do not say whether the practices she described have been adopted at Google or anywhere else. The articles do not give the date of the session within the conference or the size of its audience. The articles do not say how the Snyk research was conducted or which marketplaces were examined.

stories.Headline: iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories with a remote sandbox platform
stories.Summary:
iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories, and on November 24, 2026, OpenAI published an account of how the company scaled coding agents across all of them. The account describes iFood's Remote Agents Platform, which turns engineering tasks into API calls that run in a remote sandbox and return a merge request. Victor Coelho, a Senior Software Engineer at iFood, is quoted throughout the account explaining the platform. The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks and consumed more than 27 billion tokens, according to the account. The first major user was an internal iFood security product that scans the repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.

The platform's entry point is a simple REST API through which users submit a prompt and environment requirements, and the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox. The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript and Go, and beyond it the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes and AWS. All runs use GPT-5.6 Luna, at an average cost of four U.S. cents per run. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow, cloning the repository and setting up the working branch at the start and publishing the merge request at the end, with agentic execution in between. Results are processed using OpenAI's Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.

Coelho said solving the problem for one repository is easy and the challenge is solving it at scale, and that the platform is designed to make that possible across all 15,000 repositories. He said that before the platform there were fragmented solutions, with several teams trying to solve different problems without an agentic runtime available to them. He said the team chose GPT-5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, benchmarks showed a great balance of intelligence, efficiency and execution speed. He said the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI's model provides ensures iFood can scale sustainably given plans to scale the platform across many use cases. He said the Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI's Batch API and Agents API, and that those products directly inspired how iFood built its solution.

Coelho said that with the platform the accuracy of the security fixes more than doubled, and that the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. He said a developer can launch a code fix or a performance analysis while in a meeting, something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment. He said developers can unlock productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens. The security team did not need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration, and it needed only to call an API.

Coverage extends across iFood's more than 15,000 code repositories, and product teams have moved from building fragmented solutions to delegating agentic execution through a REST API. Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way and they all ran into the same obstacle, according to the account. What was missing was not intelligence or a use case but execution infrastructure, a dedicated runtime. The platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers, extending to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.

Task progress can be monitored in real time, and the runner's internal design alternates between deterministic steps and agentic execution. The account lists lessons for leaders, including that the bottleneck is often the runtime rather than the use case and that cost per run should be treated as an architectural decision. The team plans to bring the platform to many more use cases across iFood, expanding the range of internal products that delegate agentic execution to it. Cost per task will determine whether that expansion can be sustained, according to the account.

The account does not say when the platform was first deployed or how long the migration took. It does not give the size of the team that built the platform. It does not say which vulnerabilities the security product fixed or how many. It does not name the internal security product.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes bill to give all citizens cash payments from AI industry tax revenues
stories.Summary:
The Taiwanese government decided to provide cash payments to share economic achievements from the artificial intelligence industry boom with its citizens. Taiwan's Legislative Yuan passed a bill on November 20 to grant these payments to all citizens regardless of age or income. The main opposition Kuomintang led the effort to pass this legislation despite formal opposition from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party. This bold decision aims to return tax revenues generated by the AI industry boom back to the general public. The Legislative Yuan passed the measure with 50 votes in favor and 46 votes against the proposed cash distribution.

The Special Act for Sharing Economic Fruits with the Entire Nation and Stabilizing Livelihoods requires payments of 20,000 New Taiwan Dollars. This amount is equivalent to about 810,000 won and will be distributed to every resident without any income based exclusion criteria. The received money will be exempt from income tax and excluded from seizure, collateral, and any form of compulsory enforcement. The Executive Yuan must submit a special budget bill to the Legislative Yuan within one month of the special act taking effect. Payments must then be completed within three months after the special budget takes effect to fulfill the requirements of the bill.

The main opposition Kuomintang led the bill and claimed that local election results will determine whether the bonus is paid. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party maintains that further increases are difficult without considering fiscal conditions for the country's general budget. This ruling party stated that its proposed 2027 budget already includes a payment of 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person. The Executive Yuan raised concerns over the fiscal burden and stated the plan could be unconstitutional due to the cost. They claimed that distributing 20,000 New Taiwan Dollars to all citizens would require about 471.4 billion New Taiwan Dollars in resources.

Online opinion appears to favor the cash payments according to a poll conducted by the China Times News Network. In that poll, 92 percent of more than 8,000 participants responded that they strongly support the proposed AI bonus payments. The ruling and opposition parties have clashed ahead of local elections over how much excess tax revenue should be refunded. Citizens of all ages and income levels are affected by this decision as the bill targets every resident of Taiwan. The clash between the two parties centers on the amount of money that should be returned to the public.

Taiwan houses major companies across global AI supply chains, including TSMC, which is claimed to be the world's largest foundry company. The AI semiconductor industry boom has driven up economic growth rates and increased tax revenue, leading to calls for sharing achievements. Taiwan has previously distributed consumer vouchers and cash several times to stimulate the economy and boost overall national consumption. These past payments include 3,600 New Taiwan Dollars in the late 2000s and 3,000 and 5,000 New Taiwan Dollars during the pandemic. In 2023, the government paid 6,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person, and last year it distributed 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars per person.

The government must now determine if the Executive Yuan will submit the required special budget bill to the Legislative Yuan. It remains uncertain whether and when the cash will actually be distributed to the citizens of Taiwan despite the bill. The two political parties continue to disagree, so it is expected to take time to finalize the payment details. The articles leave open whether the ruling party will accept the fiscal burden of 471.4 billion New Taiwan Dollars. Final decisions on the exact amount and the timing of the distribution are not yet confirmed by the government.

stories.Headline: Australia and Singapore agree to expand cooperation on AI and essential supply chains
stories.Summary:
Australia and Singapore agreed to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence and essential supplies on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, during bilateral talks. Prime Ministers Anthony Albanese and Lawrence Wong met at Parliament House in Canberra to sign a joint statement regarding the emerging technology. This meeting took place during the 11th Singapore-Australia Annual Leaders' Meeting to strengthen the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership 2.0 between the nations. The two leaders committed to working together on the development of AI and international efforts to shape the governance of AI. They also announced a new memorandum of understanding to ensure the resilience of supply chains for various essential goods and materials.

The new agreement expands fuel supply chain arrangements from July to include essential supplies such as food, pharmaceuticals, and various medical goods. The leaders reaffirmed cooperation under the 2024 Memorandum of Understanding on AI and a refreshed 2026 MoU on Cyber Security Cooperation. They welcomed the inaugural Australia-Singapore Cyber and Digital Senior Officials' Dialogue that was held in July 2026 to improve digital ties. The nations will use platforms like the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science to advance international AI standards. They also aim to support Pacific-led AI capabilities by drawing on Project Atlas and the development of the SEA-LION AI model.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese stated that the agreement helps shape regional and global approaches to AI while keeping technology under human control. He emphasized the importance of ensuring that AI remains under human direction, oversight, and control to mitigate risks and boost productivity. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the practical arrangements for essential supplies will make a real difference when the next disruption comes. Wong noted that these agreements reflect the trust built between the nations and a shared commitment to keeping trade open. Both leaders expressed their ambition to seize transformative opportunities to improve lives, support employment, and advance research and innovation.

The leaders believe that the Indo-Pacific region should have a voice in shaping AI development to reflect diverse needs and values. They intend to position Australia and Singapore as trusted AI hubs for the Indo-Pacific by accelerating adoption across business and government. The agreements affect the workforce through planned capability and skills development and the strengthening of links between businesses and the government. Research institutes are affected as the countries seek to turn innovation into commercial opportunities through strengthened collaboration and greater digital interoperability. The public is affected by efforts to build trust in AI through implementing safeguards and preparing for emerging AI-enabled threats.

The initial deal on fuel and gas was signed under the Singapore-Australia free trade agreement in response to a previous oil crisis. This earlier arrangement ensured that trade in fuel and gas would continue to flow during periods of disruption between the nations. The current cooperation on AI seeks to foster inclusive and sustainable economic growth for both countries and the wider surrounding region. The leaders recognized that AI can enhance service delivery and support innovation-led growth while safeguarding privacy and security through data governance. They also welcomed opportunities to share experiences in developing multilingual AI that reflect local languages, cultures, and specific regional priorities.

The countries will now explore greater interoperability in digital infrastructure and cross-border data flows to enable further innovation and secure data. They will cooperate on emerging cyber and AI security challenges to ensure that the deployment of the technology remains safe and responsible. Singapore's 2027 ASEAN Chair Year is seen as an opportunity to advance practical cooperation on AI governance and testing standards. This effort supports the ASEAN Working Group on AI Governance in building a trusted, secure, resilient, and interoperable regional AI ecosystem. stories.Headline: Meta launches Muse in the UK as the ICO and CMA monitor its data access
stories.Summary:
Meta launched the Muse agentic AI assistant in the United Kingdom on 24 November 2026. This digital tool aims to organize the lives of users by performing various tasks. British data watchdogs are now keeping a close eye on where the system sends data. The release is being overseen by the CMA and the ICO. These two organizations worked with Meta to ensure the product follows UK data privacy laws.

The assistant requires access to emails, calendars, apps, and digital wallets to function. It can declutter an inbox or make purchases for users at retailers like Debenhams and Argos. Free users have usage limits, while premium Power and Maximum users get expanded problem solving capabilities. The ICO is concerned about this sweeping access to data and the ability to make purchases. The watchdog warns that privacy must be built into consumer facing agentic products.

The Information Commissioner's Office issued a warning to people who might use Muse or other agentic agents. They told consumers to ensure their privacy settings are set up correctly. The agency also advised users not to share too much of their personal information. The ICO is specifically worried about the amount of data the assistant can access. They are monitoring the product to protect the privacy of British citizens.

Child safety experts have provided widespread criticism regarding the levels of data the AI can access. Security researchers have also exposed numerous flaws within the system. Some reports indicate that the assistant has read private messages without receiving permission. Users are affected by significant data privacy risks when handing over so much personal information. The tool is claimed to be the most data hungry AI assistant currently available.

The assistant moves beyond answering questions to carry out a range of tasks on behalf of users. It can hoover up almost every type of data available for it to access. Retailers have integrated the shopping capabilities of Muse into their own checkouts. The product promises to be the ultimate digital assistant for those who want their lives organized. These features create the crux of the concerns held by the ICO.

The ICO and CMA will continue to oversee the assistant to ensure it remains compliant. Watchdogs will keep monitoring the flow of data from the consumer facing agentic product. The articles do not state if Meta will change the data access levels for users. It is unclear if the security flaws found by researchers have been fully fixed. The future of the retail integrations remains open as scrutiny continues.

stories.Headline: Onclusive finds AI citations vary by category as Webflow reports median brands appear in 16% of AI answers
stories.Summary:
On November 25, 2026, The Drum published a member article by Aya Elbaoudi of Onclusive, a field marketing assistant, arguing that brands’ AI visibility problems are local, sectoral and specific. Onclusive analyzed 1,972 unique earned-source domains cited by five AI systems, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Grok. The analysis covered 12 industries, 24 categories and six countries: France, Italy, Mexico, Spain, the UK and the US. On November 24, 2026, IT Brief Australia published a report by news editor Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin on Webflow research finding most companies have limited visibility in AI answer engines. Webflow’s study found the median company appeared in 16% of responses across a sample of 2,000 websites.

Onclusive said the closer you get to the question your audience actually asks, the less the global list matters. Its analysis split the 12 industries into 24 product and service categories, and it said sources AI systems cite can change from one category to the next within the same industry. It said the top of its Industry Citation Guide is led by Il Sole 24 Ore, El Economista (Mexico) and Les Echos, ahead of Forbes and CNBC. It said Reddit appears in retail’s top sources nearly three times as often as in automotive’s, with about 29 mentions against 11. It said Toyota holds a 24.7% share of voice in hybrid SUVs and appears in 92.5% of AI answers there, while in electric cars its visibility drops to 1% and Tesla is chosen in 95% of answers.

Onclusive said B2B sectors such as banking, enterprise software, insurance and pharma lean on journalism, institutional sources and regulators. It said B2C sectors such as consumer tech, retail, fashion and travel draw more on reviews, creators and community discussion. It said regulated industries such as healthcare and telecoms are shaped heavily by government and policy sources. It said a source that dominates in the US might barely register in France, Italy or Spain. It said the same source can be essential context in one category and background noise in another.

Webflow said the median company was cited with a link only 6% of the time, and appeared 15% of the time whenever any company was mentioned. It said the systems got facts wrong roughly one-third of the time when a company was mentioned, producing an accuracy score of 63 out of 100, with message pull-through at 24 out of 100 and median sentiment at 57 out of 100. It said B2B SaaS and software companies were mentioned 20% of the time against 14% for B2B industrial and manufacturing groups, with citation rates of 13% and 6% respectively. It said companies in the Forbes AI 50 were mentioned 31% of the time against 16% across all 2,000 websites, and cited 8% of the time against 6%. It said Progressive had the strongest visibility in the Ad Age Top 50 US Ad Spenders group, with a mention rate of 44%.

Onclusive said its analysis identified 70 media sources linked to 220 articles where Toyota is either absent or described negatively, including Edmunds, KBB and Auto Express. It said its AI Visibility Playbook sets out six steps, from mapping cited sources to measuring change in AI answers over time, and includes a 90-day plan for PR, comms, content and digital teams. Webflow said its assessment covered 2,000 websites and used 123 scoring gates, drawing on roughly 325,000 lines of code, more than 29,000 automated tests, more than 5,200 lines of prompts and 100 source modules across more than 500 large language model sessions. Webflow said it queried four answer engines with buyer-style questions and scored responses against a common rubric, measuring quality metrics across the 1,579 domains mentioned at least once. Webflow said Forbes AI 50 companies’ content had been updated within the previous six months at three times the rate seen across the wider sample, and those businesses were recognised as thought leaders 60% more often.

Webflow ranked Krea.ai highest overall among the Forbes AI 50, followed by Abridge, BaseTen and Cohere, and ranked AllState highest in the Ad Age group, followed by Capital One, Pfizer and Progressive. It said none of the Cannes Grand Prix winners reviewed reached the top tier of its scoring, with Columbia, Heineken, Suncorp Insurance and Adidas ranking highest in that group. It said Google, represented by deepmind.google, ranked as the most mature in the MANGOS group of Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI and SpaceX, with Nvidia following on a mention rate of 86%. Onclusive said the next phase of generative engine optimization is about finding the handful of sources that repeatedly shape the answers you want to influence in your industry, market and category. Webflow said that for many brands the issue is not only whether they appear in an answer, but whether the answer links back to them and describes them accurately.

stories.Headline: David-Russell urges Tubman University graduates to use AI for Liberia’s development
stories.Summary:
Dr. Elizabeth David-Russell challenged graduates to use innovation and emerging technologies to address development challenges during a keynote address on November 24, 2026. This event took place in Harper, Maryland County, during the commencement ceremony for the 2026 graduating class of William V.S. Tubman University. The former university president urged the students to move beyond their academic qualifications to improve their local communities and lives. She specifically encouraged the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence and other new technologies as tools for solving critical national problems. These challenges include the fight against diseases, the need for infrastructure development, and the ongoing struggle with national food insecurity.

The speaker requested that graduates use their professional skills to create practical solutions for Liberia rather than being passive consumers of technology. She called for agriculture graduates to help achieve rice self-sufficiency and for engineering graduates to address the country's various infrastructure challenges. Education graduates were urged to strengthen community learning, while business graduates were encouraged to provide support for local entrepreneurship efforts. Health sciences graduates should promote disease prevention, and Arts and Sciences graduates should advance research and preserve the cultural heritage of Liberia. These requirements for the graduates were delivered at the William V.S. Tubman University ceremony held in Harper, Maryland County.

Dr. David-Russell stated that the university's commitment to academic excellence must be reflected in professionalism, creativity, ethical leadership, and meaningful national service. She explained that true academic excellence requires the ability to apply knowledge and think critically rather than simply memorizing various pieces of information. The former president cautioned the graduates against compromising their integrity for the sake of personal gain, convenience, or gaining more popularity. She asked the graduates to consider if they would be proud of the person they see when looking into a mirror. She maintained that genuine success is measured by the positive impact individuals make on society instead of just professional achievements.

The graduates of William V.S. Tubman University are the primary people affected by these challenges to integrate technology into their careers. These students are expected to uphold the core values of their institution and become responsible professionals committed to the development of Liberia. The speaker urged them to make their professional decisions based on ethical principles and facts rather than personal interests or convenience. By applying their specific degrees, these new professionals are tasked with solving the diverse problems facing the people of Liberia. They are encouraged to use their education to produce practical results that will benefit their communities and the entire nation.

The articles note that Dr. David-Russell previously served as the president of William V.S. Tubman University during her professional tenure there. During her time as president, she worked to improve the technological infrastructure of the university through the implementation of internet connectivity. She also recalled her efforts to establish intranet systems and provide online academic services for the students and faculty of the institution. This background in technology informs her current challenge to the graduates to embrace Artificial Intelligence for the benefit of the country. Her previous leadership focused on enhancing the digital capabilities of the university to better prepare students for their future professional roles.

The graduates are now expected to enter their respective fields and apply the innovation and integrity that Dr. David-Russell described. They must now decide whether to become innovators or remain passive consumers of the emerging technologies available in the modern world. The articles do not state if the university has provided specific training in Artificial Intelligence to the 2026 graduating class. It remains open whether the graduates will successfully achieve rice self-sufficiency or solve the infrastructure challenges mentioned in the keynote address. The text does not mention any specific government policies that will support the graduates in implementing these technological solutions.

stories.Headline: Oyo governor's aide urges developers to use AI for governance and to include SMEs
stories.Summary:
Oladayo Ogunbowale, the Special Assistant on Communication to the Oyo State Governor, called on technology developers, innovators and digital entrepreneurs to use Artificial Intelligence to tackle governance challenges and promote economic inclusion. He made the call in a keynote address at the 2026 edition of DevFest Ibadan, held in Ibadan, the Oyo State capital. He spoke on the theme ‘Building the Future: How AI and Digital Innovation Can Transform Governance and Society.’ He urged developers to move beyond commercial products and build solutions that address challenges facing individuals, communities and public institutions. He said technology is a critical instrument for a more responsive, transparent and inclusive system of governance. He said the Oyo State government was already laying the foundation for digital transformation, citing internally generated revenue of N103 billion in 2025, which he said exceeded the combined revenue of the two preceding administrations.

He attributed that to strategic deployment of science, data and technology in government operations, particularly in plugging financial loopholes, reducing fraud and improving revenue in lands and housing. He said the state’s experience shows technology can improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen financial management. He said the ultimate objective of technological advancement should be more accessible government services, greater accountability in public resources and economic opportunities for a wider section of society. He identified small and medium-sized enterprises as the bedrock of Oyo State’s economy and said digital transformation would remain incomplete if SMEs were excluded. He said that if AI serves only big business and government while SMEs are left on the far side of the digital divide, then digital transformation is a half-finished product.

He said Nigeria must move from being a consumer to a creator of technology and must become creators of intelligence rooted in the country’s reality. He said that if the country relies only on foreign AI models, they will not understand its nuances, culture and people. He said the country needs an AI that understands the meaning of words such as ‘akwa,’ ‘ekaabo’ and ‘sannu’ and not just translates them. He said this year’s DevFest theme, ‘Building Safe, Secure, and Scalable Solutions with AI and Cloud,’ captured the technical pulse of the moment with precision. The Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Kakanfo Inn and Conference Centre, Adedamola Are, said he was delighted to co-host DevFEST 2026 and that the facility hosted the 2026 edition on 21 November 2026.

He said the emphasis was on AI and machine learning, agentic AI, Google Cloud, Flutter, Web3, distributed systems, product design, data privacy and tech community and mental health discussions. He said the primary goal of DevFest is to educate developers, builders and tech enthusiasts on Google’s latest technologies while fostering community-driven learning and local networking. The Lead Organiser of GDG Ibadan, Abidemi Tiamiyu, said the team volunteers with Google Developer Group Ibadan, which organises DevFEST Ibadan, to equip young people with skills. He said speakers came from Accra in Ghana, Lagos, Ado-Ekiti and other parts of the world, and that DevFEST has a presence in Accra, Nairobi, Lagos, Ibadan and Ogbomoso. Tiamiyu said DevFEST recorded 2,500 participants in 2025 and about 3,000 participants at the 2026 DevFEST, and that the crowd was far larger than in 2025.

He said the organisers were targeting over 3,000 attendees for the 2026 festival and that training programmes provided by DevFEST for over a decade have helped many youths gain skills to earn a living. The Co-Lead of GDG Ibadan, Joshua Olajide, said one major objective of DevFest was to transform participants from ordinary consumers of technology into independent product builders. He said advancements in AI were making it possible for individuals to develop websites, create graphics and build digital products without depending on external professionals for every task. The Co-Lead Organiser of GDG Ibadan and software engineer at Resilience17, Joshua Odejide, said the programme had equipped many participants with website development capabilities and other digital skills to become self-reliant. He said tasks such as designing graphic flyers could now be completed within seconds using AI tools.

The Developer Ecosystem Programme Manager at Google, Sodiq Akinjobi, said developers, engineers, programme managers and product managers are currently building for Nigeria’s markets. He said they are building their apps in Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo, not just in English, so that information, instruction and technology can reach everyone whether learned or not. He said user research was making it easier to apply these technologies in day-to-day activities. He commended the government for implementing initiatives from secondary schools aimed at utilising new technologies and taking advantage of AI opportunities. He said many participants in the conference hall were within the 22 to 25 age bracket and that he had spoken to a lady building prototypes in robotics for healthcare.

The event was organised by the Ibadan Google Developer Groups in collaboration with Kakanfo Inn and Conference Centre and took place at the facility in Ibadan at the weekend, attracting about 3,000 young people from across Nigeria and beyond. It was the seventh annual Google Developer Groups event. It featured panellists including the Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Zeeh Africa, David Adeleke, investor and community builder Michael Toyinbo, the Director of Expansion, Strategy and Operations at Chowdeck, the Founder of Prine, Gbolahan Alli, and the Developer Relations Lead at ALATPay, Haastrup Adegoke, among other dignitaries. Tiamiyu said many participants were already showing interest in how to use AI to drive products and services. He said taking that away from the event was 100 per cent valuable for anyone.

The articles do not state what specific AI solutions, if any, were commissioned or adopted at the event, nor do they give a date for any follow-up. They do not say whether the Oyo State government made any commitment or announcement in response to the call. They leave open how the target of over 3,000 attendees was set against the figure of about 3,000 participants reported at the 2026 event. They do not say what the 2025 revenue figure of N103 billion will be measured against in future years. They do not state any outcome from the panel discussions or any plan to repeat the SME focus at later DevFest editions.

stories.Headline: David Fincher details his AI filmmaking vision while promoting his new film
stories.Summary:
Director David Fincher detailed his vision for using artificial intelligence in filmmaking during a Wednesday episode of the Big Picture podcast. He spoke about these ideas while promoting his latest film, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, in November 2026. Fincher attended a special screening of the movie at the BFI IMAX Waterloo in London, England, on November 24. Controversy has swirled around the production because some early screenings led attendees to bemoan the use of AI technology. The filmmaker has been open lately about his interest in using these tools to expedite the overall filmmaking process.

Fincher imagines a world where humans still do great work like sculpting, painting, aging, and doing makeup on a handcrafted set. He suggests shooting a master shot 20 or 25 times while simultaneously performing surface capture to derive close-ups and over-shoulders. Actors would then sit in chairs and perform from the clavicles up after the crew moves to pre-light the next stage. This process would allow him to avoid missing focus or failing a dolly shot, reducing the required takes to 15. He believes the results will still be based on real human beings and the way they move and traverse sets.

Fincher stated that he is not a Luddite and does not fear the unknown regarding the use of artificial intelligence. He argued that the art form is only a hundred years old and that artists should continue iterating their processes. The director questioned why filmmakers should not use existing tools that allow them to change the color of a person's eyes. He told the Big Picture host, Sean Fennessey, that this manner of working totally appeals to him for future productions. Fincher believes AI can cut down on the repetitive aspects of production that often provoke violent and vitriolic responses.

YouTuber and director Patrick Tomasso claimed the film features some of the most blatant and egregious AI use from a major studio. Tomasso said he felt completely gutted and insisted that AI-generated footage is visible in the trailers posted online. Other moviegoers on social media called the amount of AI astounding to an absurd degree and vowed to stop watching Fincher. Some critics disagreed, suggesting that the visuals people thought were AI might actually just be bad CGI in the film. These viewers are affected by uncanny and inconsistent visuals that make the movie feel like slop rather than a polished production.

The film is a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood and is set in 1977, about a decade after the original. It stars Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth, a former stuntman turned fixer for Hollywood elites who also works as a bartender. The plot focuses on Booth's romance with agent Karen Crosby and his work for actor Charlie Peters to protect his wife. Other filmmakers like Christopher Nolan, Guillermo del Toro, Seth Rogen, and Kane Parsons have rejected or questioned the arrival of AI. Netflix recently invested in generative AI by acquiring Ben Affleck's startup, InterPositive, for around 600 million dollars earlier this year.

The movie is scheduled to premiere on November 25, and Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied the use of AI. InterPositive's models are designed to generate assets from production footage to tweak lighting or remove unwanted elements from the background. One trailer features baffling shots of people sitting backward in a carriage, which has increased suspicion among many viewers. The articles leave open whether the visuals are actually AI-generated or simply the result of poor CGI work by the studio. It remains unclear if the final release will address the criticism regarding the meticulous attention to detail expected from Fincher.
