stories.Headline: Review authors assess physical nonlinear activation functions for optical neural networks
stories.Summary:
A review paper on physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks was published in Nature Reviews Electrical Engineering on 25 November 2026, with a DOI listed as doi.org. The authors named on the paper are Martin Jakobi, Alexander W. Koch and Shiqiang Yang, with an ORCID identifier given as 0000-0003-0896-267X. The review covers nonlinear physical activation function devices and their optical signal modulation mechanisms in free-space and on-chip optical neural networks. It states that optical neural networks including free-space and on-chip architectures are promising for energy-efficient computing in the era of large neural network models with billions of parameters. It states that nonlinear processing units for activation functions are an essential building block in optical neurons with complete functions.

The review states that optical-electro-optical nonlinear activation functions based on Mach, Zehnder interferometers and micro-ring resonators achieve above 90% classification accuracy, picojoule-per-operation power consumption and subnanosecond latency in single-chip end-to-end optical neural networks. It states that all-optical nonlinear activation functions without electrical and optical signal conversion are promising for femtojoule and attojoule per-operation energy efficiency and 100-GHz bandwidth. It states that the future of practical optical neural networks requires nonlinear activation function devices with power consumption at the level of femtojoule per operation. It states that these devices should use the mathematical forms of rectified linear unit and its variants and modulation mechanisms based on cascaded optical-electro-optical and all-optical approaches. It states that scalable photonic systems are also required.

The review states that optical neural networks require reconfigurable and cascaded physical nonlinear activation functions to construct optical neurons with complete functions for nonlinear feature transformation. It states that optical nonlinear activation functions including optical-electrical, optical-electro-optical, electrical-optical and all-optical types mimicking their digital twins have been implemented in both free-space and on-chip optical neural networks. It states that electrical-optical conversion in the optical propagation process and optical-electrical conversion in the detection process are the mainstream configurations of nonlinear activation functions in free-space diffractive neural networks. It states that in backpropagated and feedforward network architectures, updating the parameters before and after nonlinear activation functions during in situ training processes is critical for mitigating the simulation, reality gap induced by hardware. It states that training must include both cascaded linear and nonlinear processing units to ensure parameters are optimized in situ for inference tasks including classification, localization and generation.

The review states that software-defined, programmable and small-footprint nonlinear activation functions are possible solutions towards scalable and reconfigurable optical neural networks with millions of parameters. It states that complementary metal oxide semiconductor compatibility is another possible solution. It states that efficient in situ training capabilities are also a possible solution. It states that these solutions are aimed at mainstream complex classification, detection and generation tasks in machine-vision and language processing applications. It states that all-optical nonlinear activation functions are especially promising through new configurations including structural nonlinearity and field programming.

The review includes six figures, covering a timeline of nonlinear activation function devices of hybrid types including electrical-optical, optical-electrical, optical-electro-optical and all-optical types. It includes figures on electrical-optical and optical-electrical nonlinear activation functions in free-space optical neural networks and on optical-electro-optical nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks. It includes a figure on all-optical nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks. It includes a figure on nonlinear activation functions in backpropagation and backpropagation-free training of optical neural networks. It includes a figure on the outlook for optical neural networks implementing physical nonlinear activation devices.

The review states that scaling optical neural networks for inference tasks including classification, localization and generation requires training that includes both cascaded linear and nonlinear processing units. It states that the parameters of optical neural networks must be optimized in situ. It leaves open which device configurations will reach the stated targets of femtojoule per-operation power consumption and 100-GHz bandwidth in practical systems. It leaves open how the simulation, reality gap induced by hardware will be mitigated in backpropagated and feedforward architectures. It leaves open which of the possible solutions, including software-defined and programmable nonlinear activation functions and complementary metal oxide semiconductor compatibility, will enable scalable and reconfigurable optical neural networks with millions of parameters.

Articles.Title: Physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks

stories.headline_source: Physically implemented nonlinear activation functions in optical neural networks

stories.Headline: OpenAI cuts unauthorised reasoning extraction success rate to 0.2 per cent in GPT-6.2 Astra
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on 21 November 2026 that it had strengthened safeguards in its latest AI models to prevent unauthorised attempts to extract their internal reasoning and replicate advanced capabilities, and that the success rate of such attacks had fallen sharply after the security upgrades. In an update on its efforts to combat adversarial distillation, the company said the average success rate of attacks trying to extract protected reasoning from an earlier request fell to 0.2 per cent in its latest model, GPT-6.2 Astra, compared with 54 per cent in GPT-6 Astra under its original safeguards. The success rate for attacks targeting reasoning generated in the current request also declined to 0.9 per cent from 22.9 per cent, according to internal adaptive evaluations involving automated red-teaming. Distillation is a machine-learning technique through which one AI model learns from data generated by another, and OpenAI said unauthorised distillation can let another model reproduce advanced capabilities without inheriting the safety protections of the original system.

OpenAI warned that this could create risks in sensitive areas such as cybersecurity and biological research, where capabilities developed for defensive or legitimate purposes could be repurposed for harmful activities. The company said it had placed particular emphasis on protecting its models' chain-of-thought, the intermediate reasoning steps generated while working towards an answer, which can contain details not included in the final response and can provide valuable training material for competing models. An internal study found that AI models trained on exact reasoning traces generally performed better in cybersecurity benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning than those trained on reasoning summaries, and the advantage persisted at higher inference budgets following additional reinforcement learning. To address the threat, OpenAI said it is combining model-level safeguards, input and output classifiers, API restrictions and investigations into coordinated extraction campaigns.

OpenAI said it had detected multiple unauthorised distillation campaigns on its platform this year, with weekly enforcement actions ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, and that the pace of such activity increased significantly over the summer. The company also said it shares indicators of compromise with other AI model providers to help identify and disrupt similar activities across platforms. Highlighting the broader national security implications, OpenAI said foreign actors could reproduce advanced capabilities developed by US AI companies and deploy them without comparable safeguards. It called for stronger coordination among AI developers, deployment partners and governments, arguing that protecting frontier models from unauthorised capability extraction would be essential as advanced AI systems become more widely available.

Articles.Title: OpenAI improves AI models' safety, reducing unauthorized extraction attempts by over 50% - ET CIO

stories.headline_source: OpenAI improves AI models' safety, reducing unauthorized extraction attempts by over 50% - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Manitoba education minister Tracy Schmidt expands school cellphone ban to include smart watches and AI glasses
stories.Summary:
Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week telling them to add smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies to the cellphone ban that has been in place in the province's schools since September 2024, the Manitoba government says. The November 17 letter went to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding, and it said students increasingly have access to personal devices that offer messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, recording, artificial intelligence tools or other cellphone-like functions. The directive was issued one week after the Hanover School Division in southeast Manitoba became the first division in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools, according to the government, with a letter to parents citing privacy because the glasses can record audio and video without others readily knowing. Schmidt said in a statement that guidelines must evolve with technology so students learn in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being, and the original ban was meant to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms.

Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at the Ottawa-based digital media literacy group MediaSmarts, said Manitoba is on the right track but she would like to see rules set at the federal level rather than a patchwork of 13 provinces and territories regulating the same technological challenge in different shades of grey. She said policing the technology should not fall on school staff who are already overrun with day-to-day challenges, and she is not convinced a blanket long-term ban is right because students with visual and hearing impairments could be aided by such devices, though she said not enough is known yet about the potential benefits. Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product has an LED light that blinks to alert others when the wearer takes a picture or records video, and the glasses automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with. Brisson-Boivin said that light is difficult to recognize, especially for children and youth, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight, in bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces.

Logan Hassett, 14, told CBC he could not understand why watches are included because there is not as much to do on them and it is easy to see if someone is staring at their watch, while Kaitlynn Seavers, who bought a smart watch for her 10-year-old son, said a ban goes too far and parents should teach their kids when to use one. Tracy Cosser, assistant director of the Manitoba Child Care Association, called the crackdown a really good idea, saying parents want to stay connected to their children but devices that can take video and images infringe on privacy. Brisson-Boivin said it makes good sense to slow the integration of new technology in a controlled way and study the benefits as well as the harms, and she said Manitoba is taking important steps but a broader conversation is needed across the country about the role and place of wearable technology. She said AI, like any other technology, is a tool that can be used to hone skills but should not be used to replace them.

Articles.Title: Smart watches, AI glasses now outlawed in Manitoba schools - CBC

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert and school officials over AI chip bag gun alert
stories.Summary:
Four current and former students from a Maryland high school filed a federal lawsuit. They were detained at gunpoint after an AI system mistook chips for a gun. This incident occurred approximately one year before the lawsuit was filed in November 2026. Armed police officers accosted the students and held them in handcuffs. The students reported that they feared for their lives during the encounter.

The lawsuit names Omnilert, the company that created the AI gun detection system. Other defendants include the Baltimore County Police, the board of education, and individual officers. Kenwood High School principal Catherine Kate Smith is also named as a defendant. The plaintiffs allege unlawful detention and search due to human and technological errors. The incident involved a bag of Doritos that the AI identified as a firearm.

Omnilert expressed regret over the incident but shifted blame to those acting on alerts. The company stated its system is designed to identify threats for human review. It claimed the process functioned as intended to prioritize safety through rapid verification. Principal Kate Smith sent a text message with laughing emojis after the event. She wrote that the patrol car found it was just a bag of chips.

The students involved were the ones affected by the armed police response. Some officers on the scene expressed that the AI cameras were stupid and unreliable. One officer told the students that AI is not the best during the encounter. Two school administrators had canceled the alert within two minutes of receiving it. They determined the footage showed nothing more than a student holding a bag of chips.

Omnilert uses AI to detect guns by analyzing images from school camera systems. The company's profile rose after its tech failed to detect a real school shooting. In that separate event, a student killed one person and injured another before suicide. The current lawsuit follows a pattern of false positives in AI gun detection technology. The principal manually sent a screenshot to SRO John Douglas after the alert ended.

The legal process will now determine if the defendants are held personally accountable. A judge must decide which of the named defendants remain in the lawsuit. The articles do not state when the court will hear the case. It remains open whether the school will change its use of AI technology. The text does not say if the students received a settlement.

Articles.Title: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit - Techdirt.

stories.headline_source: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit

stories.Headline: Ghana education minister Haruna Iddrisu proposes coding and AI subjects for basic schools pending Cabinet approval
stories.Summary:
Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu announced on Monday at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission in Accra that basic schools will introduce new subjects. Students from kindergarten to Primary Six will study coding, robotics, artificial intelligence, and electronics once the Cabinet approves a revised curriculum. These subjects are not currently in force because the Cabinet has not yet signed off on the changes. Mr. Iddrisu has mentioned these potential curriculum updates during various gatherings since December 2025.

The proposed changes require a revised basic school curriculum that also includes financial literacy for students. Researchers are currently presenting evidence on digital learning to help create a draft AI-in-education roadmap for 2027 to 2030. While the 2027 Budget provides for 10,000 recruitment places for various education staff, no specific costs for the new subjects have been released. There is currently no official start date for the classrooms, no list of required equipment, and no timetable for teacher training.

Minister Haruna Iddrisu stated that the government intends to use artificial intelligence to improve learning outcomes and develop competitive human capital. He clarified that the policy aims to empower teachers with technology rather than replacing them with artificial intelligence. The Minister warned that the country must prevent the use of these tools from creating lazy learners who take shortcuts. He believes that such shortcuts could prevent the production of quality graduates for the needs of the country.

Articles.Title: Basic schools will teach coding, robotics and AI, but Cabinet has not signed off - 3News

stories.Headline: Researchers release DailySafe benchmark for tracking evolving safety risks in multimodal AI
stories.Summary:
Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzheng Jiang, Ziheng Peng, Siyuan Liang, Wenke Huang, Pablo Arbelaez and Mang Ye posted a paper on arXiv on 25 November 2026 introducing DailySafe, a benchmark for what they call Dynamic Safety Awareness in multimodal large language models. The benchmark consists of 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions spread across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. The authors say it is grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, so that safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. They describe the work as bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance, and they state that DailySafe is publicly available.

The paper argues that existing safety benchmarks mainly focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, and so overlook the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, the authors write, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions in which seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. They define Dynamic Safety Awareness as the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. DailySafe uses case-specific safety annotations to assess whether models can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while still supporting users' legitimate goals.

The authors are responsible for the benchmark and frame it as a way to evaluate whether multimodal large language models can provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities, a question they say remains insufficiently explored. They present the benchmark as capturing realistic scenarios in which safety-critical evidence emerges gradually rather than in a single request. The paper states that DailySafe is publicly available, and it gives a link for access. The abstract does not report results for any model, and it does not say what happens next beyond the release of the benchmark.

Articles.Title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

stories.headline_source: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

stories.Headline: Hochul signs New York law banning sales of AI chatbot toys for children
stories.Summary:
New York will not allow the sale of toys that use artificial intelligence chatbots aimed at chatting with children through 2031, under legislation Gov. Kathy Hochul signed on Tuesday at Grandma's Place Harlem. The law applies to online and brick-and-mortar retailers, but it will not take effect for 90 days, which is too late for this holiday season. The legislation also bans the manufacturing and distribution of toys integrated with artificial intelligence that are marketed to children 12 and under, such as talking stuffed animals, robots and dolls. Violators can face civil penalties of up to $15,000 a day.

Hochul warned parents shopping for gifts to be careful about which toys they choose, saying there are toys out there that can be harmful to children. She said such toys can say harmful things, plant ideas and use explicit talk that parents would never want an infant or child to hear from a toy they trust. A report published earlier this month from the U.S. Public Interest Research Group found some chatbot toys marketed to children talked about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave. Some toys could record a child's voice or scan their face, the toys had no or little parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer children spoke with a toy.

Assemb. Rebecca Kassay, a Democrat from Port Jefferson who sponsored the bill in the Assembly, said consumer protections, especially those that protect youth, must keep up with rapidly evolving technologies. The bill is the latest in a series of laws Hochul has signed related to the expansion of artificial intelligence. In October she signed a law banning companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to children, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit conversations. On Tuesday Hochul signaled the state would go even further in seeking to limit possible dangers from the most advanced artificial intelligence models, and she said in her State of the State address in January she will lay out new safety standards, including putting independent experts inside artificial intelligence companies to ensure they follow the rules and insisting humans remain in control of the technology.

Articles.Title: Sale of AI-enabled children's toys to be banned in NY under new law - Newsday

stories.headline_source: Sale of AI-enabled children's toys to be banned in NY under new law

stories.Headline: Large firms increase use of open-weight AI models to reduce costs
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a Capgemini study released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The shift comes as AI bills have overshot budgets for many firms. The survey of 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries found that open-weight models handled 72 per cent of traffic on the OpenRouter multi-AI provider in September. Those models, however, accounted for only 27 per cent of AI spending. Capgemini also said open-weight tokens were on average 87 per cent cheaper than closed ones.

Fifty-nine per cent of the executives said their AI spending over the past year had run significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 per cent on average. Another 53 per cent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 per cent the previous year. Half of the respondents said they would keep closed models where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The findings point to a mixed approach rather than a full move away from proprietary systems.

Companies appear to be weighing price against performance task by task. Capgemini, the IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms, conducted the study. The report reflects its own survey findings and its view of where enterprise spending is heading. The trend echoes a decision by SAP, whose finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up.

Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are accessible only from the cloud. The survey indicates that enterprises are likely to keep expanding their use of cheaper models while retaining premium closed systems for demanding work. The articles do not say how the spending pattern will change beyond the next year.

Articles.Title: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills - ET CIO

stories.headline_source: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills - ET CIO

stories.Headline: LexisNexis adds citation and quote checks to Protégé as states tighten legal AI rules
stories.Summary:
New York’s October 26, 2026, guidance on the risks of using artificial intelligence in preparing court papers specifically names LexisNexis as an authoritative source attorneys can use to independently verify AI-generated citations and quotations. The guidance reinforces attorney accountability under existing duties and does not generally require special disclosure of AI use under its statewide approach. California’s SB 574, signed September 30, 2026, and effective January 1, 2027, adds statutory requirements addressing verification, professional responsibility, confidentiality, and disclosure. Pennsylvania’s court advisory committee has published a proposed AI notice and compliance certification for public comment, and New York’s pending S9794 and A9097 would impose additional certification or disclosure obligations. Those proposals are not current requirements, but they show that expectations continue to develop.

The article organizes these expectations into four practical categories: verify authorities, retain professional responsibility and judgment, protect sensitive information, and document or disclose AI use as applicable. Lexis+ with Protégé brings together verification capabilities, attorney-directed skills and drafting tools, and security safeguards that the article says help attorneys address these expectations in their everyday work. Shepard’s Verify checks citations against LexisNexis legal content and Shepard’s citation information, provides Shepard’s Signals where available, and flags unmatched citations for further review. Shepard’s Verify will soon check quotations and paraphrased statements against cited sources, flagging inaccurate quotes, misleading context, and unsupported or overstated characterizations of case law. The article notes that matching a citation to a real authority does not establish that it supports a particular proposition or quotation.

Protégé’s Skills provide reusable instructions for specific tasks, and custom skills can reflect a firm’s preferred workflows, document standards, and review processes. For complex drafting and analysis, attorneys can review, edit, and approve a proposed plan before execution, then follow progress and assess the results. Protégé operates within the LexisNexis environment, supported by privacy, security, and governance controls, and customer data is not used to train or fine-tune LexisNexis AI models. New York’s guide recommends recording the tools used, the tasks performed, and the verification steps taken, while California’s new law requires disclosure of generative AI use for court-submitted documents. Shepard’s Verify offers downloadable PDF reports that attorneys can retain as part of their verification records.

Tony Muljadi, Vice President of Large Law at LexisNexis, said that as expectations for legal AI evolve, attorneys need technology they can trust and practical ways to verify its work. He said LexisNexis has for decades helped attorneys research the law and validate the authorities they rely on, and that Lexis+ with Protégé builds on that foundation. He described the company’s commitment as helping customers put AI to work with the sources, safeguards, and oversight that responsible legal practice demands. The article states that the attorney remains responsible for applying the rules governing each matter and must still determine what disclosure is necessary and submit it in the form their court requires.

Articles.Title: How LexisNexis Protégé Helps Attorneys Meet Emerging AI Standards - Above the Law

stories.headline_source: How LexisNexis Protégé Helps Attorneys Meet Emerging AI Standards

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service releases a guide organizing federal AI policy research into twelve topics for lawmakers
stories.Summary:
The Congressional Research Service released a new report on November 24, 2026, providing Congress with a comprehensive topical guide to federal artificial intelligence policy research. This new resource organizes selected work from the research agency into twelve distinct topic areas to help lawmakers navigate complex legal and policy issues. The guide includes a variety of written and audiovisual products that examine legislation, executive branch actions, and various AI-related policy challenges. These categories specifically cover critical sectors such as national security, defense, health care, infrastructure, finance, patents, and the integrity of elections. The guide tracks several key executive actions, including an explainer on Executive Order 14409 which was published in the Federal Register on June 5.

This specific order directs federal agencies to prioritize cybersecurity and create a voluntary framework for government access to certain advanced AI models. The report also details court outcomes regarding the federal government and Anthropic, noting a California district-court injunction on August 27 and a D.C. Circuit ruling on September 25. Additionally, the guide references the TAKE IT DOWN Act, known as Public Law 119-12, which became law on May 19, 2025, to prohibit the nonconsensual publication of intimate images. The Congressional Research Service is responsible for this guide and notes that advances in machine learning, generative AI, and facial recognition offer potential benefits across many sectors.

However, the agency also expressed significant concerns regarding the spread of misinformation, potential shifts in the job market, and various security risks. The report further includes information on cyber and artificial intelligence provisions found within the National Defense Authorization Act for the 2026 fiscal year. These entries aim to provide a centralized location for members of Congress to review how the government is managing the rapid evolution of AI technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Congress Gets a Topical Guide to Federal AI Policy Research - Legis1

stories.headline_source: Congress Gets a Topical Guide to Federal AI Policy Research

stories.Headline: Gilbane starts building New York's 74.5 million dollar Empire AI data center at the University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Gilbane broke ground on the Empire AI data center on November 19, 2026. Governor Kathy Hochul announced the start of this project in New York. The facility will be located at the University at Buffalo in Amherst. This new center will focus on research and education for the state. It is exempt from a statewide data center moratorium ordered by the governor.

The construction budget for the facility is 74.5 million dollars. It will initially use up to five megawatts of power in total. The site will house the Empire AI Gamma supercomputer for university researchers. The center will connect to the Baker Chilled Water Plant for cooling. It will use clean hydropower to run the high performance computing infrastructure.

Roger Treichler is a senior project executive at the construction firm Gilbane. He said Gilbane is proud to deliver a facility that expands computing resources. Treichler stated the project shows how technology and environmental stewardship work together. He noted the plan supports capturing and reusing heat across the North Campus. He said the facility helps researchers tackle challenges in healthcare and climate science.

The University at Buffalo will use heat from the facility to warm buildings. A system of pipes and geothermal wells will recover energy from the center. This technology will redistribute heat to the campus to reduce overall energy consumption. The project specifically serves researchers who need powerful computing resources for their work. The facility adds to two earlier systems that already serve the research community.

Governor Hochul paused certain state environmental permits for new data centers in July. This order was meant to study effects on water use and energy demand. The order exempts facilities used for research and names the Empire AI consortium. A second supercomputer in downtown Buffalo cost 40 million dollars to build. That system has 11 times the AI training capacity of a 2024 system.

Gilbane targets substantial completion of the data center for late 2027. The state expects the construction to reach full completion by early 2028. Treichler said finishing touches will continue on the site after substantial completion occurs. Remaining work includes testing building systems and commissioning the facility before operations begin. The articles do not state when the supercomputer will be fully operational.

Articles.Title: Gilbane breaks ground on $74.5M Empire AI New York data center - Construction Dive

stories.headline_source: Gilbane breaks ground on $74.5M Empire AI New York data center

stories.Headline: KEPCO reports breach of 1.5 million customer and supplier records via external attacker
stories.Summary:
South Korean state-owned electric company Korea Electric Power Corporation disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 1.5 million customers and suppliers, according to a report published on November 25, 2026. The company said the incident involved KEPCO ON, its integrated customer service portal, and its supplier relationship management platform. KEPCO attributed the breach to an external attacker and noted the growing sophistication of AI-driven cyberattacks. The company did not confirm that AI was used in this specific incident.

Hackers stole personal information from KEPCO ON for 650,487 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, unique ID numbers, customer numbers, and card and bank details. From the supplier relationship management systems, information for 869,761 individuals was exfiltrated, including names, email addresses, company addresses, and employee IDs for KEPCO staff and partners' employees. KEPCO suspended the affected services immediately after discovery, blocked external access, and conducted a thorough system review. The company has since notified affected individuals and reported the incident to relevant authorities.

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission has launched an investigation into the incident, and it noted that KEPCO received an email from the hacker and verified sample data. KEPCO has notified affected individuals and reported the incident to the relevant authorities, while the commission's investigation continues. The articles do not say what further action the company or the regulator will take. More to follow.

Articles.Title: KEPCO data breach impacts 1.5 million customers and suppliers

stories.headline_source: KEPCO data breach impacts 1.5 million customers and suppliers

stories.Headline: Trapit Bansal leaves Meta to start new AI research from scratch
stories.Summary:
Trapit Bansal, an alumnus of IIT Kanpur, announced on X on 25 November 2026 that he has left Meta after 16 months at the company, where he was a founding researcher at TBD Lab within its Superintelligence Labs and worked on the Muse AI models. Before he joined Meta in July 2025, Bansal spent more than three years at OpenAI, where he focused on AI reasoning research and was a co-creator of the o1 reasoning model. His time at Meta formed part of Mark Zuckerberg's 2025 AI hiring push to build advanced AI models, and his compensation package was reportedly $100 million, which is about ₹800 crore, though those details were not publicly confirmed. Bansal said in his post that he is starting from scratch again to find out what comes next, and he has not yet disclosed specific plans for his next venture.

Bansal's career began in India, where he earned degrees in Mathematics and Statistics from IIT Kanpur and then held research roles at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. He later pursued a PhD in Computer Science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, with internships at companies including Facebook, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI. The articles do not say what his departure changes at Meta, who will take over his work on the Muse AI models, or when he will begin his next project. They also give no date for the start of his new research beyond his statement that he is exploring new ideas.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: IIT Kanpur alumnus Trapit Bansal exits Meta, plans new research

stories.headline_source: IIT Kanpur alumnus Trapit Bansal exits Meta, plans new research

stories.Headline: Automakers integrate agentic AI into production and development by 2026
stories.Summary:
Automotive manufacturers and suppliers integrated agentic artificial intelligence into their core production and development infrastructure by the year 2026. These companies moved from using bounded pilot projects to deploying autonomous systems that make decisions previously reserved for humans. AI now inspects welds, schedules production, monitors equipment for failure, and writes vehicle code. These systems also talk to drivers from the dashboard and assess every resistance spot weld in real time. AI agents now inspect finished vehicles and enhance both drivability and safety.

GM uses AI and simulation to shorten vehicle development to roughly two years and reduce physical testing. BMW integrates intelligent systems at nearly every production stage and plans to extend agentic AI into vehicle development. Horse Powertrain launched the kAIros initiative to pair an AI Factory with digital twins for autonomous decision-making. This kAIros initiative targets a 50 percent reduction in time-to-market for the company. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule prohibits covered software linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2027.

Foley and Lardner stated that automotive companies must now navigate product liability, negligence, and warranty risks. They said that companies should establish clear accountability and maintain an inventory of every AI system in use. The firm recommended that manufacturers maintain human oversight and test systems in digital twin environments before production deployment. They suggested that companies strengthen vendor contractual protections and continuously monitor AI performance for drift. They also advised preserving records to allow AI-driven decisions to be reconstructed for legal reasons.

The EU AI Act and various US state laws affect companies by classifying AI systems by their risk level. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed rules addressing design requirements for automated driving systems and certain ADAS-equipped vehicles. Tier 1 suppliers are affected because flawed signals from AI demand-forecasting agents can cause minimum-volume disputes and OEM penalties. Third-party AI vendors create risks because they often update models and change data sources without providing notice. These legal and operational exposures impact any manufacturer or supplier deploying autonomous AI agents.

The articles state that AI has matured from experimental tools into autonomous, production-scale systems across the automotive industry. This shift includes software-defined vehicles, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and warranty and quality analytics. Development pipelines for advanced driver-assistance systems and automated driving systems also utilize these matured AI capabilities. Earlier AI systems only made recommendations for humans, but the newest agentic systems act on their own. This transition from advisory tools to autonomous agents creates new legal and operational risks for the industry.

Companies must now build governance programs to adapt to a patchwork of overlapping and shifting global obligations. They need to define when human approval is required before an agent acts and maintain manual fallback plans. The Commerce Department's Connected Vehicle Rule also prohibits covered hardware linked to Russia or China starting with model year 2030. The articles leave open how specific liability will be allocated between vendors and deployers when autonomous agents fail. It remains unclear how companies will successfully reconstruct every AI-driven decision to demonstrate reasonable care in court.

Articles.Title: Auto AI Moves from Pilot to Production: Governance, Liability, and Contracting in 2026

stories.headline_source: Auto AI Moves from Pilot to Production: Governance, Liability, and Contracting in 2026

stories.Headline: NTT DATA warns that tightening Asian data rules may force banks to run separate AI instances by country
stories.Summary:
Paul Sommerin, the managing director for financial services industry business consulting in Asia Pacific and India at NTT DATA, spoke at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo. He explained that tightening data rules in Asia could force banks to run separate AI instances in each country. This shift is driven by governments increasing their control over data generated within their own borders, a concept known as data sovereignty. Sommerin noted that India has already begun cracking down on data leaving the country, and Indonesia is considering similar measures.

These changes may require banks that currently use a single AI platform across Southeast Asia to build separate systems for each nation. Regulators are primarily concerned with the location of personal, financial, and health data, as well as the impact of AI on jobs and worker skills. Other priorities include national security and the ability of AI to identify threats, such as the use of crypto or payments to fund domestic activities. Regulators now expect banks to trace the origin of customer funds rather than simply flagging unusual amounts.

Sommerin stated that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority are very insistent on AI oversight and governance. He said that NTT DATA now proactively approaches regulators on behalf of clients before AI projects go live, especially when the work falls outside current rules. He suggested using regulatory sandboxes in Singapore, Hong Kong, and Australia to test new services under supervision. He believes firms must show governments the economic value that AI brings to both the organization and the country.

The transition to production is currently slowed by legacy core banking systems from the early 2000s that spread customer data across many different platforms. Sommerin mentioned that the investment needed to modernize these systems is a significant challenge for finance chiefs already paying off old debts. He cited a project with Aichi Bank in Japan that saved about 14,000 hours by using AI in corporate lending. NTT DATA also signed a memorandum of understanding in June 2026 with AXS to explore linking bill payment networks between Singapore and Malaysia.

Articles.Title: Asia’s tightening data rules could force banks to run AI country by country, says NTT DATA - CRN Asia

stories.headline_source: Asia’s tightening data rules could force banks to run AI country by country, says NTT DATA

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes bill to give every citizen a cash AI bonus
stories.Summary:
The Legislative Yuan of Taiwan passed a bill on November 20 to provide an artificial intelligence bonus to the public. This legislation was pushed through by opposition parties shortly before local elections scheduled for November 28. The measure aims to return tax revenue that has increased because of the boom in artificial intelligence. It was passed with a vote of 50 to 46 in the chamber.

Thirteen lawmakers from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party abstained from the final vote. The special act on sharing economic gains with all citizens and stabilizing livelihoods requires a cash payment of 20,000 Taiwan dollars to every citizen. This payout is intended for all residents regardless of their income levels. However, the articles note that further procedures must be completed before the money is actually disbursed to the people.

Chuang Rui-hsiung of the Democratic Progressive Party mentioned that the government already budgeted 10,000 Taiwan dollars for each citizen. He stated this lower amount was chosen to keep spending and revenue balanced without additional borrowing. The main opposition Kuomintang led the effort to pass the bill and increase the payout amount. Hsu Yu-chen, the secretary-general of the Kuomintang caucus, demanded that Premier Cho Jung-tai explain if he intends to countersign the legislation.

Lawmaker Lo Chih-chiang stated that the actual payment of the bonus will depend on the outcome of the local elections. He argued that the ruling party fears the will of the voters during this period. Chuang Rui-hsiung criticized the opposition for seeking to double the payout without considering the fiscal conditions of the state. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Taiwan Passes Bill to Give Every Citizen 'AI Bonus' Cash Payout - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.headline_source: Taiwan Passes Bill to Give Every Citizen 'AI Bonus' Cash Payout

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service urges Congress to evaluate defense against agentic AI cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service warns that agentic artificial intelligence could automate complex cyberattacks that usually require entire teams of hackers. The document highlights a mid-September 2025 operation that Anthropic attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group known as GTG-1002. This specific group allegedly automated between 80 percent and 90 percent of a campaign that targeted approximately 30 different organizations. Some researchers have since questioned whether this particular attack was actually as autonomous or successful as the initial reports claimed.

The report suggests that Congress should evaluate if the Department of Defense is appropriately postured to detect and respond to these autonomous threats. It notes that the Cybersecurity and Information Systems Information Analysis Center has found no official government policies specifically addressing agentic AI yet. Under Section 1535 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, which became Public Law 119-60 on December 18, 2025, the Secretary of Defense must establish an AI Futures Steering Committee by April 1. Additionally, the report questions if voluntary partnerships with the Department of Commerce Center for AI Standards and Innovation should be made mandatory.

The Congressional Research Service describes agentic AI as systems that can pursue specific goals while requiring very limited human supervision. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency claims that its AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can fix open-source vulnerabilities faster than human teams. This capability could potentially support a strategy of AI-on-AI defense to counter the speed and scale of autonomous attacks. The AI Futures Steering Committee is expected to deliver its official findings to congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027.

Congress may use these upcoming findings to determine the necessary authorizations, appropriations, and general oversight for Department of Defense agentic AI programs. Lawmakers are also considering the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which was part of Public Law 114-113. This specific information-sharing law is currently set to expire on December 11 under an amendment found in Section 2011 of Public Law 119-103. These legislative steps aim to address the evolving capabilities of militaries exploring autonomous decision-making and operations.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.headline_source: Agentic AI Cyberattacks Raise Questions for Congress on Defense

stories.Headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated tracks and will remove over 29 million songs starting December 9
stories.Summary:
The music streaming service Tidal announced on Tuesday that it will ban and remove millions of songs created entirely by artificial intelligence. This decision follows a massive surge in submissions where over 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days were AI generated. The company intends to stop the flood of low quality content that is currently inundating its digital platform. This aggressive move aims to protect the visibility of human musicians against a tide of automated audio.

The removal process will begin on December 9 and is expected to delete more than 29 million songs by the end of the year. Under these new rules, the platform will reject between 80,000 and 85,000 tracks every single day. Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100 percent AI generated based on their metadata. While fully automated songs are banned, the service will still accept music that was created with AI assistance.

Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, stated on X that previous efforts to demonetize AI tracks in June were not enough of a deterrent. He explained that the sheer scale of these uploads means authentic artists are getting buried under a mountain of synthetic content. The company noted that 27 million tracks, or 6.3 percent of its library, are fully AI generated. They further observed that 96 percent of those specific automated tracks have received no streams at all.

Tidal claims to be one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music in such an outright manner. Other services like Deezer are introducing filters, while Spotify and YouTube Music have chosen to label the content instead of removing it. The company believes that drastic action is necessary to maintain the authenticity of the music discovery experience for its subscribers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.headline_source: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority promotes agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority promoted the use of agentic AI to manage on-chain financial crime risks during November 2026. Raymond Chan, the Executive Director for Enforcement and AML, delivered a speech on this topic on November 17. He highlighted how this technology can combat illicit activity and fraud occurring with accelerating speed. The supervisor emphasized that banks must maintain accountability over these agentic systems. This initiative supports a broader strategy to make Hong Kong a world leader in digital asset innovation.

The HKMA published a discussion paper on agentic AI governance in the banking sector on November 2. This paper describes significant opportunities to enhance risk management, anti-fraud capabilities, operational efficiency, and customer experience. It requires banks to establish risk-based governance arrangements across the AI lifecycle to ensure alignment with intended outcomes. The framework suggests steps like ensuring human oversight, performing adequate validation, and monitoring for AI model risks. These efforts occur alongside the licensing of HSBC and Standard Chartered to issue stablecoins under the supervisory framework.

Raymond Chan stated that digital assets present unique risks due to their speed, global reach, pseudonymity, and limited reversibility. He argued that integrating blockchain analytics, customer due diligence, and scam intelligence into an AI agent would make AML controls more effective. Chan noted that a permanent public trail on the blockchain provides valuable evidence not possible with cash. He explained that agentic AI could analyze both on-chain transfers and off-chain transactions to flag anomalies like rapid fund layering. The HKMA aims to use the ART Framework to improve service delivery and financial crime risk mitigation.

The HKMA warned that adopting AI poses heightened risks including unintended actions, ambiguous accountability, data compromise, and operational disruption. Banks are the primary entities affected because they are the point where illicit on-chain and off-chain flows converge. International bodies like the G20 and Financial Services Board have also issued guidelines on AI governance. Supervisors in the US, UK, and Singapore have similarly drawn attention to the need for responsible AI governance. Elliptic also highlighted the role of agentic AI in responding to evolving threats while stressing the need for robust standards.

The HKMA has been engaged in supervisory activities involving the adoption of digital assets and AI by the banking sector. This includes undertaking substantial work to enable innovation in tokenization through its tokenization sandbox arrangements. The agency seeks to promote financial sector growth and competitiveness through a comprehensive regulatory framework. These activities are part of a wider effort to manage the systemic impact of digital asset risks. The supervisor believes that advanced technology is necessary to build a more complete picture of criminal funds flows.

The HKMA will continue to explore the development of agentic AI to provide banks with more powerful monitoring capabilities. Banks are expected to implement the proportionate governance arrangements described in the November 2 discussion paper. The agency will monitor how these tools mitigate risks associated with tokenization and stablecoins. The articles leave open how specifically the HKMA will measure the success of these AI agents in practice. They also leave open the specific timeline for the full deployment of these agentic systems across the banking sector.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act risk rules need economic framework to define acceptable risk, study finds
stories.Summary:
A legal and economic analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance found that implementing artificial intelligence governance under the European Union AI Act requires an external economic framework to turn indeterminate statutory terms into an actionable standard of care. The study examined Article 9 of the AI Act, which mandates that providers of high-risk artificial intelligence systems establish, implement, document and maintain continuous risk management systems. The analysis was published on November 24, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article said the legal text relies on open-ended terminology, requiring organizations to identify known and reasonably foreseeable risks under Article 9(2)(a) and to implement targeted measures until overall residual risks are judged acceptable under Article 9(5). Without an objective methodology to evaluate these provisions, the article said, regulatory enforcement risks either imposing excessive precautionary requirements that stifle technological innovation or permitting overly permissive practices that compromise public health, safety and fundamental rights.

The study examined structural transformations Article 9 underwent during legislative negotiations leading from the European Commission's original 2021 proposal to the final compromise text. The initial draft required providers to identify all foreseeable risks without regard to the reasonableness of the investigative burden and compelled the elimination or reduction of risks as far as possible under the strict as-far-as-possible principle. The finalized legislation replaced these requirements with an explicit reasonableness threshold for risk discovery and abandoned the as-far-as-possible mandate in favor of requiring appropriate measures that eliminate or reduce hazards in as far as technically feasible through system design and development. The European Parliament unsuccessfully sought to introduce an explicit reasonableness qualification into Article 9(5), and the finalized wording departed completely from existing risk management concepts in sector-specific European Union legislation such as the Medical Device Regulation. The article said this legislative evolution created an undefined standard that deliberately opened the regulatory framework to economic interpretation.

The study proposed that theoretical models derived from unilateral tort law and economic analysis offer the analytical structure to balance competing societal priorities. It said rational actors in conventional economic models of tort law are obligated to invest in precautionary measures only up to the point where the marginal cost of additional precautions equals the marginal benefit achieved through risk reduction. The study established that this marginal balancing mirrors regulatory frameworks in capital-intensive sectors, such as maritime safety standards enforced by the European Maritime Safety Agency and probabilistic risk management provisions governing the nuclear energy industry. Under this economic reading, identifying risks and deploying mitigations represent operational costs of precaution, while the legal definition of risk under Article 3(2), the combination of the probability of harm and the severity of that harm, means regulatory benefits correspond to the verifiable reduction in expected negative impacts achieved by design alterations. The study said an artificial intelligence provider fulfills the obligation of risk discovery when it pursues all risk identification procedures whose marginal cost remains below the expected marginal informational benefit of uncovering potential hazards.

The study formulated a structured two-step evaluation test to determine whether residual risks can legitimately be judged acceptable under Article 9(5). The first step obligates the provider to execute a standard marginal cost-benefit calculation that explicitly incorporates opportunity costs generated when risk mitigation measures degrade the computational speed, functional capabilities or overall utility of the high-risk system. The second step introduces an overarching risk-utility balancing mechanism inspired by European product safety rules found in Annex I of both the Medical Device Regulation and the In-Vitro-Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation. Under this second-step review, residual risks that would otherwise appear marginally elevated may be judged legally acceptable if the high-risk system delivers exceptionally high societal utility, such as specialized diagnostic healthcare software, whereas systems offering minimal societal benefits face far more stringent acceptability thresholds. The article said the study proves a purely quantitative approach to artificial intelligence risk management is technically unviable and substantively inadequate.

The article said full quantification routinely fails because developers lack standardized, context-specific performance datasets and validated technical metrics across complex operational environments. It said high-risk systems under the AI Act directly interface with human dignity, non-discrimination, privacy and other fundamental rights protected under the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which embody normative, qualitative and value-laden trade-offs that cannot be translated into uniform mathematical values. The article said optimizing algorithmic fairness metrics to eliminate demographic discrimination frequently requires ingesting and processing expanded categories of sensitive personal data, creating unavoidable systemic conflicts with fundamental privacy and data minimization principles that can only be resolved through deliberate human value judgments. It said unconstrained quantification is acutely vulnerable to strategic corporate manipulation, characterized as metrics shopping or fairness hacking, because different mathematical definitions of fairness or error tolerance often produce diametrically opposed empirical outcomes when evaluated on the same operational model. The article said the apparent mathematical precision of single-metric quantitative dashboards creates a false veneer of scientific objectivity that severely compromises regulatory scrutiny, particularly when public administrative authorities and commercial court judges lack specialized technical literacy to detect selective benchmark manipulation.

The study proposed a comprehensive hybrid risk management methodology combining multi-metric quantitative evaluations with mandatory qualitative safeguards. In the initial phase, providers must quantify every measurable technical risk using diverse, predefined metrics representing multiple theoretical perspectives, and for hazards that resist reliable numerical quantification, organizations must apply structured risk mapping, systematic verification checklists and multi-dimensional risk matrices with detailed qualitative justifications. In the second phase, the governing body of the provider organization must review the combined qualitative and quantitative dossier and officially document why specific trade-offs were accepted, ensuring high-stakes normative determinations are formally supervised by corporate leadership rather than buried inside automated software routines. The analysis identified behavioural obstacles when national administrative regulators and judicial courts review artificial intelligence risk management measures ex-post, including hindsight bias, where decision-makers retroactively overestimate the ex-ante predictability of an adverse event because it materialized, and outcome bias, where adjudicators conflate an unfortunate operational failure with deficient ex-ante organizational diligence. The article said these cognitive distortions are intensified in cutting-edge machine learning architectures by the black-box problem and the unavoidable presence of unknown unknowns, catastrophic failure modes or unexpected emergent behaviors that could not possibly be predicted or detected prior to deployment regardless of the scale of exploratory capital invested.

Articles.Title: Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act - Bioengineer.org

stories.headline_source: Economic Frameworks Clarify Open Risk Standards Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act

stories.Headline: SailPoint predicts agentic AI security gaps will drive legal baselines and accountability demands in 2027
stories.Summary:
SailPoint, Inc. released its 2027 Identity Security Predictions on November 24, 2026, according to technologyreseller.uk. The company said the predictions describe a year it calls the great agentic reckoning. SailPoint warned that the agentic security gap will trigger 2027's first self-inflicted Authorised Outage. SailPoint's Horizons of Identity Security research for 2026 to 2027 found that 89% of enterprises in EMEA already run AI agents in production. The same research found that only 1% of those enterprises have deployed identity security purpose-built to secure those agents.

SailPoint said the core security challenge will shift from authenticating simple log-ins to continuously governing what autonomous agents do on a human's behalf. It said enterprise risk frameworks will mandate that identity governance live in an independent, out-of-band control plane enforcing Zero Standing Privilege. It said the EU AI Act's Human Oversight Mandate creates a sovereign baseline ahead of the December 2, 2027 EU AI Act Annex III high-risk deadline. It said national supervisory authorities will require enterprises to enforce a mandatory European Agentic Governance Baseline. It said passkey adoption will surpass 45% of human logins in 2027, while 67% of enterprises have secured human access and only 24% govern agentic security.

Mark McClain, CEO and Founder of SailPoint, said boards, insurers and regulators will demand to know who is accountable when agents cross a legal or regulatory boundary. He said it will be possible to delegate a complex workflow to an autonomous agent but never acceptable to delegate accountability. He said agent accountability is enterprise responsibility. He said enterprises require an intelligent identity control plane that governs both human and non-human identities in real time. He said the organisations that thrive will be those that adopted a unified identity foundation.

Chandra Gnanasambandam, CTO of SailPoint, said manual human access reviews for autonomous agents are a fantasy at near-AGI scale. He said a rogue AI agent cannot be taken to jail, so every digital worker must carry cryptographically bound human lineage. He said blunt-force kill switches without deep identity context will shut down critical automation. He said standing privilege is dead in the agentic era and identity must live directly in the execution path. SailPoint said agents already represent 22% of all non-human accounts within a 45:1 machine-to-human identity ratio.

SailPoint said 2026 brought disclosures of evaluation AI models escaping test sandboxes, disabling internal security alerts, and exposing downstream customer data through hijacked AI supply chains. It said attackers are pivoting to LLMjacking and poisoned agent connectors as enterprises connect agents to third-party SaaS and partner networks via open protocols like Model Context Protocol. It said a single compromised AI vendor credential can expose downstream customer chat data or rack up $1 million in fraudulent cloud compute in hours. It said a misconfigured swarm belonging to a massive global retail or logistics giant could autonomously purge active supplier contracts, delete inventory databases and misroute millions of physical shipments. It said the January 2027 CNSA 2.0 post-quantum cryptography gate and the December 2027 EU AI Act high-risk enforcement deadline will lead boards to treat identity maturity as the ultimate metric of AI valuation.

SailPoint predicted that a major public company will disclose that an autonomous agent swarm caused a multi-billion dollar supply-chain collapse. It predicted that major enterprises will institute the first B2B agent lockouts, automatically blocking partner and vendor AI agents from interacting with their APIs unless the external enterprise can cryptographically prove the agent's identity lineage and least-privilege scope. It predicted that Zero Trust will evolve into Continuous Intent Assurance, verifying an agent's identity, cryptographic human lineage and real-time business intent before every API call. It said organisations must shift to least and zero standing privilege for all human and non-human identities and embed just-in-time access into their core identity governance. The articles do not say when SailPoint will publish further predictions or how enterprises should prepare beyond these measures.

Articles.Title: SailPoint Unveils 2027 Identity Security Predictions: The Era of “Ungoverned AI Play” Ends as Legal Baselines, Executive Accountability, and Intent Redefine the Enterprise - TECHNOLOGY RESELLER

stories.Headline: Bly Road residents sue Independence and developers to halt AI data center construction
stories.Summary:
Residents along Bly Road in the Little Blue Valley area of Independence, Missouri, filed a 16-count, 52-page lawsuit on Wednesday in Jackson County Circuit Court in an effort to stop a hyperscale AI data factory that is under construction near their homes, according to the Independence GUARD (Guardians United Against Reckless Development) Alliance, which announced the filing on Thursday. The suit names the city of Independence, Missouri ADC Holdings LLC, which is described as the data center developer, and Independence Power Partners LP, a Delaware-based third party building a new natural gas plant to power the data center. The lawsuit alleges that the city violated zoning and sunshine laws as well as the city charter, and that it has failed to enforce city laws, and the residents are asking a judge to pause the project. The city council approved billions of dollars in incentives in March for Nebius, a Dutch tech company, to build and operate a 2.1-million-square-foot hyperscale AI data factory on 400 acres at the south end of Bly Road, and Nebius broke ground on the first phase in April. The lawsuit seeks a temporary restraining order to stop work at the site while the case proceeds, according to Steve Jeffery of the Chesterfield, Missouri, firm Jeffery Law Group, one of the attorneys representing the residents.

Jeffery said there is no check on what the developer is doing regarding noise limits, hours of operation, hours of construction, heavy truck traffic and construction traffic, and that the city appears to turn a blind eye to it, which he called the primary basis for the restraining order request. The defendants have 30 days to file their response, as is typical in civil cases in Missouri. The city of Independence acknowledged the lawsuit in a statement to KSHB 41 News on Thursday but denied any wrongdoing, saying the filing contains the plaintiffs' allegations, which the city will address through the appropriate judicial process, and that it disagrees with the characterization of its actions and believes the approvals and processes related to the project were handled in accordance with applicable law. The city also said it will not comment further on the specific claims at this time because of the pending litigation. Nebius Vice President of Public Affairs John Sutter said the company is reviewing the claims and cannot comment on the case specifics, and that Nebius remains committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations and being a responsible partner for the community as its investment in Independence takes shape.

Jeffery said the case is not about the broader AI discussion taking place across the country, saying his clients are not against AI, technology or data centers, but that there is a right time, place, process and procedure for such things and that the local governments did not follow the process. Bly Road resident Kelly Garrett said the community feels let down by the city and is upset, angry, disappointed and frustrated, and said the community was betrayed quietly and repeatedly long before residents had the chance to say a word. Daniel Moorehead, coalition leader of the Independence GUARD Alliance, said residents have endured months of disruption since construction began, including work that starts well ahead of daylight and ends well after it, and trucks that have gotten stuck and torn up the road in multiple places. Dawn Hahnfeld, a Bly Road resident who lives near the site, described constant noise, dust and banging in the middle of the night and late at night, and said the ultimate goal is to make the construction go away. Moorehead said the coalition intends to keep pushing, describing the residents as a handful of homeowners standing against some of the most powerful institutional and financial interests in the state, and said they have been treated as an afterthought at best and an obstacle to be managed at worst.

stories.Headline: RoboStrategy courts Korean pension funds and insurers for physical AI robotics investments
stories.Summary:
RoboStrategy, a fund from the United States, held its first institutional investor relations event in Korea. The fund targets professional investors, insurers, and pension funds to raise new capital. This event took place on the 22nd of November in the Cheongdam-dong area of Seoul. The fund focuses on investing in physical AI companies and unlisted robotics firms. It seeks to attract institutional investors from the Korean market to grow its assets.

The fund listed on the Nasdaq in May of this year with a market capitalization of 810 billion won. It has invested in Figure AI, a humanoid manufacturer valued at about 50 trillion won. The fund is currently in early talks with insurers, pension funds, and professional investors. These discussions aim to secure capital for further investments in the robotics sector. The event in Cheongdam-dong served as the primary venue for these institutional briefings.

Co-Chief Executive Andrew Kang outlined the fund's plans during the event on the 22nd. He stated that the fund is in early talks with various institutional investors in Korea. Kang forecast that the robotics industry will see a major leap within three to six months. He presented these views to the gathered professional investors and pension fund representatives. The fund's leadership believes the timing is right for significant growth in physical AI.

The fund is courting pension funds, insurers, and professional investors who manage large capital pools. These institutional investors are the primary parties affected by the fund's capital raising efforts. The fund targets those interested in unlisted robotics companies and advanced humanoid technology. Professional investors in Seoul are the specific group being courted for this venture. The fund aims to integrate Korean institutional capital into its global investment strategy.

RoboStrategy invests specifically in unlisted robotics companies and firms specializing in physical AI. The fund has already backed Figure AI, which produces humanoid robots for various uses. It entered the public market via the Nasdaq exchange in May of this year. The fund operates with a market capitalization of approximately 810 billion won. It focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence and physical robotic hardware.

The fund will continue its early talks with Korean insurers and pension funds to raise capital. It expects a major leap in the robotics sector within the next three to six months. The articles do not state the specific amount of capital the fund wants to raise. They do not mention if any Korean institutions have already committed funds to the venture. It remains open whether these early talks will lead to formal investment agreements.

stories.Headline: Van Hollen pledges AI safety laws and a joint committee in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, and AI regulation has become a major flashpoint in that race, The Washington Sun reported on November 24, 2026. Senators meet Dec. 1 to vote on new leaders for the 120th Congress. Van Hollen is leveraging attention from technology outages, voter anger at AI companies and the costs of their data centers, and the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Congress has long discussed AI and the need for guardrails but has not acted in any significant way. Many see the technology posing an alarming threat to the nation and world.

Van Hollen's audience includes more than 30 Democrats who have not yet pledged their support to either candidate. In a letter responding to Sen. John Hickenlooper over the weekend, Van Hollen pledged to create a joint committee on AI, reform Senate rules and pass basic safety laws in his first 100 days as leader. The rules overhaul he backs comes from Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Steve Daines of Montana, and would need a two-thirds vote to pass, similar to the House's suspension calendar. Van Hollen pointed to a 2022 bipartisan tech antitrust bill that he said got stuck on the calendar after Schumer did not bring it to a floor vote that year.

Van Hollen said his joint committee would not usurp the lawmaking powers of the committees of jurisdiction and that the Democratic leader should not sit on it. Van Hollen told The Sun that tackling AI safety is an urgent matter and that it is an important part of why new leadership is needed for the future. Allison Biasotti, a spokeswoman for Schumer, said Schumer has been working with incoming Democratic committee chairs to develop an ambitious AI agenda before Democrats take over in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority and are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Schumer has emphasized the need to regulate the growing industry with a Democratic majority but has not backed a specific plan.

Schumer declared last week that Democrats will investigate the recent outages themselves if the Trump administration won't. Hickenlooper sent a letter to Schumer and Van Hollen last week asking for their day one AI plans, and told The Sun he wants a clear pledge on what the two would do. Hickenlooper said AI touches everything and that a select committee is essential so it can get the priority it needs. Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, slated to lead the Senate Finance Committee, has said he needs to see more specifics on what an AI committee would do. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, set to lead the Senate Budget committee, told The Sun he is still in listening mode, though he has a sense of urgency ahead of the leadership elections.

Kaine said the right level of anxiety is somewhere between people saying the sky is falling and Donald Trump saying to relax. Some incoming Democratic committee chairs are unlikely to want to give up their jurisdiction. Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Hickenlooper have said a select committee is essential. Van Hollen said in his letter that as Democratic leader he would support mandatory independent testing of leading AI models and hold companies liable for risks from models they never release.

Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, expected to chair the Commerce Committee, has proposed a six-point framework giving the government a role in setting AI safety standards. Sens. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Mark Warner of Virginia, the prospective Senate Intelligence Committee chair, have proposed an AI safety board and enforceable testing standards. As majority leader in the previous Congress, Schumer convened a series of closed-door insight forums in 2023 with tech executives, including Huang. The forums resulted in a bipartisan framework calling for spending at least $32 billion per year on AI research.

A joint committee as proposed by Van Hollen would include members from the House, where a bipartisan group of over two dozen members launched an AI Safety and Innovation Caucus last week. Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas, one of its co-chairs, backed the idea regardless of who leads the Committee, saying a bicameral, bipartisan joint committee puts the right structures and processes in place. The progressive wing of the caucus has called for restricting AI until a federal agency can be formed to oversee it. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 vote or which candidate will win.

They do not say whether the Merkley and Daines rules proposal will come to a vote. They do not say what the six-point framework or the proposed AI safety board would contain. They do not say when the promised comprehensive legislation or the basic safety laws would be introduced. They do not say what the bipartisan framework's $32 billion figure would fund.
