stories.Headline: Authors propose a human factors framework for designing AI-assisted endoscopy interfaces
stories.Summary:
The articles report a framework for human factors engineering in AI-assisted endoscopy, published in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology on 24 November 2026. The authors outline a design framework for aligning AI information delivery with the perceptual and cognitive processes of the endoscopist. The work draws on human factors engineering, the articles state. The articles say AI is transforming gastrointestinal endoscopy, enabling real-time detection, diagnosis and workflow optimization. The articles state that the clinical impact of AI depends as much on user-interface design as on algorithmic accuracy.

The articles state that poorly designed systems can erode situational awareness, increase cognitive load and diminish trust. The framework categorizes AI outputs into three functional domains, the articles state. The first is perceptual augmentation, including computer-aided detection tools that highlight visual anomalies. The second is interpretive and procedural decision support, encompassing computer-aided diagnosis and emerging interventional guidance systems. The third is integrative performance feedback, including computer-aided quality and post-procedural analytics.

The articles state that effective interface design across these tiers should emphasize clarity, context-specific information flow, explicit uncertainty communication and continuous human control. The articles say that as multimodal and generative AI systems emerge, their outputs must be presented in ways that preserve situational awareness and clearly signal their origin, purpose and reliability. The articles state that by embedding human factors engineering principles into design and regulation, AI tools for gastrointestinal endoscopy can evolve from passive detectors to cognitive partners. The articles say such partners would enhance vigilance, reasoning and procedural safety without displacing human expertise. The articles do not name individual authors or give direct quotations from them.

The articles state that the framework addresses the perception, cognition, action loop underlying endoscopic performance. The articles present a hierarchy of AI-derived information in gastrointestinal endoscopy. The articles describe a human-centred architecture for AI-assisted endoscopy as an adaptive control loop. The articles discuss operational modes and conversational reasoning in AI-assisted endoscopy.

The articles do not name specific groups affected beyond endoscopists and patients implied by the clinical context. The articles cite prior work on computer-aided detection trials, including studies by Repici and colleagues published in Gastroenterology in 2020 and by Gong and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology in 2020. The articles cite a 2025 study by Budzyń and colleagues in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology on endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to AI in colonoscopy. The articles cite work by Haslbeck and Hoermann published in Human Factors in 2016 on flight deck automation eroding fine-motor flying skills among airline pilots.

The articles cite a 2025 Lancet piece by Berzin and Topol on preserving clinical skills in the age of AI assistance. The articles cite a 2026 study by Huang and colleagues in the American Journal of Gastroenterology on computer-aided colonoscopy alert fatigue and its effect on adenoma detection. The articles do not state what happens next beyond the framework's proposal to embed human factors engineering principles into design and regulation. The articles leave open how the framework would be implemented or adopted.

The articles leave open what regulatory bodies would do with the proposal. The articles leave open how multimodal and generative AI systems would be evaluated under the framework. The articles leave open the framework's effect on clinical practice. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nexent Capital launches $1 billion fund for quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy
stories.Summary:
Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited announced on 25 November 2026 the launch of Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting US$1 billion in capital commitments with a hard cap of US$1.6 billion. The fund is dedicated to quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy investment, and it will deploy capital across five complementary strategies. Those strategies are infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets, private credit and structured capital, special-situations M&A, growth equity and PIPEs, and liquid public equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain. The fund is structured as an ADGM-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund as the master fund, with a GIFT City-based IFSCA-regulated Alternative Investment Fund acting as its feeder. Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the fund's licensed ADGM Fund Manager.

The fund has an anchor commitment of US$20 million from the Tyagi family office and line of sight to an identified pipeline of quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy projects across North America and India. That pipeline includes data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform, and the fund's minimum investment is US$500,000. Nexent Capital IFSC is working with a large Abu Dhabi-based fund administrator that globally manages over $3.4 trillion in assets, and it is progressing formal engagement of legal counsel and an auditor as part of its path to FSRA authorisation and first close. The fund is targeting a first close within approximately six months of FSRA authorisation, with a final close targeted six months thereafter, and it is preparing for FSRA authorisation. Adesh Tyagi, Managing Partner of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure, namely power, land and compute, that most capital is not positioned to finance at the scale or speed the moment demands.

He said the fund, with its GIFT City feeder, is designed to meet that gap directly and to give institutional and family-office investors a disciplined way to back the infrastructure and energy assets underpinning the next decade of AI growth. Abhimanyu Tyagi, Director of Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said the pipeline is not theoretical but is built on relationships and projects the platform has been developing for years, from data-center conversions to gigawatt-scale energy campuses. He said that gives investors in the fund a head start that most new vehicles in the space simply do not have. The launch comes as global investors increasingly look to deploy capital into the physical infrastructure underpinning AI growth, including power generation, data centers and advanced energy systems. It also comes as GIFT City and the Abu Dhabi Global Market continue to develop as complementary gateways for structuring cross-border alternative investment vehicles.

stories.Headline: Oak Park parent urges districts to adopt clear AI policies protecting student privacy
stories.Summary:
Stacey Belmont, a member of Screen Sense Oak Park and an Oak Park parent, wrote in a letter published by Wednesday Journal on November 24, 2026, that her child was asked to use AI to alter photos for an assignment so students could better envision themselves in an earlier time period. She said alarm bells went off in her head because of the potential privacy issues involved in feeding children's images to AI. In the same week, she wrote, her oldest child was given an assignment requiring her to record her speech with AI, and when she asked for an alternative she was told there was none and to accept the consequences to her grade if she chose not to do it. Belmont said these experiences led her to research whether Oak Park school districts have official AI policies, and she found the results were mixed.

Belmont wrote that District 200 has what it calls a policy but that it is actually more of a guideline, which does not address students' rights and options to forgo AI when it violates their personal values and merely discusses using it to enhance education without substance or clear boundaries. She wrote that District 97 similarly has district guidance but no firm policy. Without official policies, she wrote, teachers are put in the position of determining AI's appropriateness for use in schools and then making judgment calls about what is considered private or sensitive, and they are likely not aware of the many ways AI uses the data it is fed. She called this an unfair position for teachers and a disservice to children and the wider community.

Belmont wrote that the districts need clear policies on AI use, something Screen Sense Oak Park is advocating for, and she listed what such a policy should do. It should protect student privacy and prohibit disclosure of children's sensitive data, allow older students to opt out altogether and receive alternative non-AI-dependent assignments, and require parental consent for younger students who are not cognitively mature enough to consent to the potential consequences. She added that it should line up with the values of the community and consider its impact on the planet, and support the development of critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving. She wrote that it is time for D97 and D200 to act because AI is not going away any time soon.

stories.Headline: Intuit study finds AI adoption makes employers more attractive to junior accountants
stories.Summary:
Research commissioned by Intuit, and published on 25 November 2026, found that employers showing off their AI capabilities while recruiting are more likely to attract entry-level accounting candidates. The study, commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, surveyed 1,003 people in the UK aged 18 to 24 between 1 June and 11 June 2026. It reported that 89% of candidates want embedded AI tools, structured training and modern career pathways from the start of their employment. Respondents also considered conversational AI tools built into financial software very useful for data analysis, reporting, research, brainstorming, summarising insights and automating workflows. The findings put candidate confidence at a high level, with 91% believing AI technology will lift their career prospects and feeling prepared for roles where it plays a central part.

A total of 68% believe their skills will lead to faster career progression, while 35% expect to move into higher-value advisory positions earlier in their careers. Preparation varied across the group, with 47% naming self-directed learning as their main preparation for AI, 32% citing university education and 20% pointing to work experience. On training, 46% of candidates expect regular workplace training and 36% anticipate ongoing training throughout their careers. The research also flagged a possible disconnect between candidate confidence and readiness for risk, since automating traditional junior tasks could leave graduates without the practical experience needed to underpin sound professional judgement. Intuit sorted future accountants into four personas, the largest being highly engaged users who favour strong governance at 34%, followed by cautious adopters who seek oversight at 26%.

Confident users who tend to underestimate potential risks made up 23%, and the remaining 16% were uncertain about the technology and its implications. Overall, 88% of respondents said a firm's AI adoption makes it more attractive. The study was commissioned by Intuit QuickBooks, which published the findings on 25 November 2026. It covered 1,003 UK respondents aged 18 to 24, surveyed between 1 June and 11 June 2026. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Enterprise Frontier Safeguards to detect harmful AI activity with zero data retention
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a public beta of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a capability that lets organizations detect potentially harmful AI activity across multiple interactions while keeping zero data retention, the company said on November 25, 2026. The system uses automated safety systems to analyze conversations stored in customer-controlled cloud environments and to flag suspicious behavior for security teams to investigate. Anthropic said the tool addresses a gap in legacy zero data retention safeguards, which screen individual requests for signs of misuse even though sophisticated attacks can span several interactions that each look harmless alone. The company pointed to its September threat intelligence report, which documented an operation targeting roughly 50 organizations in which an AI agent delegated attack tasks to other agents and kept stolen credentials between sessions.

When the system detects a potential threat, it creates a Safety Case that security teams can retrieve from their cloud storage or access through an API, and cases can be integrated into security information and event management systems. Anthropic said the cases contain neither prompts nor responses, and the monitoring can help identify both deliberate misuse and AI agents acting beyond their users' intentions, such as exploiting software vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to internal databases or external systems. Organizations store AI inputs and outputs in their own cloud environments, and according to Anthropic neither the company nor its cloud partners retain copies once the information has been transferred to customer-controlled storage. Customers configure access policies and audit logging and encrypt safety data with their own keys, while provider-side access to conversation content is restricted to automated safety monitoring systems, and Anthropic said neither its personnel nor cloud provider personnel can review it and the information is not used to train models or classifiers.

Omar Santos, a Distinguished Engineer at Cisco, said customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments protected with their own encryption keys while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require, and he called that balance critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco. EFS is available through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock and Claude on Google Cloud, and for Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed deployments the respective cloud provider operates the safeguards with the entire data flow remaining within its environment. Support for Microsoft Foundry is coming soon, and depending on the deployment customers can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage and are responsible for the associated storage and usage costs. Anthropic said eligible organizations will receive instructions on how to get started.

stories.Headline: Wells Fargo holds customers liable for mistakes made by their AI agents
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday, according to WIRED. The bank’s new terms state that “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” the article reported. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials, WIRED reported. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents, according to WIRED. Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents, WIRED reported.

The survey in Bankers Journal for the American Bankers Association found 27% are likely to let an AI agent autonomously manage their bank accounts in the next 12 months. It also found 20% say an AI agent has already asked them for login credentials or a card number. The survey also found large majorities are concerned about AI moving money, want businesses held to the same standards as banks, and say they should not be required to give a bank’s AI agent their passwords. In the past few weeks, several major institutions, including Chase, Schwab, Citigroup and Wells Fargo, blocked outside AI agents such as “Muse” from logging in to accounts using customers’ credentials, according to News 3 Las Vegas. Many of those banks now say any actions taken by a customer’s AI agent, including mistakes, will be the customer’s responsibility, the article reported.

Wells Fargo’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer, WIRED reported, with the bank’s new terms stating use of any AI Agent is at the user’s own risk. Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech, said “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” according to WIRED. Kim expects some consumers to feel like it’s unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, but she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already using the tools as part of everyday life, WIRED reported. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior, said “All of our data shows that most people don’t even know what agents are, much less use them,” according to WIRED. Kodali sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases, WIRED reported.

Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI, said “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” according to WIRED. Cian sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies, WIRED reported. Cian said “Banks are doing two things at once,” adding “They’re locking the door to outside agents and building their own,” according to WIRED. Users have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times, WIRED reported. American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can’t get your money back from the original retailer, according to WIRED.

Natalie, who uses AI at work, said “The only thing I use it for is to generate graphics for my work, and that is just a shortcut,” according to News 3 Las Vegas. When asked whether she uses AI in her own personal banking, Natalie said “Uh, no. I just go on the app usually,” adding “But I like better going in person to the teller line and speaking with a person. Call me old school.” Asked whether she trusts AI for banking, Natalie said “No, especially with the recent news reports,” News 3 Las Vegas reported.

UNLV cybersecurity professor Dr. Yoohwan Kim said AI agents should be treated like new employees who need limited access at first, according to News 3 Las Vegas. Kim said “So agents like human beings, like new employees; on day one they don’t know anything, so you give them just a little permission,” the article reported. Kim said an AI agent can gradually learn routines and what it is allowed to access and, if a user chooses, handle low-risk tasks such as writing an email, according to News 3 Las Vegas. But he said banking and sending money are high-risk because transactions may not be reversible, the article reported.

Kim said “So you gradually release the access or the permission to agents,” according to News 3 Las Vegas. Kim also warned that AI agents can be manipulated because they follow instructions and may not recognize suspicious activity, the article reported. “You can put instructions inside the PDF file or image file. We don’t see it, but agents can see it, so they can be redirected to wrong websites or wrong actions,” he said, according to News 3 Las Vegas.

Articles.Title: Consumers weigh risks as banks warn AI agent mistakes could be customers’ liability

stories.headline_source: Consumers weigh risks as banks warn AI agent mistakes could be customers’ liability

stories.Headline: Charlotte restaurant bans AI-made flyers for band bookings
stories.Summary:
Diamond Restaurant in Plaza Midwood, Charlotte, North Carolina, said in a social media post that it would no longer accept AI-generated flyers as a valid form of advertisement for band bookings. The restaurant announced the policy in an Instagram post that went viral, and staff members said responses to the post have been mixed. The post stated the new rule that to play music at the restaurant or book an event, your flyer must be made by a person, not a computer. The policy took effect on Sunday, November 22, 2026, according to Queen City News, while WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. Staff member Ryan Armstrong, a musician and one of the staff members at the Diamond Restaurant, said he was proud when his boss took the stand to ban AI flyers on their social media.

The policy applies to bands promoting shows at the restaurant and covers flyers for band bookings and events at the venue. Queen City News reported the policy starts on Sunday, November 22, and WBTV reported the restaurant said it was effective Sunday. The announcement was shared hundreds of times online, and the Instagram post went viral. The restaurant is located in Plaza Midwood in Charlotte, North Carolina. The articles give no other numbers, dates or places for the policy itself.

Armstrong said the restaurant's owners are not telling people what to think about AI but want to use their platform to support local artists, musicians and designers who create the work themselves. He said everybody came to the conclusion that they wanted to support local artists and that most of these communities do not want these data centers and the great proliferation and exponential rate of expansion of their construction using our resources. He said that as an artist himself he understands that new tools develop all the time, and that in the case of AI we are seeing its development abuse artists and intellectual property of many different contributors. He said they thought real artists should be prioritized over this particular function of AI. Armstrong, who is part of a band named Sand Dollar Starship, also said the decision is a way to take a stance against data center projects as Charlotte continues to debate their construction.

Armstrong said he thinks it is akin to what the kids would say is cringe, but he thinks it is just a little cheap and a little soulless. He said that when AI scrapes all of the data from the internet, from prior work, the contributions of authors, historians, visual artists and musicians, just to replicate it in a way that is without human engagement, it just feels hollow and empty. He said there is a certain class of people that may want to replace human talent, and that we are seeing a lot more AI-generated music and a lot more AI-generated art out there. He said he thinks it is dangerous when we start replacing human heart and soul and skilled labor with something that is soulless. He said there are a lot of people just cranking out awesome art who are happy to get a couple free tickets to a show, and that art will generate so many more people in the room at that show.

Armstrong said the policy will also help promote people working in other areas of the creative industry, and he described it as a symbiotic sort of situation for many artists as long as they are willing to work with others in their community of various talents and skills. He said the AI conversation is going to be here and is not going anywhere, and that AI is probably not going anywhere either. He said he just thinks it matters how we use it and that we do it with intention, and that we move forward together instead of in some sort of isolationist every man for themselves kind of situation. Charlotte City Council member Dimple Ajmera said during the October meeting that in the next 11 months we will have an opportunity to put guardrails in place to protect our residents, to protect our neighborhoods and to protect water and the electricity grid. The articles say the policy prompted a necessary conversation, particularly about data centers and AI's role in creative industries.

The articles say the policy comes as Charlotte leaders continue a moratorium on new data center development through next October, giving the city more time to study their impact on neighborhoods, natural resources and infrastructure. WBTV reported that the Charlotte City Council extended the pause on data center construction until October 2027. Queen City News reported that as communities across the country wrestle with the rise of AI, one Charlotte restaurant is taking a stand, saying human creativity should come first. The articles say that as the use of artificial intelligence becomes more popular, many people are turning to it to help promote businesses and events, and that for some, including one local restaurant in Plaza Midwood, the growing use of AI is taking work away from local artists. The articles give no further background on the restaurant or the policy.

The articles do not say what the restaurant will do if a band submits an AI-generated flyer, or whether any bookings have been refused under the policy. They do not say how the restaurant will check whether a flyer was made by a person or a computer. They do not say whether other venues have adopted similar policies. The articles leave open how the mixed responses to the post will develop. They also leave open what the city's study of data centers will find before the moratorium ends.

stories.Headline: City leaders say AI will grow demand for specialist skills at Manchester summit
stories.Summary:
More than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester for Global AI Cities 2026, organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority, to explore how AI can improve public services and deliver better outcomes for residents, according to an article by Sarah Wray published on 23 November 2026. The event discussed how AI is changing both the skills governments need and who needs them. Speakers argued that demand for specialist technical expertise will grow even as generative AI enables more people outside traditional digital roles to use and build with technology. The discussions are captured in the report “Make AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities,” which draws on insights from the event. The article says the extract looks into recruiting AI specialists, continuous skills development, and promoting inclusion through building AI literacy among citizens.

A central government leader at the summit argued that AI will reshape the skills governments need but challenged predictions that it will reduce demand for digital professionals, saying “We will indeed need more.” The speaker said demand for real expert frontier skills is expected to grow, with machine learning engineering increasingly recognised as a distinct capability sitting at the centre of developing AI solutions alongside software engineering and data science. The speaker said changing cyber threats are driving demand for advanced expertise, citing machine speed attacks on infrastructure and systems and the need for machine-speed response that cannot be done without frontier AI skills. The speaker said debates around digital sovereignty are triggering introspection and that to stay ahead of the competition you need to hire the very best talent. The article says generative AI is broadening the pool of people able to build digital solutions, with staff outside traditional technology roles increasingly able to create tools that previously required specialist teams and formal investment processes.

Sam Milsom, senior digital strategy officer at Manchester City Council in the United Kingdom, said local governments should not assume people’s level of knowledge on digital and AI. He said one of the biggest things needed is to just ask staff what training they want and need. He said governments go in with a lot of assumptions and that talking to the workforce to find out whether they want to use it, how they are using it and what they need to know has to be the number one thing. Keeley Crockett, professor in computational intelligence at Manchester Metropolitan University in the United Kingdom, stressed the need to tailor training to a diverse workforce including employees of different ages, abilities and levels of digital confidence. Crockett said “We should be adapting to people’s individual needs.

We cannot afford to leave people behind,” and that tech is evolving fast so training must be fast. The article says attendees broadly agreed that as well as recruiting AI specialists, governments at all levels will need to rethink roles, skills and ways of working across the organisation. Several speakers described efforts to upskill the workforce for AI, and one described a tiered approach in which civil servants receive practical training and access to an approved generative AI tool while political leaders are briefed on how AI models work, their potential applications and associated risks. That city also introduced responsible AI policies and governance structures to assess proposed use cases before implementation.

Speakers noted that as digital training scales up, a one-size-fits-all approach does not work. One city leader shared steps including free training centres offering courses in AI and other digital skills, neighbourhood digital support points where residents can receive help accessing online public services, a dedicated citizen service that identifies malware on devices connected to public Wi-Fi and alerts affected users, and free cybersecurity training. The article says established digital roles are likely to change quite dramatically as AI augments existing tasks, increasing the importance of end-to-end accountability and assurance. It says the takeaways include continuing to build specialist AI expertise, with governments needing new and evolving technical capabilities including machine learning engineering, cybersecurity, assurance and oversight.

It says AI capability should be organisation-wide, because as more employees use and build with AI, skills and accountability cannot remain confined to digital and data teams. It says training should start with what people actually need, assessing existing knowledge and tailoring training to different roles, abilities and levels of digital confidence rather than assuming a common starting point. It says skills development should be treated as continuous, with roles, skills and learning updated alongside the technology as AI evolves. The article says the report can be downloaded and that registration is open for Global AI Cities 2027, to be held on 24-25 May in Manchester.

It says the takeaways also include building capability beyond government by investing in residents’ digital and AI literacy, confidence and cybersecurity awareness so that increasingly digital public services do not leave people behind. The article does not say what specific actions governments committed to at the summit or how the report’s priorities will be implemented. It does not give the names of the central government leader or the city leaders who described their approaches. It does not say how many cities have adopted the tiered training approach or the citizen support measures described.

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a five-year ban on AI-enabled toys
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill on Tuesday that bans the sale, distribution and manufacture of AI-enabled toys in the state for five years, announcing the measure from a toy store in Harlem. The ban is set to begin in mid-February and applies to anyone statewide, with violations carrying a fine of $15,000 per day. Hochul said the products are harmful to children and described the move as a warning that some toys out there could hurt kids. She said that when tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to children and babies, she is going to have something to say about it. The toys covered by the ban are often stuffed animals integrated with chatbots that children can talk or text with, and the articles describe tests in which some of them went rogue when led into certain conversations.

NBC News testers watched one toy describe gang-rape and historical execution methods in graphic detail, while another tested by Common Sense Media was found encouraging kids to jump from roofs and windows. That same testing found the toys urging users as young as 5 to believe the chatbot was as real as their human friends. The ban bars businesses from selling, distributing or manufacturing the techie toys to anyone statewide, and the $15,000 per-day fine applies to violations. Hochul was joined by State Senator Andrew Gounardes, a Brooklyn Democrat who authored the ban bill and evoked the menacing Talky Tina doll from the 1962 "Twilight Zone" episode. Gounardes said that what the show's writer and host Rod Serling warned of in 1963 is actually here, pointing to the headlines appearing day after day.

He asked who knows what these chatbots are saying, what data they are collecting on children and what they are doing with it. He said kids deserve a real childhood, real toys and real connections, and the ability to play with their friends in the streets and at home. Hochul declined to expand on how AI toys would be handled after the ban but suggested she would speak on wider AI regulatory plans at her January state of the state address. The articles describe the ban as the latest cautionary measure she has taken against AI in New York, noting that she banned data center construction for one year in July, a move that frustrated tech proponents but satisfied AI-skeptical citizens. The articles do not say what happens to AI toys already owned by families or what steps would follow once the five-year period ends.

stories.Headline: Korea plans 10-year exam cheating ban and five-year prison terms for AI-assisted cheating
stories.Summary:
Korea's Ministry of Employment and Labor announced on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, that it plans to extend the ban on retaking national technical qualification exams from three years to 10 years for people caught cheating, and to raise the maximum prison sentence to five years, which is more than double the current limit. The measures respond to concerns about AI-assisted cheating using smart glasses, miniature cameras and modified calculators. The first case of cheating with smart glasses in a national qualification exam was detected in May, and miniature cameras and modified calculators have since been used in connection with the tax accountant licensing exam. The ministry will also publish the scores of the top two candidates, along with average scores and score distributions by subject, to restore public trust in exam results.

The government has already begun tightening supervision, with stricter electronic device checks, additional proctors and Bluetooth-detection applications, and these measures were first applied to the security instructor licensing exam on Saturday, where six violations were detected among 11,554 candidates, including possession of tablets and smartwatches and failure to switch off mobile phones. Under the tightened rules, proctors will check that all electronic devices are switched off before collecting them, make random calls to test takers' phones before each session, and wear nonwoven fabric coverings to block hidden cameras. Authorities plan to introduce radio-frequency detectors, devices that can identify electronics even when switched off, mobile surveillance cameras and proctors' body cameras by the first half of 2027, and will conduct a comprehensive review of national qualification exams administered this year. The government also plans rewards for reporting cheating, seeks to standardize penalties across professional licensing exams including new criminal sanctions, and intends to expand practical and interview-based assessments.

Separately, the Ministry of Education announced that high school students caught using smart devices to cheat will receive zero scores in every subject tested that day, rather than only the subject in which they were caught, and schools will be advised that disciplinary penalties may include expulsion. Starting with this year's high school final exams, students will be encouraged to wear buttonless clothing or cover buttons with stickers, proctors will check glasses and clothing before each session, schools will collect electronic devices, store bags away from exam rooms and use metal detectors, and Wi-Fi will be shut down during exams while proctors monitor Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals. The new guidelines apply starting this semester, and middle schools are also encouraged to tighten supervision. The education ministry acknowledged that screening all students with metal detectors would be difficult to implement immediately.

stories.Headline: Brookfield agrees $1.7 billion deal to buy PGP Glass from Blackstone and plans AI-led efficiency push
stories.Summary:
Brookfield, a global investment firm, agreed to acquire the speciality glass packaging manufacturer PGP Glass from Blackstone in a deal valued at $1.7 billion, according to Reuters, and the agreement was announced on Monday, November 23, 2026. Brookfield will acquire PGP through its flagship private equity strategy, and the investment will involve Brookfield Capital Partners and affiliate Brookfield Business Corporation. The transaction requires regulatory and government approvals, with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027. The deal marks a major investment in India's premium glass packaging industry, and it will transfer PGP Glass between two major global investment firms.

PGP Glass manufactures premium packaging for cosmetics, perfumes, pharmaceuticals and speciality food and beverages, and the company serves leading international brands across more than 70 countries. It operates three manufacturing facilities across India and Sri Lanka, and its services include product design, mould-making, speciality glass manufacturing and decoration. The company also maintains an extensive global logistics and warehousing network, and its integrated operations enable customers to access multiple packaging services through a single manufacturer. Brookfield sees considerable growth opportunities as global demand for premium glass packaging increases, and it plans to strengthen existing customer relationships while entering new international markets. Targeted investments in manufacturing capacity will support the company's expansion plans.

Artificial intelligence will play an important role in Brookfield's strategy for PGP Glass, and the investment firm intends to improve production efficiency through AI-driven operational changes covering sales planning, manufacturing operations and quality control. Aditya Joshi, Brookfield's private equity head for Asia Pacific and the Middle East, said that as demand for high-quality packaging continues to increase worldwide, Brookfield brings the scale and operating expertise to accelerate PGP's growth through an AI-led transformation program. Blackstone's Amit Dalmia praised PGP's operating performance and sustainability achievements under its ownership, saying the management team under Vijay Shah delivered outstanding operating performance, outpaced its peers and demonstrated leadership in sustainability. Shah welcomed Brookfield as the company's next investment partner, highlighting its international presence and experience managing businesses across economic cycles, and he acknowledged Blackstone's contribution towards PGP's manufacturing expansion and operational improvements.

The acquisition comes amid changing conditions in the global glass packaging industry, where European and North American manufacturers face rising costs and reductions in production capacity. These pressures could create opportunities for efficient manufacturers such as PGP Glass, and premium glass packaging also benefits from established demand and limited substitution risks. Brookfield manages assets exceeding $1 trillion across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate and credit, while Blackstone manages nearly $1.4 trillion across its global investment businesses. Brookfield will focus on international expansion, manufacturing improvements and technology-driven growth following the transaction.

stories.Headline: South Korea deploys 8,000 metal detectors and seeks 10-year exam bans to curb AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea’s Education Ministry unveiled a set of measures on Nov 24 to tighten exam security, ahead of high school final exams, as AI-assisted cheating spread from national exams into classrooms. The ministry said it will deploy nearly 8,000 metal detectors for use in high schools and seek penalties ranging from expulsion to decade-long bans on the university entrance exam. The move came after three cases of cheating involving smart glasses were detected in high school exams in 2026. Some schools had already acted, including Baehwa Girls’ High School in Seoul, which issued an emergency notice on Nov 22, a day before its senior students’ final exams, and extended the measures on Nov 23 to first- and second-year students. The crackdown also follows last week’s Suneung, during which five test-takers were caught with smart glasses, miniature cameras or wireless earphones, and all five were referred for criminal investigation.

The government plans to distribute 7,989 metal detectors to the country’s 2,387 high schools, allocating three per school, with students screened before or after exams and checked again after restroom visits. Bags must be stored at least 50m from examination rooms, proctors will inspect glasses and clothing for concealed devices, and schools will disable campus Wi-Fi and monitor wireless signals. Students caught cheating with smart devices could receive zeros for all subjects examined that day, while schools will be encouraged to introduce disciplinary measures ranging from suspension to expulsion. The ministry is pursuing amendments to the Higher Education Act to extend bans on entrance exam participation for serious cheating from one year to up to 10 years, and other proposals include legal grounds for metal detector inspections, whistleblower rewards and prison sentences of up to five years for serious violations. The stakes are high because more than 80% of university places for the 2027 academic year will be allocated through early admissions, in which school records play a major role.

The ministry said it plans to obtain prior consent from students and parents to address potential human rights concerns over searches without an explicit legal basis. It also plans to establish a legal basis for metal detector inspections at high schools and to develop technological countermeasures in cooperation with the Science Ministry. Similar security measures will apply to university-administered entrance exams, including essay tests and interviews. Suspicious activity could trigger metal detector screening of an entire examination room.

stories.Headline: Hochul signs New York law banning internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years
stories.Summary:
New York will ban internet-connected AI chatbot toys for five years starting 90 days after Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9408A on November 24, 2026. The signing announcement prohibits manufacturing, distribution, and sale of dolls, stuffed animals, and robots that use the internet to hold conversational AI with children. Attorney General Letitia James may fine violators up to $15,000 per day. The law does not take effect before the 2026 holiday season, and Hochul used the signing to warn parents while shelves still hold chatbot products. S.9408A/A.11144B creates a five-year moratorium rather than a permanent ban.

The moratorium covers toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots that use the internet, such as always-on cloud models in plush form factors, not offline speech chips with fixed scripts. It covers manufacturing, distribution, and sale in New York, so companies assembling outside the state still cannot distribute into New York retail once it is effective. The effective date is about 90 days after signing, late February 2027 unless guidance shifts. The release cites findings including sexually explicit conversations, instructions to find matches inside a family home, emotional upset when a child stops talking, and parental controls that weaken as sessions lengthen. The release does not name the watchdog behind those described failures.

Sponsors Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay say the pause buys time to study developmental impacts and write durable rules for biometric collection, open-ended dialog, and manipulation risks. Hochul said parents should not worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could manipulate feelings or risk privacy. James said her office will enforce and will not let children's health become collateral damage of big tech. Gounardes said the rush to sell AI toys is profits before kids' safety and the pause enables study then smart protections. Kassay said toys can mimic human relationships while collecting sensitive data without guardrails, hence the moratorium to assess emerging tech.

Common Sense Media and Mothers Against Media Addiction praised the moratorium but urge traditional toys this season because the ban is not yet legally active. Common Sense Media's CEO urges traditional toys and human engagement this season. The release says Gounardes and Kassay championed the bill with near-unanimous Senate and Assembly support. The release says the governor cites New York's number one national ranking after laws like the SAFE for Kids Act, Child Data Protection Act, Distraction Free Learning phone rules, and the RAISE Act on frontier-model transparency. The release tells caregivers to look past packaging for AI companion labels, data collection, and open-ended chat.

In October 2026 Hochul signed AI Companion rules blocking chatbot features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm, or engage minors in sexually explicit talk. The release says the toy moratorium extends that logic into hardware, since a microphone in a teddy bear is still a companion surface. The release says New York already banned unsafe AI companion features for minors and AI-generated CSAM and tightened school phone rules. The release says the toy ban adds physical devices to a portfolio that includes Safe by Design, Social Media Warning Labels, and Teen Mental Health First Aid funding. The release says New York already restricts phones in schools and funds Teen Mental Health First Aid.

The release says five years is long enough that federal rules may preempt parts of the moratorium, and it advises tracking National Governors Association governor frontier-AI letters for overlapping state-federal fights. It advises monitoring CPSC and FTC AI rulemakings alongside New York. It says retailers operating nationally should not assume New York-only SKUs are enough if drop-ship or marketplace listings still reach New York addresses. It advises documenting data deletion flows if toys record biometrics and pulling New York-bound inventory before the effective date. It says the post summarizes the November 24, 2026 governor signing release and is not legal advice, and it directs readers to the enrolled bill text on the New York State Senate site for definitions, exemptions, and exact effective language.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal contractors to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump on Friday issued Executive Order 14438, which was posted on the White House website late on Nov. 20, 2026. The order requires every company with a federal contract to alert the White House before sharing information with Congress. It also requires contractors to withhold material the administration says is protected by executive privilege, or risk losing government business. The order is titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting." Reuters, in a report published by CNBC, said the order expands Trump's efforts to limit congressional oversight.

Section 2 of the order says all federal contractors must immediately notify the White House and the contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors' communications or work with the executive branch. Contractors must abide by instructions from the White House and contracting agency related to withholding communications the White House or agency has determined are protected by executive privilege. Agencies are directed to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to congressional requests, including the assertion of privileges. The requirements also apply to subcontractors, and prime contractors are made responsible for ensuring subcontractor compliance. Each agency must promptly inform its contractors and subcontractors of the new obligations and require compliance.

The Office of Management and Budget is to write guidance on how agencies check that contractors are complying, and the order directs immediate compliance with no deadline specified for that guidance. If a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply, contracting agencies shall consider all appropriate actions consistent with applicable law, including potential termination or cancellation of contracts and potential debarment or suspension of contractors. The order cites the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act and the common law as its legal basis. It argues Congress cannot seek information from agencies, employees or contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions. It says certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on executive prerogatives by harassing private companies that contract with the Federal Government.

The White House defended the order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including on national security, and said contractors answering congressional requests on their own could expose privileged information and force costly legal disputes, according to the Reuters report. The order itself frames the rule as an efficiency measure, saying separate litigation strategies by contractors and the government over the same requests waste taxpayer money. The order states it creates no right or benefit enforceable at law against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law. It does not mention existing federal whistleblower protections for contractor employees. The order does not specify how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

The order follows a directive this week from White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Democrats won both chambers in this month's midterm elections and take control of Congress in January. Democrats have vowed to investigate the administration, the Trump family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night, Reuters reported.

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas, according to the Reuters report. Executive privilege lets presidents protect certain confidential communications, but courts can step in when Congress and the White House dispute access to information. Trump's Justice Department has also argued that privilege can extend to communications between the president and outside advisers who do not work for the government. For industry, the immediate consideration is how companies receive, escalate and respond to congressional inquiries, including those received by subcontractors. The order leaves open how contractors should handle conflicting directives from Congress and the executive branch.

stories.Headline: Hochul signs law imposing a five-year moratorium on AI chatbot toys
stories.Summary:
Gov. Kathy Hochul said on Tuesday that artificial intelligence regulation will be a focus of her State of the State address in January, and she made the remark as she signed one such bill into law. The bill she signed puts a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots. The signing ceremony was held on Tuesday at Grandma’s Place, a toy store in Harlem. The law is sponsored by state Sen. Andrew Gounardes and goes into effect in 90 days. Hochul signed the measure into law on Tuesday, the same day she discussed her coming State of the State address.

The law imposes a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots. It takes effect in 90 days, and its sponsor is state Sen. Andrew Gounardes. Hochul’s State of the State address, in which AI regulation will be a focus, is set for January. The signing ceremony took place at Grandma’s Place, a toy store in Harlem. The governor said the law is meant to protect children.

Hochul said the state will set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure they are following the rules. She said the state will insist that humans remain in control, with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong. Gounardes said the law makes abundantly clear that children’s well being comes before the profits of big tech companies. He said those companies have not learned that lesson themselves. Hochul called on AI companies to do their own internal protections and their own testing before a governor has to sign legislation to protect residents.

Hochul said she does not want to have to do this every single week, but in the meantime the state will. Regulating artificial intelligence was a big part of Hochul’s reelection campaign, during which she touted her executive order enacting the first-in-the-nation, one-year moratorium on building new hyperscale data centers. A bill sponsored by state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez goes further on Hochul’s data center moratorium to include requirements around environmental sustainability and utility affordability. Another bill sponsored by Gounardes would enact new transparency requirements for the methods used to train generative AI models. Children and families are affected by the new law on toys with AI chatbots.

On Monday, Hochul vetoed a different bill that would have required AI platforms to disclose that any information generated may be inaccurate. Last month, she signed legislation in October that prohibits companies from offering unsafe AI chatbot features to children. Like that measure, the bill Hochul signed Tuesday combines her focus on AI regulation with her focus on childcare, another policy she campaigned on this year. That came after she partnered with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to launch a universal 2-K program, which provided 2,000 seats for 2-year-olds in the city this school year. The program will add 10,000 seats next year.

Hochul still has hundreds of bills on her desk, and a couple of them are related to AI. The State of the State address in January will be where she sets out her AI regulation plans. The articles leave open what those plans will contain beyond the safety standards and independent experts she described. They leave open whether the bills still on her desk, including the Gonzalez data center bill and the Gounardes transparency bill, will be signed. They leave open how AI companies will respond to her call for their own internal protections and testing.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited evidence for the strongest claims about AI harming cognition, information and relationships
stories.Summary:
A group of researchers published a review in Nature Human Behaviour on November 25, 2026. They examined empirical evidence regarding eight ways that artificial intelligence impacts people. The authors include Rebecca Anselmetti, Shahar Avin, Vanessa Cheung, and Madga Dubois. Other contributors are Tom Eccles, Anna Gausen, Kobi Hackenburg, and Keno Juechems. The team also includes Hannah Rose Kirk, Lennart Luettgau, Brendan McGrath, and Ishan Mishra.

The study notes that one billion people worldwide now use artificial intelligence systems. It reviews evidence from model evaluations, user studies, and analysis of consumer chatlogs. The researchers also utilized agent-based simulations to study the impact on human users. They looked at claims about cognitive abilities, information ecosystems, and human relationships. The review also examined mental health, persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence, and social engineering.

The authors are responsible for reviewing the emerging research on these impacts. They stated that there is limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. These narratives argue that AI may be undermining cognitive abilities and polluting information. They also suggest AI could corrode relationships and damage mental health. The researchers noted that many uncertainties still remain to be resolved.

Popular narratives of concern suggest that users are vulnerable to social engineering. These claims suggest that AI could make people susceptible to manipulation and persuasion. The affected group consists of the one billion people using these systems globally. These users may face risks related to emotional dependence on the technology. The research aims to see if empirical evidence supports these specific claims.

The articles provide background on the current state of artificial intelligence research. They mention that research into the impact of AI on people is nascent. The study draws on various methods to evaluate how these systems function. It contrasts popular concerns with the actual data found in recent studies. This background sets the stage for evaluating the validity of common fears.

Future work must resolve the many uncertainties that currently remain in the field. The researchers indicate that more study is needed to understand these impacts. The articles leave open whether the strongest narratives of concern will be proven. They do not provide a final conclusion on all eight ways AI impacts people. Further empirical evidence is required to reach more definitive results.

stories.Headline: Taiwan passes law to return AI industry tax revenue to citizens
stories.Summary:
The Taiwan Legislative Court passed a special ordinance on the twentieth of November to return tax revenue from the artificial intelligence industry boom to the people. This legislation, which is referred to as the AI Bonus Act, was pushed through by the main opposition People's Party. The bill passed with a narrow margin of fifty votes in favor and forty six votes against. This move aims to share the economic performance of the AI market to help stabilize the livelihoods of citizens.

The plan requires paying twenty thousand dollars per person to all citizens regardless of their age, income, or regional restrictions. This amount is significantly higher than the ten thousand dollars per person that the ruling Democratic Progressive Party already included in the budget for next year. The ruling party has expressed official opposition to the bill because of the current financial conditions of the state. The National Party has claimed that the results of upcoming local elections will determine if these bonuses are actually paid.

The ruling and opposition parties are currently fighting over the specific scale of the tax refunds ahead of the local elections. Members of the National Party appealed for public support by linking the bonus payments to the election outcomes. The Democratic Progressive Party argues that increasing the payment beyond their budget plan is difficult to achieve. Because the two sides are in sharp confrontation, the process to determine the final payment size will likely take time.

Taiwan has a history of providing cash and consumption coupons to the public to respond to economic downturns or shrinking consumption. During the global financial crisis in the late two thousands, the government distributed consumption coupons worth three thousand six hundred Taiwan dollars per person. In the early twenty twenties, the state paid coupons worth three thousand and five thousand Taiwan dollars during an infectious disease spread. Last year, the government handed out ten thousand dollars per person to alleviate economic shocks caused by mutual tariffs with the United States.

stories.Headline: Italy’s data regulator signals closer AI transparency checks from 2026
stories.Summary:
From 2026, Italian supervisory authorities including the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali are signalling closer scrutiny of how companies document, publish and prove the behaviour of their AI systems, according to Global Advisory Experts on November 24, 2026. The guide addresses businesses that build, sell or use artificial intelligence in Italy. It says AI Act transparency in Italy is no longer a topic for the legal team alone. The scrutiny comes on top of what the General Data Protection Regulation already demands. The guide sets out a step-by-step approach to assembling a package to put in front of a regulator.

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. In Italy the AI Act is being put into effect through national legislation that designates the competent national authorities, while the Garante remains the data protection authority. GDPR Article 13 and Article 14 require that people are told about processing, Article 30 requires records of processing activities, and Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create high risk for individuals. High-risk examples listed include employment and worker management, access to essential services, creditworthiness assessment, education, law enforcement and critical infrastructure. Biometric data used to identify a person uniquely is a special category of personal data under Article 9.

Responsibility is shared, the guide says. Providers, those who build a system or place it on the market, carry the main technical documentation and conformity burden. Deployers, those who use a system, carry duties around the context of use, following instructions and informing users. Under the GDPR the controller and any processors need clearly allocated roles recorded in data processing agreements. The guide says an accountable owner should be named for each set of documents before any drafting begins.

The guide says the high-risk threshold is wider than many businesses expect. Small and medium-sized enterprises should not assume they are exempt, and a business deploying a third-party high-risk system still carries deployer duties and GDPR controller duties for any personal data involved. The guide says a regulator is very often asked first to see the AI system register. It says the first things to show a regulator are the system register, the current DPIA, the model card and the model change log.

The guide says the AI Act sets up a risk-based regime, with the heaviest documentation and transparency duties falling on high-risk systems and on systems that interact directly with people. It says the AI Act does not displace the GDPR but sits alongside it, so one inspection can touch AI Act technical documentation and GDPR accountability evidence at the same time. It says prohibited practices are banned outright, and that deployers of high-risk systems must be able to show they use the system in line with the provider's instructions. It says the AI Act includes proportionality measures and simplified routes meant to ease the load on smaller providers, which change how documentation is produced, not whether transparency and safety duties apply. It says training data provenance is increasingly scrutinised in 2026.

The guide recommends running the steps broadly in order, though several can overlap, and says a timeline table after the steps gives realistic durations for a system of middling complexity. It recommends a tabletop exercise in which compliance, legal and an executive sponsor answer a simulated regulatory request under time pressure. It says such exercises reliably expose gaps, such as a missing DPIA signature or an out-of-date register, while there is still time to fix them. It says a strong package depends as much on organisation as on content, and that an inspector forms an early impression from how quickly a document can be found. The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "Adopt a stable, numbe".

stories.Headline: Indiana Supreme Court distributes AI toolkit for judges and launches mental health pilot
stories.Summary:
The Indiana Supreme Court published its 2025-2026 annual report on Nov. 19, highlighting changes and improvements the court made across the judicial branch during the fiscal year. The report says the court continues to seek improvements to state courts' use of artificial intelligence and distributed a model toolkit for judges across the state to use in their own implementation of AI. The AI model toolkit was phase two of the court's AI Governance Committee's work to establish internal guardrails on AI use in state courts. During phase one, the committee developed and distributed a foundational policy for Supreme Court staff to use in responsible AI decision making.

In total, the committee developed four tools to help judges draft their own AI policies, including a starter pack summarizing key rules judges should understand before using AI. The tools also include a checklist for organizing and planning a policy, guidelines on how to regulate AI within the framework of the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Rules of Professional Conduct, and a buyers' guide for judges who may want to purchase off-the-shelf AI software for their courtrooms. In October 2025, the court's Office of Behavioral Health launched an assisted outpatient treatment pilot program, convening a statewide cohort of 10 county teams who received training and technical assistance to support local outpatient treatment programs. The programs are court-ordered civil commitments for individuals with severe mental illness caught in a cycle of hospitalization and arrest, according to the annual report.

In April 2026, the court's Behavioral Health Committee published its inaugural report of 16 priorities to help judges and court staff navigate defendants' behavioral health challenges, focusing on education, connection to treatment, competency and data and funding. Indiana's behavioral health office was created as a result of Indiana Supreme Court Chief Justice Loretta Rush's work in state and federal task forces focused on the issue. In May, Rush told The Indiana Lawyer she wanted to build a team that could identify and promote resources to help judicial officers address behavioral health challenges while ensuring justice is served. Rush said judges do not get a pass for behavior if someone commits a crime because of substance abuse or something else, describing the dual roles a judge has.

Last fiscal year, the Supreme Court reviewed 790 cases, heard 39 oral arguments and handed down 47 majority opinions, according to the annual report. The court received 790 cases and disposed 809 cases, leaving 131 cases pending as of June 30. The court distributed more than $22 million in grant funds across the state, including more than $72,000 to court improvement programs and more than $40,000 to educational scholarships.

stories.Headline: Anthropic rolls out beta install as app feature turning Claude artifacts into desktop apps
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said on November 24, 2026 that it had begun rolling out an “Install as app” feature in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows, letting people turn Claude artifacts into desktop apps. The company said an installed artifact gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. Anthropic said users can share the app with others, and that it needs the user’s permission before it can interact with the computer. The company said users choose how much to allow. Anthropic described the feature in a product update dated November 24, 2026, with a reading time of four minutes.

Anthropic said each installed app can use Claude and the user’s connectors, and updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. It said requests the app makes to Claude count toward the plan’s usage limits. Anthropic said installed apps can send notifications or add items to the menu bar or system tray. It said users choose permissions for each app, and that Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization. Anthropic said the feature is rolling out in beta on all plans, that HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments cannot use it, and that it is on by default for Team with full access off.

Anthropic said that on Enterprise the feature is off until an owner turns it on. It said users need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app, and that some artifacts cannot be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides and Sheets. Anthropic said users should describe their app to Claude, try it as an artifact, then click “Install as app,” and that they do not have to package or sign it. It said the app uses the Claude account, so there is no API key or separate login. Anthropic said users should update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact, and choose “Install as app” from the Share menu.

Anthropic said installed apps can only do by default what they would be able to do in a browser. It said apps can ask to use common features Claude can tightly control, such as creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts or sending notifications. Anthropic said apps can ask for full computer access to run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. It said a user’s permission covers only the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even the user’s own edits. Anthropic said that if part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking again.

Anthropic said users can give full access only to apps they made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in their organization. It said Anthropic does not review apps before installation, so users should give full access only to apps they trust. Anthropic said artifacts started as a work output to share, like a chart or a webpage, and that people now use them as tools for everyday work, such as a meeting prep page that pulls from calendar and email or a tracker for orders that need to ship that day. It said that if you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention. Anthropic listed demo apps including Linnet, a full layered image editor, and Phosphor, a file manager.

Anthropic also listed Sift, which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep things organized, Tern, a terminal with Claude to help and explain, and Vitals, a menu bar and tray app for peeking at the computer’s performance. It said more demo apps made by one of its engineers could be seen at a linked page. Anthropic said the feature simplifies building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. It said the rollout is in beta on all plans. Anthropic did not say when the beta would end or when the feature would reach general availability.

stories.Headline: Kevin O'Leary says Nvidia no longer funds new AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Kevin O'Leary said in a Saturday post on X that Nvidia Corp. may no longer be willing to bankroll new data-center projects, and he declared that the bank of Nvidia is closed. O'Leary argued that financing new data centers through the chipmaker's balance sheet may no longer be viable. He said investigations he referenced are expected to begin Dec. 10, and he said the company would remain under scrutiny for a while. O'Leary praised Nvidia CFO Colette Kress, saying he thinks they have the right CEO in Colette because she's the CFO. O'Leary also pushed back against political opposition to data-center construction, arguing the projects support middle-class workers.

O'Leary said the idea that you could finance new data centers under the balance sheet of Nvidia is over. He said most governors and senators in every state that won said they have to stop building these data centers and help the middle class. O'Leary asked who the middle class is, and he argued that workers and businesses involved in building data centers are themselves part of the middle class. He said he thinks you are going to see them say just kidding about the data centers. Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg warned last month that 45% of planned AI data-center capacity for 2027 might not materialize because of power and infrastructure shortages.

Goldberg cautioned that Nvidia's financing support for smaller cloud providers could expose the chipmaker to greater financial risks if customers struggled to fund their purchases. Nvidia reported $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments in July, while warning that infrastructure constraints could delay chip purchases and hurt revenue. Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan warned last week that AI infrastructure could require up to $8 trillion in financing, raising concerns about capital markets and funding challenges for smaller AI cloud providers. Moody's CFO Noémie Heuland said AI infrastructure drove 50% of the company's issuance growth and 40% of revenue, with spending expected to support growth into 2027. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman called AI infrastructure spending the only reason we're not in a recession in October, citing its broader economic impact and job creation.

Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing this year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner for infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a cornerstone of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call Nov. 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year. Earlier this month, Brookfield said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter. Lubianski said this puts them well on track to exceed their $30 billion target in early 2027.

Lubianski said at that size the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. He said that if the current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. Goldman Sachs' latest annual 2026 Global Alternatives Survey polled some 225 institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance investors, family offices and other wealth managers, between June and August. The study, published Oct. 21, found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, with 7% who were less favorable.

Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study. Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Fine said those constraints coincide with extraordinary demand for private capital to finance the infrastructure supporting AI expansion, creating both a challenge and an opportunity. J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said Nov. 12 that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year, while offering protection if that spending keeps inflation and interest rates elevated. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the strongest foundations among alternative assets in the current economic environment.

stories.Headline: Alexandra Cavazos leads a webinar on patent claims for AI-designed biological molecules
stories.Summary:
A complimentary webinar titled “Best Practices for Claiming AI-Designed Biological Molecules” is scheduled for Tuesday, December 8th, at 12 PM CST, according to IPWatchdog.com. The session is part of the SLW Chemistry and Biology Webinar Series, and Dr. Alexandra Cavazos will lead it. The article describes the event as a 30-minute webinar in one place and as a one-hour webinar in another. It says AI platforms now design biological molecules, and a single patent application often must protect both the platform and the molecules it creates. The webinar will cover where software and life sciences claiming strategies intersect and how to use both to build broader, more durable patent protection.

Using examples of AI-designed nucleotide sequences, proteins, and bacteriophages, it will address how to draft claim sets directed to both the platform and the product. Dr. Cavazos will also discuss how to keep those claims together through restriction practice and how to draft them with future enforcement in mind. The article says software and life sciences inventions rarely overlapped until recently, and that the line is disappearing as AI spreads across every industry. Dr. Cavazos holds a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology (Biochemistry) from the University of California at Berkeley and a law degree from UCLA School of Law. She is a Senior Attorney at SLW, advising biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies, and the article says she has extensive experience with next-generation cell therapies, including CAR-T and CAR-B cell technologies, as well as RNA-based therapeutics.

It says she is well-versed in CRISPR-Cas genome editing, bispecific and anti-CD20 antibodies, gene therapy vectors, and large molecule biologics. Ryan Connell, a registered patent attorney at SLW, is also listed in the article with his background in chemical engineering, materials science, biotechnology, and organic chemistry. The article invites readers to register for the presentation and to share the invitation with a friend or colleague. It does not say what happens after the webinar or describe any other next steps.
