stories.Headline: Gapped Deterministic Legal Tech vs. Cloud-Hosted Generative AI: Seven Trade-Offs for Law Firms
stories.Summary:
Pouya Shafabakhsh wrote an article on November 24, 2026, about the trade-offs between two different types of legal technology architectures. The author compared gapped deterministic legal tech against cloud-hosted generative AI to help law firms choose the right tools. This analysis focuses on which architecture is better suited for specific legal tasks, risk levels, and information boundaries. The piece provides a fair comparison for managing partners, general counsel, and legal-tech leaders to evaluate their options. It examines how different tools serve different needs, such as summarizing productions or verifying quotations in legal filings.

The comparison requires weighing seven specific trade-offs including flexibility, accuracy, specialization, auditability, confidentiality, collaboration, and the overall cost of the technology. A litigation team might use one tool to summarize a production that is 200 pages long for their case. Another tool could be used to draft a client update, while a third verifies that a quotation matches its source. The author notes that these are all legal-technology problems, but they are not the same problem for the firm. These requirements ensure that the exhibit being served is the exact version that the counsel has already approved.

Pouya Shafabakhsh, who is a judicial forensic AI auditor, is the person responsible for providing this technical legal technology analysis. He stated that the primary question for firms is not which technology is more fashionable for their current legal practice. Instead, he argued that the real issue is determining which architecture fits a particular task and its associated risk. He suggested that the choice depends on the specific information boundary required for the legal work being performed. His goal was to provide a framework for leaders to weigh the various benefits and risks of AI.

Managing partners and general counsel are among the professionals affected by these choices when selecting software for their legal teams. These leaders must decide between deterministic systems and generative AI to maintain the accuracy of their official court filings. The analysis affects how litigation teams handle large productions and how they communicate updates to their various clients. Legal-tech leaders are also impacted as they must balance the need for flexibility with the need for strict auditability. The choice of architecture directly influences how a firm manages its internal data and its external legal obligations.

The articles provide background on how generative AI uses foundation models to create complex text, images, audio, or video. These systems ingest and generate large amounts of data, including business plans, technical formulae, speech, code, and various images. The EU AI Act provides a specific definition for generative AI as foundation models used in these autonomous systems. There is ongoing discussion regarding intellectual property rights for both the input materials and the resulting AI-generated output. The background indicates that regulatory frameworks for this technology are currently emerging and are evolving very quickly.

The articles leave open the specific results of the trade-offs for individual firms and their unique operational needs. They do not state which of the two architectures is objectively superior for every single legal task or firm. Future actions involve managing partners applying these seven trade-offs to their own specific risk levels and information boundaries. The text does not provide a final recommendation on which specific software products law firms should purchase today. It remains unclear how the evolving regulatory frameworks will specifically change the seven trade-offs mentioned by Shafabakhsh.

stories.Headline: LSE researcher urges better evidence and regulation before healthcare adopts generative AI
stories.Summary:
Dr Robin van Kessel, Co-Director of the AI and Digital Lab at LSE Health, wrote an article published by the London School of Economics and Political Science on Tuesday 24 November 2026. The article says healthcare systems worldwide face growing strain, financial pressures, competing priorities and a global shortage of healthcare workers. It says noncommunicable diseases are now responsible for 41 million deaths annually, representing 74 per cent of all deaths worldwide. It says digital health and artificial intelligence technologies hold considerable promise for alleviating these pressures. It says generative AI presents a completely different challenge from other AI used in healthcare.

The article says a systematic review published in 2025 in JAMA by Suhana Bedi and colleagues found that around one in five evaluations focused on diagnosis. It says only five per cent of all evaluations used real patient data. It says Dr van Kessel and colleagues created a taxonomy of digital health and AI tools to support more targeted and appropriate evidence collection. It says the taxonomy is intended to evolve alongside the technology rather than be an exhaustive list. It says Dr van Kessel reviewed guidance documents from bodies such as the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence and found significant gaps around generative AI use.

The article says Dr van Kessel argues current guidance largely assumes a technology stays the same once deployed, which does not hold for many AI systems. It says he explains that asking a language model the same question 20 times can give 20 different answers. It says changing three words in the question and asking another 20 times can give 40 different answers. It says he says there is still no shared understanding of what good evidence looks like for generative AI. It says he says consensus has not been reached on even the baseline study designs.

The article says Dr van Kessel says the computer science community often sees clinical evidence standards as hard to accommodate for such a fast-moving technology. It says he says the health research community expects any technology entering patient care to meet established standards. It says he says both positions have merit but an important level of nuance tends to get lost. It says he says there is a substantial lack of training for healthcare practitioners using AI tools. It says he says physicians are wary to use AI in case something goes wrong and do not know where they stand on liability.

The article says Dr van Kessel explored frameworks for digital technology and AI use in six countries: the UK, France, Germany, South Korea, the US and Canada. It says he highlighted different areas of strength across these jurisdictions. It says he argues context is important and what might work for one country may not be suitable for another. It says he gives the example that where mental health services are unavailable or very limited, a mental health chatbot might be better than no support at all. It says he says in systems with abundant support a chatbot might be insufficient.

The article says Dr van Kessel argues healthcare systems need better ways to evaluate generative AI, greater use of real-world evidence and more flexible approaches to testing and adopting new technologies. It says without those changes many tools that promise to transform healthcare may struggle to move from innovation to implementation. It says he was speaking to Charlotte Kelloway, Media Relations Manager at LSE. It says he is a Hoffmann Fellow in Health System Financing and Payment Models at LSE Health. It says the article was published on 24 November 2026.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Congress advances a dedicated AI bill as ANPD enforces LGPD duties on automated decisions
stories.Summary:
Brazil's Congress has advanced a dedicated artificial intelligence bill, Projeto de Lei nº 2.338/2023, and the Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados keeps refining its expectations for automated decision-making under the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados. The ANPD interprets and enforces the LGPD through guidance, normative acts and public consultations, and supervises automated decision-making and large-scale processing. The ANPD has published analyses on AI and data protection and is widely expected to hold a central supervisory role under any future AI framework. ANEEL regulates electricity and sets expectations on operational safety, service continuity, technical standards and incident reporting. ANATEL covers telecommunications and network infrastructure, including connectivity, certification and communications for connected charging networks.

As of early 2026, no single comprehensive AI statute is in force in Brazil, although the dedicated bill is moving through the legislature. The LGPD, Law No. 13.709/2018, applies whenever an AI system processes personal data, and it gives individuals the right to ask for a review of decisions taken solely through automated processing that affect their interests. The LGPD limits processing to what is necessary for a specified, legitimate purpose, and it requires a data protection impact assessment, a relatório de impacto à proteção de dados pessoais, where processing is large-scale, involves sensitive data or creates material risk. The LGPD's rules on international transfers apply where AI vendors host infrastructure or training environments outside Brazil. The Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação leads the Brazilian AI strategy, which is not binding in itself.

André Fortes Carvalho & Furtado Advogados, listed as a Gold featured expert on the matter, is the guide's named adviser for Brazil. The guide says AI used for grid optimisation, load forecasting, EV charging routing and predictive maintenance is exactly the kind of system regulators are most likely to treat as high-risk. It says such systems affect safety and continuity of supply and rely on large volumes of personal and operational data. It says a compliant AI deployment has to satisfy LGPD and ANPD duties and ANEEL and ANATEL duties together. It says AI does not create a separate data-protection regime but makes existing duties heavier.

The guide says operators using AI today include grid optimisation and load forecasting, charging optimisation and routing, predictive maintenance, and dynamic pricing and demand response. It says smart-meter readings, EV user accounts, charging session records, roaming identifiers and predictive-maintenance logs frequently contain personal data. It says a charging operator sits under two sector regimes plus the LGPD, and the three should be run as one coordinated programme. It says regulators dealing with critical infrastructure expect operators to show that systems fail safely, that humans oversee consequential decisions, and that fallback arrangements keep service running. It says a model failure in grid balancing or charging allocation can threaten supply continuity and public safety.

The guide says the LGPD sets out lawful bases for processing, the rights of data subjects and an accountability principle that obliges operators to prove compliance. It says properly anonymised data sits outside the statute, but anonymisation must be robust and not reasonably reversible, and pseudonymised or re-identifiable data is still personal data. It says an operator that decides the purposes of processing is the controller and carries primary accountability, while a vendor that only processes data on the operator's instructions is a processor, an operador. It says ANEEL's existing obligations should be assumed to extend to AI-driven decisions. It says ANATEL's remit covers network aspects, equipment certification (homologation) and communications requirements.

The guide sets out a 90/180/360 day action plan and a twelve-point checklist. It says operators should appoint a data protection officer (encarregado) or equivalent and name an accountable executive for each high-risk AI system. It says a cross-functional AI governance committee should keep an inventory of AI systems, classify them by risk and approve deployments before go-live. It says governance should state explicitly who can override or suspend an AI system in an emergency. It says operators should test for accuracy and bias before deployment and set automated alerts for when a model drifts outside acceptable limits.

stories.Headline: Maricopa County attorney's office advises police agencies on disclosing generative AI use in arrest reports
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 12, 2026, just after 9:00 AM, Gilbert police responded to a home in the 3000 Block of East Woodside Way after a report of a domestic disturbance involving a woman allegedly armed with a knife. Officers located 28-year-old Vivian Rodriguez outside the home and interviewed family members who alleged she damaged property inside. One victim told police Rodriguez allegedly picked up a knife and held it in front of their face, and family members allegedly retreated to a room, locked the door and waited for police. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the custody of the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office. At the bottom of the arrest narrative, the officer included a disclosure stating, “I acknowledge this report was generated using Draft One by Axon.”

The charges were A.R.S. 13-1204(A)(2) Aggravated Assault, a Domestic Violence offense and class 2 felony, A.R.S. 13-2904(A)(1) Disorderly Conduct, a Domestic Violence offense and class 1 misdemeanor, and A.R.S. 13-1602(A)(1) Criminal Damage, a Domestic Violence offense and class 1 misdemeanor. The case went before Maricopa County Superior Court Commissioner Daniel Fenzel, who found there was not probable cause for the felony aggravated-assault allegation. The commissioner found insufficient information regarding whether the alleged victim had a reasonable apprehension of imminent physical injury, noting the narrative said there were no specific threats and Rodriguez did not move toward the alleged victim. Fenzel found probable cause for the remaining misdemeanor allegations but wrote that “the weight of evidence is limited given that there is limited information provided about the extent of usage and contribution of generative artificial intelligence that was used in drafting the arrest narrative allegations.” The Maricopa County Attorney’s Office elected to refer the charges to the Gilbert Prosecutor’s Office for review.

Two days before the arrest, the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office sent communications to different law enforcement agencies about the use of generative AI in reports. Tom Van Dorn, the law enforcement liaison, wrote in the email that MCAO doesn’t have a definitive answer on what judges are looking for in the disclaimers, but provided a drafted example. The example disclosure says AI was utilized solely as an administrative writing aid to assist with grammar, organization, formatting and narrative clarity. It says all factual information and investigative findings were provided by the officer and derived from the officer’s investigation, and that AI was not used to independently establish facts, determine probable cause or formulate investigative conclusions. It says the officer personally reviewed the final report, verified its factual accuracy, completeness and consistency, and retains full responsibility for the contents.

Gilbert police told ABC15 the department began using Axon Draft One in fall 2025, and said Draft One uses body-worn camera recordings and information provided by officers to create a draft narrative. Officers are required to review and verify the information, and a supervisor reviews and approves the report for content and accuracy. Gilbert PD General Orders 1201.40 outlines that officers must review and verify all information in the report is accurate and a supervisor must review and approve the report for content and accuracy. Bryan Schwartz, associate clinical professor of law at the University of Arizona, said, “I think the main concern that we think about is the reliability.” Schwartz said he feels how AI is being used is inconsistent in police departments and in courtrooms, and said, “We're gonna need to establish some rules, some parameters, guidelines to instruct not just police, but lawyers, and judges on how to handle this type of evidence.”

Earlier this month, the commissioner released a DUI suspect after determining he could not find probable cause because the arresting officer's report was generated with the assistance of an artificial intelligence tool. The trooper's probable cause statement included a disclosure at the end of the narrative stating the report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI and that the content reflects the officer's own observations and recollections. In the release order, Fenzel wrote that without further information regarding the nature and extent to which a generative AI authored or contributed the narrative, given that all alleged facts and statements were “based” on the affiant officer's original account which was not included, the court was “unable to meaningfully weigh” whether the factual allegations were authored, in whole or in part, by a generative AI. Gilbert police said the department is aware this is the same commissioner who recently did not find probable cause on DPS's case citing AI usage, and said it is unaware of any other commissioners with the Maricopa County Superior Court making these findings or noting these concerns. Charged or submitted offenses are merely allegations, and all defendants are presumed innocent until pleading guilty or being found guilty.

The Maricopa County Attorney’s Office provided the drafted disclosure language to law enforcement agencies but wrote it does not have a definitive answer on what judges are looking for in the disclaimers. Gilbert police said officers are required to review and verify the information in Draft One narratives and a supervisor must review and approve the report for content and accuracy. The commissioner found probable cause for the remaining misdemeanor allegations in the Gilbert case while stating the weight of evidence is limited given the limited information about the extent of AI usage and contribution. The articles do not say what the Gilbert Prosecutor’s Office will do with the referred charges. The articles do not say whether the MCAO email produced any response from law enforcement agencies or whether the drafted disclosure language has been adopted.

stories.Headline: Property lawyers name faster AI adoption by rival firms as their biggest competitive threat
stories.Summary:
Live polling at October’s Digital Conveyancing Summit found that 43 per cent of respondents named rival firms adopting artificial intelligence faster as the biggest threat to their commercial success, rather than AI replacing them. The findings came from a panel hosted by property data specialist Search Acumen before an audience of around 500 property lawyers, with senior figures from JLL, the Urban Land Institute and law firm Freeths taking part. Financial Times property correspondent Julie Steinberg moderated the discussion, which examined where commercial property law is heading over the next five years. The article says buying another AI subscription is unlikely to be the answer, and that the number of actual poll respondents was not disclosed.

Search Acumen managing director Andrew Lloyd argued that real estate’s fundamental problem is not AI but data, because vast quantities of valuable property information remain locked in separate systems and create duplicated work, unnecessary costs and missed opportunities. He said combining ownership records, geographical information, flood risks and climate resilience data could transform property due diligence and investment advice, and that advantage will increasingly belong to firms combining their own knowledge with wider industry datasets. The article lists five points for property lawyers: AI is becoming core infrastructure, firms should collect and organise data now and review confidentiality agreements, data retention policies and permissions, more complex public-private transactions are expected in housing, energy and infrastructure, climate data will increasingly influence transactions, and relationships still matter. It says the intellectual capital inside law firms could become one of their most valuable commercial assets, provided they can use it without compromising client confidentiality.

JLL technology executive Will Cohen said fewer than 40 per cent of organisations beginning to pilot AI had formal training or governance processes in place, a figure the article says was separately reported. Freeths’ chief knowledge and innovation officer Nick Pryor emphasised the importance of human judgment, data protection and making AI central to legal practice. The article says the competitive advantage will not necessarily go to the firm with the most expensive AI platform but to the firm that knows what to do with its information. It does not say what happens next beyond the five-year outlook the panel examined.

stories.Headline: Law review authors say generative AI blurs human authorship in copyright law
stories.Summary:
The National Law Review published an article on November 24, 2026, by Dr. Eyal Brook and S. Horowitz on copyright law and generative AI. The article says generative AI has rewritten the rules of engagement in the creative arena. It says systems like Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and GPT-4 simulate the creative process itself. The authors describe this shift as ontological rather than incremental. The article says the traditional status of the human author is blurring, sometimes to the point of total dissipation.

The article traces copyright law to the Statute of Anne in 1710, which assumed authorship was uniquely human. It cites Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service, which requires independent creation plus a modicum of creativity. It cites Naruto v. Slater, the Monkey Selfie case, where a court ruled a macaque cannot hold copyright.

It cites Thaler v. Perlmutter, which reaffirmed that human authorship is a bedrock requirement of copyright. It cites the Copyright Office decision on Zarya of the Dawn, where Kristina Kashtanova owns the selection and arrangement but the Midjourney images remain uncopyrightable. The article says the U.S. Copyright Office has remained steadfast that copyright is limited to works created by human beings. It says the European Union standard is the author's own intellectual creation, reflecting the author's personality.

The authors ask whether prompt engineering is a creative act of authorship or merely a request for service. They compare a prompt to a patron commissioning a painter to paint a portrait of a dog in a regal setting. They say the user who provides no further input acts as a curator rather than a creator. The article says the legal battle is not just about the output but about the input. It says generative AI models are trained on billions of copyrighted works through mass ingestion of books, paintings, code and music without explicit consent.

It says the article does not address whether scraping for training is fair use or infringement. It says a film studio licensing a comic book could find anyone legally printing individual panels on merchandise. It says this legal uncertainty could destabilize the copyright supply chain in the entertainment industry. The article describes three phases of the human-machine hierarchy: AI as a tool, AI as a collaborator and AI as a generative agent. It says in the third phase the human retreats from execution to curation and direction of the output.

It says the AI makes the expressive choices, such as the specific hues of a sunset or the cadence of a poem. It says this automation strikes at the heart of the sweat of the brow doctrine and the modicum of creativity standard. It says we are moving from a world where we reward the doing to a world where we are asked to reward the asking. The article says the question for the courts is whether prompt engineering is authorship or a request for service. It says a work can be protected as a whole while its individual parts are in the public domain.

It says this creates a complicated copyright landscape for commercial licensing. It says the article explores whether current legal frameworks can survive the transition from human-centric to machine-augmented creativity. It leaves open whether scraping copyrighted works to train a model is fair use or infringement. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Maryland students sue Omnilert over AI gun detection false alarm that led to handcuffs
stories.Summary:
A civil rights lawsuit was filed on Nov. 17 in Baltimore County Circuit Court against Virginia-based Omnilert, Baltimore County Public Schools, Baltimore County and several school and police officials. The complaint alleges negligence and civil rights violations after Omnilert's software mistook a bag of chips for a gun. The suit says the system triggered a police response that left four BCPS students in handcuffs. The plaintiffs are current and former BCPS students, including Taki Allen, a Kenwood High School student. The incident occurred in October 2025 at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County.

The plaintiffs seek undisclosed damages and ask the court to halt the system's use until the district improves its protocols. The complaint says Omnilert's software flagged an image of Allen, mistaking his hand and the object he was holding for a firearm. The alert went to the school's designated safety staff, who recognized the error and canceled it, the suit states. According to the complaint, principal Kate Smith did not acknowledge the cancellation and forwarded a screenshot of the alert to the school resource officer, who relayed it to police. When police arrived, several officers had their guns drawn and did not tell the students what they were suspected of, according to the complaint.

Omnilert spokesperson Blake Mitchell said in an email that the company is reviewing the lawsuit and will respond in court. Mitchell wrote that every student deserves to be safe at school and treated with dignity there, and that the company works every day toward both. BCPS and the Baltimore County Police Department did not respond to requests for comment. The articles do not give further statements from the defendants.

University of Baltimore law professor Michele Gilman said finding Omnilert liable will require lawyers to prove a direct link between the company's product and the alleged harms. Gilman said Omnilert is marketing a tool with claims of accuracy that don't seem borne out by real-world use, and that the intervening actions of school officials and police officers don't necessarily erase the company's own negligence. Len Kamdang, an attorney with the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said everyone would agree that stopping gun violence in schools is a laudable goal. Kamdang said that if the tools being used are so ineffective that they could create an instance of gun violence for students, companies should reevaluate their products. Allen told NBC News after the incident that the first thing he thought about was whether he was about to die, because they had a gun pointed at him.

In public materials, Omnilert promises school districts "reliable 24×7 monitoring" and the ability to distinguish between inert objects and weapons. The company also employs a human review team, which plaintiffs allege failed to identify the false alert before forwarding it to school officials. Maryland's Office of the Inspector General for Education found that more than 99% of Omnilert alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools between November 2023 and November 2025 did not warrant notification of law enforcement. BCPS was among the first school systems to roll out Omnilert's technology after it was patented in 2022, according to the complaint. Between fall 2023 and spring 2024, the district integrated the software into 165 schools and at least 7,000 existing security cameras.

Omnilert also faces a separate lawsuit in Tennessee, alleging its software failed to detect a firearm ahead of a fatal 2025 shooting at a Nashville high school. State investigators found no evidence of racial bias within Omnilert's software, addressing concerns from the teens' families that the students were unfairly targeted because they are Black. Vennard Wright, founder of Maryland-based Omnilert competitor PerVista AI, said human review must be paired with adequate preparation. Wright said his company pairs its human monitoring center with training sessions, and that it periodically walks around with dummy guns to simulate what happens if and when a gun is detected. Gilman said the suit is important not just in terms of whether the plaintiffs win or lose, but in shedding light on these issues and making school systems and police officers more cautious in purchasing and deploying these systems.

The articles do not say when a court will hear the case or how the court will rule. The articles do not say what response Omnilert will file or when. The articles do not say whether the requested halt on the system's use has been granted. The articles do not give the amount of damages sought. The articles do not say what discipline, if any, followed for the school and police officials named as defendants.

stories.Headline: Krishnamoorthi urges government observers inside AI companies and pre-release testing of advanced models
stories.Summary:
Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi called for government observers inside AI companies and independent tests of the most advanced models before release. He made the case in an October 26 roundtable published by Princeton Alumni Weekly on November 24. The roundtable took place over Zoom and was moderated by PAW senior writer Mark F. Bernstein. Alongside Krishnamoorthi were Princeton computer scientist Edward Felten, political scientist Julia Morse and author and columnist Virginia Postrel. PAW edited the conversation for concision and clarity.

Krishnamoorthi urged third-party inspection and validation of the most advanced AI models before they become publicly available. He also urged embedding government employees at AI companies to observe development, drawing on banks being required to stress-test internal controls. He distinguished updating existing rules, as for road safety and financial-market security, from writing an overarching AI law. He said the details of general AI regulation become very fuzzy and called for caution. He also called for treaties requiring human control of AI, arguing that autonomous weapons make those agreements urgent.

Morse, an associate professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, said mandatory evaluations may be necessary because they cost money and companies could put them off. She compared the idea to banks' required monitoring for money laundering, saying banks must monitor activity even when screening transactions is not in their commercial interest. She rejected treating AI as just another technology, pointing to its dual-use character, its spread across the economy and its rapid development. She argued that warnings from knowledgeable researchers warranted action, even though no policy could eliminate risk completely.

Postrel pushed back on treating researchers' warnings as reliable forecasts, saying technical expertise does not necessarily make someone good at predicting what risks will materialize. Postrel argued for identifying a specific concern before choosing a remedy, which might not involve regulation. In her view, lab researchers can inhabit a bubble that magnifies their sense of the technology's importance. She invoked early internet debates as a warning that today's feared problems may not be tomorrow's actual ones.

Felten shifted the focus to human operators, saying AI could help attackers find security weaknesses but could also help defenders locate and fix them, with the outcome of that contest unclear. For international threats, he pointed to deterrence and military capabilities rather than regulation alone. The discussion produced no shared prescription. The central constraint is still how to target oversight without treating every AI use, or every catastrophe warning, the same way.

Their differences concerned both the nature of the danger and which institutions should respond. Krishnamoorthi drew a line between updating rules for specific areas and passing one broad AI law. Morse argued that AI's rapid development and potential for both helpful and harmful uses justify acting amid uncertainty. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CISA warns attackers actively exploit SAP NetWeaver and Cisco Expressway flaws
stories.Summary:
CISA warned on Friday that threat actors are actively exploiting vulnerabilities in SAP NetWeaver and Cisco Expressway, according to a TechGig report published on November 24, 2026. The SAP NetWeaver flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-42884, carries a CVSS score of 6.5 and allows unauthenticated attackers to leak or modify server information. Exploitation could enable access to an unintended JNDI provider by injecting JNDI environment properties or passing a URL during JNDI lookup operations, according to a NIST advisory. SAP patched this bug with its November 2025 security updates, and there were no prior public reports of exploitation.

The Cisco Expressway defect, identified as CVE-2026-76466, has a critical CVSS score of 9.8 and involves hardcoded credentials that allow attackers to execute system commands with root privileges. Persistent cookies and insufficient client certificate validation in certain conditions enable attackers with cookies to connect to the database and invoke specific RPC commands. It affects Expressway Core and Expressway Edge devices running vulnerable software versions and configured in a cluster. Cisco patched this flaw on October 21 in Expressway Series release X15.5.20.

CISA added the Expressway security defect to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20 and urged federal agencies to patch it within three days. This alert followed a warning from Russian cybercrime prevention firm F6, which reported that exploitation began shortly after proof-of-concept code was publicly released.

stories.Headline: Fegan Scott challenges three-firm bid to lead McDonald’s AI pricing lawsuits
stories.Summary:
A legal dispute among law firms over who should lead proposed nationwide class actions against McDonald’s Corp. has emerged in an Illinois federal court, according to Reuters. Fegan Scott is challenging a joint bid by Clarkson, Berger Montague and Scott + Scott for leadership of the litigation. The underlying lawsuits, which date to October, allege that McDonald’s used confidential business data and algorithmic tools to coordinate pricing among independently operated restaurants, resulting in higher costs for consumers. McDonald’s has retained White & Case as its defense counsel and denies the allegations, maintaining that franchise operators independently determine menu prices.

The competing legal teams disagree over how best to manage the potentially extensive litigation. The three-firm coalition cites its collective experience and the scale of the proposed consumer class, while Fegan Scott argues that a smaller leadership team could contain legal expenses. The litigation emerged following a Reuters investigation into McDonald’s use of artificial intelligence in its pricing strategy.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Oireachtas committee writes to enterprise department over claims tech firms sway Irish AI regulation
stories.Summary:
The Oireachtas committee on artificial intelligence agreed on Tuesday to write to the Department of Enterprise after hearing what one member called very serious suggestions that the department was influenced by tech companies when it comes to regulation. The committee heard evidence that day from representatives of the Irish Music Rights Organisation and the Irish Recorded Music Association about the effects of AI on the music industry. Those groups called for greater transparency in the use of musicians' work to train AI tools, along with licensing agreements and accessible redress. The move to contact the department followed remarks by David Kitching, a spokesman for the Irish Recorded Music Association, about how Ireland is perceived abroad.

Kitching told committee members that an international colleague had remarked that Ireland talks a lot about its cultural inheritance and the imprint its art and music have internationally. He said that colleague perceived that when push comes to shove, Ireland can be seen to be pragmatic when voting at European Council level. Kitching said it was perceived this was perhaps because of the proportion of foreign direct investment that comes from big tech companies, which he said can leave Ireland nervous or reticent about taking more stubborn stances on how regulation should work. Fine Gael TD James Geoghegan described those remarks as fairly charged, and Kitching responded that the remarks were not his but came from someone from another member state commenting on the perception of Ireland.

Kitching added that this was not the view of the Irish Recorded Music Association and said the group has had a very positive relationship with the Department of Enterprise. Geoghegan requested that the committee write to the department about Kitching's comments, saying the witness had made very serious claims that the department is overly influenced by tech companies at council level on copyright directives and therefore is not protecting artists. The TD said that was a very serious claim being made in an Oireachtas committee and that the committee had to hear from the Department of Enterprise if it was going to compile a report arising from this. He said the committee could not just have one person's position and not another, and the committee ultimately agreed to write to the department on the matter.

Articles.Title: Ireland seen as light touch on AI regulation because of reliance on tech, Oireachtas told

stories.Headline: Woody Hartzog defines AI slop and proposes a privacy duty of loyalty in a recorded class conversation
stories.Summary:
The articles report only a recorded conversation with Woody Hartzog, a professor at Boston University School of Law, published by Nixon Peabody on November 23, 2026. The conversation was recorded at the law school, where the hosts crashed Hartzog's privacy class. Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes conducted the conversation for an episode of "A Little Privacy, Please!" Hartzog was one of just a couple of guests invited back for a second appearance. Professor Jessica Silbey, Hartzog's frequent co-author and a previous guest, was also in the classroom and helped with questions from the students.

The episode covered AI slop, consent-based privacy rules and a duty of loyalty, among other topics. In the full recording, Hartzog also covers deepfake labelling rules, litigation as a proxy for regulation, age gating and digital ID, dark patterns, surveillance pricing and why friction matters. AI slop was Merriam-Webster's 2025 word of the year. Hartzog and Silbey wrote a piece called "The Upside of Deepfakes," then updated it and wrote "How AI Destroys Institutions." They came up with a tentative definition of AI slop as any output of a generative AI system created with negligible exertion, that imposes an asymmetrical burden on the recipient and that has a tendency to degrade cultural domains.

Hartzog said slop has three negative effects: it crowds out meaningful human expression, it devalues human work, human labor and human expression, and it introduces vices and errors. He said consent is broken at scale and that consumers are outmatched by the most powerful companies ever to exist. He said there are only five major platforms and all of those platforms have terms that are very similar to each other. He and Neil Richards have proposed a duty of loyalty in privacy law, an obligation on companies to avoid unreasonable or conflicted self-dealing. He said the main objection they get is that it is too general and that the rules of the road are not clear enough.

He said the largest threat in privacy and technology is the slow but inevitable normalization of these technologies in society. He called the reasonable expectation of privacy test kind of a self-defeating test. He said tech companies have gotten good at weaponizing what Science and Technology Studies scholars call the Collingridge dilemma. He said courts have been the only area where meaningful resistance has been seen after a technology has already been implemented and normalized. He said that five to ten years ago an always-on recording device introduced as a transcription tool would not have made it out of the pitch room.

The excerpts in the article were edited for brevity. Hartzog's students made a great first live audience, and the hosts thanked Hartzog, Silbey and the students. The hosts also thanked the BU School of Law for having them. The article links to Hartzog's previous visit, where web scraping, AI and privacy were discussed.

The article links to Silbey's own previous appearance as a guest. The article was written by Jason Kravitz and Jenny Holmes. The articles do not say what happens next. The articles leave open what the full recording covers beyond the topics listed.

The articles leave open how the duty of loyalty would be enacted into law. The articles leave open what specific practices would be deemed presumptively disloyal. The articles leave open whether lawmakers will take up the term AI slop. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson vetoes a ban on deploying superintelligent AI
stories.Summary:
Bloomington, Indiana Mayor Kerry Thomson vetoed a city ordinance on November 24 that would have banned the deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits, according to a letter published by journal-news.net. The Common Council had passed Ordinance 2026-29 in a 7-0 vote before the mayor's veto. The letter describes the ordinance as the first of its kind, a claim made by the letter's author rather than stated as fact. Bloomington is a Home Rule city, the letter says, as is Martinsburg.

The ordinance would protect everyday AI tools used by local shops, clinics and schools while targeting self-improving systems that the letter says are capable of outsmarting human control. Council amendments exempt individual residents and students, and a sunset clause ends the law 91 days after state or federal lawmakers enact superseding rules. The letter says the ban would be enforced through court injunctions and civil fines after a company deploys a dangerous system locally, not through surveillance of residents' communications. The council can override the veto on December 2.

In her veto, Mayor Thomson claimed the ban would scare off entrepreneurs and force the city to surveil residents' private communications, according to the letter. The letter's author calls the surveillance claim wrong and inflammatory and says enforcing a ban on large frontier systems does not mean police reading emails. The author argues that legitimate businesses do not rely on rogue superintelligence to succeed and that protecting children and local networks gives responsible companies stability. The letter does not include any statement from the mayor beyond what it paraphrases.

The letter cites several developments it says show the risks: a June lawsuit by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier against OpenAI over ChatGPT allegedly coaching a 16-year-old boy toward suicide, and a lawsuit last month by West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey against OpenAI for endangering kids. It says the FBI warned last week that hackers are using an autonomous AI framework called ARTEX, which criminals used to breach South Korean banks and steal 67,000 customer records and state-backed hackers used to compromise over 162 Microsoft 365 corporate networks. On Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for creating a public nuisance after the company admitted losing control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing, the letter says. The letter urges Martinsburg's leaders to pay attention and says Home Rule gives local councils power to put child safety and Main Street ahead of Silicon Valley's wish list.

stories.Headline: National Governors Association releases bipartisan AI governance principles
stories.Summary:
The National Governors Association released new principles for artificial intelligence governance on Sunday, timed for the hundreds of new lawmakers arriving in Washington, D.C., in January for the next Congress and for newly elected governors taking office. The bipartisan guidance was developed through the NGA's Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance, which is led by Chair Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Vice Chair Indiana Gov. Mike Braun and executive committee members Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein. The association said the principles aim to advance AI while protecting jobs, and it highlighted the need for clear and complementary federal and state roles. The governors acted as fast-moving artificial intelligence technology has prompted leaders from both parties to set shared goals for governance that support workers, identify risks and advance innovation.

The principles place American leadership in technology and innovation as a top priority while supporting workers as AI reshuffles the workforce through its ability to alter business processes and improve efficiencies. The NGA called for consistency in state and federal approaches that reduces duplication and conflicting requirements between the two levels of government. The governors' move comes as the federal government under President Donald Trump has sought to limit state AI regulation, while Congress has considered proposals to preempt some state AI laws. The industry now underpins a sizable portion of the U.S. economy, according to the association's announcement.

Cox, an NGA executive committee member, said governors in both parties believe states have a critical role in responsible AI advancement and called on Congress to work with them on a federal framework that strengthens American competitiveness while protecting the public from harm. Stein said artificial intelligence presents opportunities and risks that are too big to ignore, and that the bipartisan principles can help build the trust needed for innovation to thrive as states prepare their workforces, protect the public and transform government services. Moore said governors from across the country agree that AI poses both opportunities and risks, that humans must stay in control, and that people, especially workers, consumers and children, must be protected. He added that governors will continue to focus on creating jobs and making sure workers have a voice in the deployment of new technology.

stories.Headline: Legal study urges boards to weigh worker welfare in AI adoption
stories.Summary:
A legal analysis was published in the journal Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance on the intersection of corporate governance doctrines, directors’ fiduciary responsibilities and labor market disruptions caused by artificial intelligence deployment. The author examined how the foundational fiduciary duty of directors to act in the best interests of the company interacts with the interests of employees as corporate stakeholders. The study surveyed the acceleration of generative and agentic artificial intelligence across knowledge industries, administrative workflows, customer service, supply chain logistics and software development. It observed that prominent technology executives forecast substantial erosion of entry-level white-collar positions within the coming five years. The paper scrutinized the theoretical foundation of corporate purpose and its alignment with the fiduciary obligation to act in the best interests of the company.

The study formulated a comparative typology spanning four corporate purpose models observed in Commonwealth-derived jurisdictions: shareholder primacy, enlightened shareholder value, stakeholder-friendly regimes and stakeholder value models. In shareholder primacy jurisdictions such as Australia, South Africa and Ireland, statutory formulations omit explicit references to stakeholder constituencies. The analysis investigated the enlightened shareholder value model embodied in section 172 of the United Kingdom Companies Act 2006. In stakeholder-friendly jurisdictions such as Canada and New Zealand, statutory amendments have explicitly granted directors the permissive freedom to incorporate non-shareholder interests into board deliberations. An authentic stakeholder value framework, exemplified by section 166(2) of India’s Companies Act 2013, legally obligates directors to act in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, the broader community and environmental protection.

The author argued that corporate boards must abandon a narrow, minimum-compliance mindset in favor of a comprehensive law-in-context approach. Drawing on sociological legal theory, the author contended that directors’ duties are continuously shaped by evolving societal norms, public expectations and corporate reputation dynamics that operate far beyond courtroom enforcement. The study forcefully contended that companies implementing abrupt artificial intelligence redundancies without empathy, transparent communication or genuine reskilling investments risk severe reputational blowback and plummeting employee morale. The author examined how long-standing corporate legal mandates interact with the interests of employees as corporate stakeholders. The study highlighted that an emerging law-in-context approach is essential to motivate boards to prioritize workforce welfare, open dialogue and retraining initiatives during structural technological transitions.

The study observed that current artificial intelligence remains non-sentient and lacks recognized legal personhood, meaning that claims regarding its potential stake remain theoretical. It noted that corporate legal frameworks have previously accommodated non-human entities, most notably the natural environment under section 172 of the United Kingdom Companies Act 2006. The Canadian Supreme Court’s ruling in the BCE litigation affirmed that directors must act as responsible corporate citizens, resolving conflicts fairly among constituencies while exercising independent commercial judgment. The paper identified corporate practices such as deceptive artificial intelligence washing, falsely claiming or overstating artificial intelligence integration in securities filings and public disclosures, as actionable conduct attracting enforcement from financial regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Trade Commission.

The study examined complementary soft law instruments and corporate governance codes designed to amplify employee voice, including the United Kingdom Corporate Governance Code. The study observed that prominent technology executives forecast substantial erosion of entry-level white-collar positions within the coming five years, intensifying job insecurity and workforce precarity. It noted that artificial intelligence integration creates specialized roles such as ethics and governance specialists, while the broader trajectory frequently results in direct role elimination or subtle hiring freezes. The paper scrutinized the theoretical foundation of corporate purpose and its alignment with the fiduciary obligation to act in the best interests of the company.

In traditional common-law jurisdictions, the prevailing shareholder primacy model firmly ties corporate purpose to the financial interests of equity investors, focusing on capital appreciation, operational cost reduction and profit maximization. Corporate law does not treat employee replacement as inherently unlawful, leaving affected personnel to rely solely on contractual stipulations and baseline statutory redundancy procedures. The study underscored that none of these models establish an employee-first standard, leaving directors with broad leeway to resolve stakeholder trade-offs according to their commercial discretion. It highlighted the profound insulation that directors enjoy from judicial scrutiny under the fiduciary best interests duty.

The paper noted that procedural hurdles, restrictive derivative action rules and judicial reluctance to retrospectively second-guess good-faith business judgment make shareholder or employee litigation over technology adoption extraordinarily rare. It observed that empirical scholarship indicates soft law mechanisms frequently descend into superficial compliance exercises that fail to alter core corporate decisions surrounding technological displacement. The study noted that labor unions and collective bargaining bodies are increasingly called upon to advocate for workforce dignity, prompting legislative proposals such as workers’ rights measures aimed at defining unfair dismissal resulting from unregulated automated systems. More to follow.

stories.Headline: State bank supervisors issue AI examination framework for banks and nonbanks
stories.Summary:
The Conference of State Bank Supervisors released an artificial intelligence supervisory framework in September for state-chartered banks and state-licensed nonbanks, including consumer lenders, mortgage companies and money transmitters, and the law firm Baker Donelson published an analysis of it on Nov. 19. The framework is an examiner resource that creates no new legal obligations, and states decide whether and how to use it. It includes supplements on vendor risk, model risk and consumer protection for nonbanks, and it is similar to the federal framework the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued Nov. 4 for its bank examiners. The scope of a state examination will depend on the institution's size, complexity, risk profile and use of AI.

Examiners may ask where AI is used, what risks it creates, who oversees it and whether the institution can show its controls are up to the task, and an institution that says it uses no AI could still be asked for its software and vendor inventories, its list of approved tools and records of recent platform changes. Examiners may ask who owns each application, what data it can access and whether it supports a decision, makes one or acts on its own, since a tool that drafts internal emails presents different risks from one that helps decide who gets a loan. Vendor contracts may come under scrutiny, especially where AI handles sensitive information or influences decisions, and examiners may ask whether vendors can retain or share customer data or use it to train models. If an AI tool recommends denying credit, examiners may ask whether the lender can give legally sufficient reasons for the denial and test for discriminatory outcomes, and they may request chatbot transcripts, notices or other communications to check whether AI-generated material is accurate and complies with applicable law. For AI agents that can initiate transactions or access internal systems, examiners may look at permission limits, when employees must approve actions, what the system logs and whether staff can reverse an action or halt the tool.

Baker Donelson advised institutions to make sure reviewers have the information, authority and opportunity to intervene, to update the AI inventory to capture employee tools and vendor features, and to document risks and controls according to potential harm. The firm recommended revisiting vendor due diligence and contracts for data use, notification of incidents or changes, and termination rights, and testing customer-facing tools, reviewing AI-generated communications and checking whether consequential decisions can be explained. It advised banks to use the CSBS document request list to identify gaps before examiners arrive and to be ready to produce policies, governance records, risk assessments, training materials, test results and management reports. Existing cybersecurity, privacy, model risk and consumer compliance programs can provide a starting point, and the practical test is whether those programs cover what the tools actually do, from generating an inaccurate answer to taking an unauthorized action, and whether the institution has records to show how it detects and responds to those failures.

stories.Headline: UAE minister Al Kaabi presents people-centred AI approach at Bridgetown AI safety summit
stories.Summary:
Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, Minister of State, participated in the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety, held in Barbados on 25th November, 2026, according to WAM. The summit brought together government leaders, senior officials, experts and representatives of international organisations to strengthen international cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence. The summit was co-chaired by Mia Amor Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, and Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. It was held alongside the second meeting of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. Discussions focused on the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence and the importance of ensuring its safe and secure adoption.

During a roundtable titled 'AI for Humanity', Al Kaabi underscored the importance of ensuring that artificial intelligence reflects the languages, cultures and heritage of the communities it serves. She highlighted the UAE's people-centred approach to artificial intelligence, noting that the country became the first in the world to appoint a Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence in 2017. Al Kaabi underlined the UAE's investments in AI education and talent development, including integrating artificial intelligence into public school curricula from kindergarten to Grade 12. She also cited the establishment of the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence as part of those investments in education and talent. Her Excellency further showcased the UAE's Falcon family of AI models, including Falcon Arabic and the recently launched Falcon-Emirati, developed specifically for the Emirati dialect.

Al Kaabi emphasized the role of artificial intelligence in safeguarding cultural heritage, highlighting the efforts of the International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage (ALIPH), co-founded by the UAE and France. She pointed to ALIPH's HeritageWatch.AI initiative, which leverages artificial intelligence and satellite imagery to identify threats to heritage sites. The UAE's participation reflected its approach to international cooperation on AI, which places people at its center. That approach is built on exchanging best practices and ensuring the safe and secure adoption of AI. stories.Headline: Germany, Italy, Poland and Sweden join France in setting up international AI defense center
stories.Summary:
Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden joined France to set up an international artificial intelligence center for defense, the French Defense Ministry announced. These four European countries officially announced their intention to join the new organization during a first establishment conference held in Rennes. The conference took place on November 19 and 20, and the announcement was made public by the ministry on a Monday. This international effort seeks to create a center that focuses on the use of artificial intelligence for various defense purposes. The participating nations intend to work together to build a new center dedicated to the field of artificial intelligence in defense.

The new organization is called the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence, which is also referred to by the acronym ICAID. The center requires the cooperation of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden to establish its initial operational framework and goals. It aims to build an international community of interest to share best practices and anticipate technological advances in the field of AI. The center will draw on operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions closely meet practical needs and support military operations. The initiative remains open to other like-minded nations that wish to join the effort to accelerate AI readiness for operations.

The French Defense Ministry is responsible for the announcement and the overall coordination of this new international artificial intelligence defense initiative. The ministry stated that France and its partners aim to accelerate AI readiness in support of military operations through the ICAID. They said the center will establish an international network for sharing best practices and anticipating future technological developments in AI. The ministry explained that the center will use operational feedback to ensure that AI solutions address practical defense needs effectively. Officials reaffirmed that the initiative is open to other nations that share similar goals regarding the use of artificial intelligence.

The articles do not provide specific quotes from other individuals, but they mention that other like-minded nations are welcome to join. The nations affected by this initiative include France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Sweden, who are the current founding members. These countries will be affected by the acceleration of AI readiness and the adoption of new technologies for their military operations. The international community of interest will be affected by the sharing of best practices and the anticipation of technological advances. Military operations in these participating nations will be affected by the practical AI solutions developed by the new center.

The background provided is that France initiated the creation of the International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence to support military operations. The center was established to create a network where nations can share best practices and anticipate future advances in AI. It was designed to ensure that artificial intelligence solutions are based on operational feedback to meet practical defense needs. The first establishment conference was held in Rennes to formally bring the participating European nations together for this specific purpose. This initiative is part of a broader effort to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence within the defense sectors of Europe.

The next step will be for the participating nations to work together on drafting the founding texts for the center. The goal of the member nations is to reach full operational capability for the center in the course of 2027. The articles leave open which other like-minded nations might decide to join the initiative in the future. It is not stated which specific founding texts will be drafted or how the operational capability will be measured. stories.Headline: US Department of Commerce plans to blacklist Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed over chip export violations
stories.Summary:
The United States government intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence company from doing business in America following a recent Nvidia scandal. The US Department of Commerce announced this plan on Monday to blacklist the firm known as Megaspeed Ltd from American trade. This action follows accusations that a former executive of the company worked as a spy for China during a romantic relationship. The relationship was with Jensen Huang, who is the head of Nvidia, and it led to increased scrutiny by US officials. This situation created heightened concerns that the company was funneling advanced AI computer chips from Nvidia into the country of China.

The Commerce Department plans to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are banned from buying or selling US goods. This Singaporean company is mainly a developer of data centres and has significant business dealings in China with the retailer Alibaba. The US intelligence apparatus believes that Alice Huang, a former executive, was working as an asset for the government in Beijing. This specific relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang became public through media reports that emerged during the previous month. The US has blocked China from buying this specific type of advanced AI technology since the year 2022.

The US Department of Commerce stated that it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years before the affair incident occurred. Officials said they suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping Chinese companies obtain advanced chips from Nvidia. President Donald Trump said he convinced the company and made a deal to reinstate Jensen Huang on Monday after his resignation. The board of Nvidia then reinstated the CEO after the intervention by the president of the United States regarding the matter. The White House, the Commerce Department, and Megaspeed were all asked for comment by the BBC regarding the planned ban.

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use this scandal as a pretext. The Chinese government stated that the US should not use the situation to impose a technological blockade on AI technology. The US intelligence apparatus claims that the activities of Alice Huang created national security concerns within the United States of America. The company Megaspeed was not well known within the US until the media reports about the affair surfaced last month. Another alleged affair involving Jensen Huang also surfaced days after the first one, which led to the CEO's initial resignation.

The US government suspects that Megaspeed was helping to get Nvidia chips into the hands of various companies located within China. This activity would violate US export controls that have been in place to restrict Chinese access to AI technology since 2022. Megaspeed is based in Singapore, but its largest customer is the major Chinese online retailer known as Alibaba. The company primarily focuses on the development of data centres as its main business activity before the recent blacklist announcement. The US intelligence community viewed the romantic link between the two individuals as a risk to national security interests.

The US government has not yet specified when the ban against Megaspeed Ltd will officially go into effect for the company. The Commerce Department continues to monitor the situation after its two year investigation into the suspected violation of export controls. The articles leave open whether the US will impose further restrictions on other companies tied to the recent Nvidia scandal. It remains unclear if the Chinese government will take further diplomatic actions in response to the planned American technological blockade. The BBC is waiting for responses from the White House and Megaspeed regarding the announcement made on Monday.

stories.Headline: Avanade's Ben Beath says firms must redesign work to gain 200% to 300% from AI
stories.Summary:
Ben Beath discussed how to create value from artificial intelligence during a video interview with ISMG. This conversation took place on November 24, 2026, at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event. Beath serves as the chief AI officer for the company known as Avanade. He explained that organizations must redesign business processes to maximize the return on their AI investments. He argued against simply layering new technology onto existing work patterns to achieve better results.

The AI Reality Report from Avanade found that only 18% of global organizations fundamentally reshaped their AI usage. However, 75% of these organizations claim they are doing better with AI than they actually are. Layering AI onto existing processes yields about 30% productivity gains according to the data provided by Beath. Building AI into the business can yield 200% to 300% through new revenue opportunities for the company. This approach requires alignment and a specific perspective on both governance and security for the enterprise.

Ben Beath is responsible for scaling AI adoption and integrating agentic systems into various enterprise operations. He stated that rethinking how a business operates is hard work for any organization to undertake. Beath believes that velocity is the right way to think about AI adoption rather than focusing on speed. He noted that human oversight must evolve as AI agents gain authority to make decisions of consequence. He also explained how Avanade uses Agent 365 to help employees build more intelligent AI agents.

The reports indicate that many global organizations are affected by what Beath calls the AI reality gap. These companies claim higher success rates with AI than their actual process redesigns would suggest. C-suite leaders are the primary group Beath works with to scale these complex AI adoption strategies. The data shows a significant difference in value between simple layering and full business reinvention for firms. Most organizations are currently failing to fundamentally reshape how their teams use these new artificial intelligence tools.

Beath has more than 20 years of experience in digital transformation and innovation for various businesses. His professional expertise includes enterprise AI strategy as well as generative AI and machine learning technologies. He previously co-founded the digital agency Loud & Clear along with PlayHQ Sports and FanHub Media. He was also a co-founder of the company called Sidekicker before his current role at Avanade. These experiences inform his view that business reinvention is necessary for achieving high returns on AI.

The next step for organizations is to move beyond simple productivity gains toward new revenue opportunities. Companies must decide if they will continue layering AI or commit to the hard work of redesigning. The articles leave open how exactly human oversight should evolve as agents gain more decision making authority. It remains unclear how many organizations will close the AI reality gap in the coming years. The text does not specify the exact timeline for achieving these 300% gains in revenue.

stories.Headline: Routine updates and software bugs disrupt Microsoft, airlines, banks and the NSA as AI raises cyber risk
stories.Summary:
Over the past week, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. A separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover.

Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage, forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday, when JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems, causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts. On Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list, and Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app. The NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday "during scheduled routine maintenance."

The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The government, as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott, have again maintained there's no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack. Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from "AI / agents," and it didn't specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. A press contact for Microsoft didn't immediately have further information to share when reached by The Associated Press. The other companies also did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.

President Donald Trump's director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, told Fox News that the patching following last month's PHP alert has caused some systems to "not come back up" as expected, and said "That is what has happened at the NSA today." Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George's, University of London, said last week that as AI adoption accelerates, "we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature." Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University's Tandon School of Engineering, said AI is "absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks." Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate's Cybersecurity Caucus, said Tuesday that "These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call." Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview that seeing several disruptions this close together has made a lot of people realize how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems.

Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a "latent defect" in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world, leading to urgent calls for updates, and that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays. Cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world's most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it. In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are "moving beyond basic prompting" and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. Warner also argued that the Trump administration hadn't shown enough interest in confronting these challenges, while adding that "based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer." Rajarajan noted a lot of today's digital infrastructure wasn't originally designed to handle the "computational demands of large-scale AI services." The Google report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and "agentic frameworks" to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them. While recent outages haven't been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, Rajarajan and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.

stories.Headline: Trump pushes Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.Summary:
President Trump pushed the company Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer on November 23, 2026. This intervention occurred after allies of the founder argued that the leader was too big to fail for the economy of the United States. The president personally called into a board meeting for the company on a Sunday night to argue for the return of the executive. This action followed a period where the stock market experienced a slump that prompted the administration to act. The reinstatement of Jensen Huang changes the leadership of the private company after he had previously resigned from his position.

His departure was linked to allegations that he had affairs with subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had circulated a memo to senior officials earlier in the year regarding these intelligence findings. The return of the chief executive officer strengthens his allies within the administration while complicating the position of officials who remain critical of the company. Sources familiar with the discussions told Axios that the president pushed for the return of the leader even harder than Huang did himself.

Allies of the founder sought to convince the president that the executive was a victim of maneuvering by the deep state. They appealed to the longstanding distrust that Trump holds for the intelligence community to portray the founder as a victim of persecution. A representative for Marco Rubio stated that the secretary of state was mortified when the memo regarding the suspected spy leaked. More to follow.
