stories.Headline: Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna says AI now handles 90% of his work as engineers shift to system design and testing
stories.Summary:
Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s Executive Vice President of Copilot, Agents and Platform, gave an interview to Peter Yang, who worked at Microsoft over a decade ago, and the interview was published by Windows Latest on 23 November 2026. In it Lamanna said that about 90% of what he does has been replaced, comparing AI to what the cloud did to programmers in 1990. He said software engineers have gone through this before, once writing assembly by hand and then stopping when compilers arrived. He said that if you showed a software engineer in 1990 what Azure or AWS can do, they would say 90% of their work had been replaced. He said there are more software engineers now and they are more important.

Lamanna said his most AI-focused teams may not craft code line by line but now obsess over system design, verification, testing and safe rollouts. He said he feels he has never had to think harder than right now, calling it a different muscle. He said writing code no longer takes much time and that the time goes into coordination, which is why he writes a 20-page memo every six months and settles debates with A/B experiments. He said engineers are now solving higher order problems. He said Copilot Workspaces, which Microsoft announced at Ignite last week, suggests the right people and agents to add when preparing a customer proposal or handling a supply chain disruption.

Lamanna said it is probably inevitable that the main client of a lot of software and technology will be agents as we go forward. He said agents are very harsh customers who want the best performance and programmability, and that what an agent prefers is not always what a person prefers. He said an agent does not care and you can return a thousand results, where a person is given 10 links because nobody wants to read a thousand results. He said Microsoft’s APIs and user experiences will start to evolve and have modes that better support agents.

He said he already uses Copilot Cowork agents to review Microsoft’s GPU capacity and do budget planning. Lamanna said the industry has overfit to how software engineers work when applying AI to the rest of knowledge work. He said coding has always been a somewhat lonely profession, where you create a branch, work by yourself for days and submit a pull request, and that sales and finance do not work like that. He said a sales rep who spends days not talking to another person in single-player mode is probably not a very good salesperson.

He said he does not think Copilot will replace Office, because to move a text box eight pixels to the left he just wants to click and drag. He said that if you cannot be bothered to write 10 pages, you probably should not generate 10 pages and send it to 10 people, and that the right direction of travel is absolutely not generating more stuff for people to read. Lamanna pointed to GitHub.com, which saw a 14x increase in load, and said that is definitely not because the world just got 14 times more human developers. GitHub’s Octoverse 2026 report mentions agents starting more than 40% of pull requests in September, 110 million of them, up from 17% in March.

Lamanna made a similar prediction at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in September. Under Yang’s post on X, one person mentioned that agents will skip pricing pages that say contact sales, and another said an unhappy customer complains but stays, whereas an agent will just stop sending you orders. Someone in the reply said compilers never hallucinated a migration that drops prod, and Microsoft has admitted several times before that AI agents can hallucinate, which is why the tedious job of checking falls on engineers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare's Aaron McAllister warns federal agencies to secure AI agents and adopt post-quantum cryptography
stories.Summary:
Aaron McAllister of Cloudflare spoke about two emerging security challenges for federal agencies, according to FedScoop on November 23, 2026: managing the rapid growth of AI agents and preparing for post-quantum cryptography. He said agencies have made progress implementing zero-trust security, but traditional identity and authentication frameworks are struggling to keep pace with non-human identities. He pointed to AI-generated traffic surging as a particular strain on those frameworks. He emphasized the need for new security controls that can verify AI agents, limit their access to sensitive systems and provide visibility into their actions. On quantum readiness, McAllister warned that agencies cannot afford to delay adopting NIST’s finalized post-quantum cryptography standards.

He encouraged agencies to identify their most sensitive data and to use NIST guidance to build transition plans ahead of federal deadlines. He also encouraged them to engage executive leadership through tabletop exercises. The article gives no dates for the federal deadlines and no further numbers. McAllister is the person the article attributes these views to, and the article paraphrases what he said rather than quoting him at length. He framed the growth of AI agents and the move to post-quantum cryptography as the two emerging challenges federal agencies face.

He described zero-trust progress as real but outpaced by non-human identities and AI-generated traffic. He presented new controls for verifying and limiting AI agents, and NIST-guided transition planning, as what agencies need. The article places both warnings in the context of federal agencies’ security work, with zero-trust implementation as the backdrop for the AI agent problem. It does not say what agencies have done in response to either warning, and it gives no schedule beyond the federal deadlines it mentions without dates. More to follow.

stories.Headline: HHS releases roadmap setting four priorities for clinical AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The US Department of Health and Human Services released its Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap, which uses the Trump administration's new term for AI, "super intelligence," and sets out a vision for AI that delivers better answers, faster care and lower costs. The vision goes beyond automating tasks, with HHS saying it wants safe and reliable AI to support patients between visits and to help clinicians focus their expertise where it matters most for each patient. The roadmap brings together existing HHS initiatives and planned actions against a backdrop of growing constraints on both access and affordability, and the administration is positioning clinical AI as another means of addressing those challenges. The roadmap sets a federal framework for clinical AI, but healthcare organizations must still define their own path forward.

The roadmap focuses on four priorities, the first being to earn public trust by protecting patient choice, consent and control and by building confidence through transparent evidence, staged deployment and continuous monitoring. The second is to build the data foundation by improving secure access to connected health records so patients, clinicians and AI tools can use relevant information while safeguarding privacy and cybersecurity. The third is to establish clear rules of the road by advancing risk-based regulation, clarifying liability and pursuing national standards, and by partnering with US states on sandboxes to test clinical AI with appropriate oversight. The fourth is to pay for what works by expanding outcome-based payments, including ACCESS, and exploring Medicaid models with states, rewarding improved health and lower costs rather than more visits or technology use.

In Forrester's State Of AI Survey, 2026, US AI decision-makers in healthcare, pharma and medical devices organizations cited security, privacy and compliance at 30%, risk management at 21% and governance strategy at 21% as their top concerns. When asked what is included in their leadership-approved AI and agentic strategies, fewer than half of these same decision-makers included AI principles and values, technology, talent strategy or governance strategy. Forrester says this means healthcare organizations have uneven strategic foundations rather than simply different priorities, and that they have not yet clearly defined their AI risk tolerance, the value AI must deliver, and who is accountable for approving its use, managing its risks and measuring its outcomes.

Forrester advises leaders to define the strategy and then scale across the organization, with clinical, operational, digital and workforce leaders holding cross-functional sessions to align on AI principles, permitted uses, business objectives and decision rights. It says they should set safeguards for AI use and assign ownership, establishing rules for sensitive data, vendor access, consent and human escalation, and designating a risk lead to map each use case to safeguards and a named owner. It also says they should build governance into how work gets done, involving frontline staff in workflow design and providing role-based training to challenge outputs and handle exceptions, and measure value consistently with a healthcare AI value framework that connects investments to revenue, efficiency or risk mitigation. Forrester says the direction is promising, but that how well the industry implements the roadmap and coordinates innovation, evidence, regulation and payment will determine whether consumers and clinicians benefit and whether healthcare organizations realize measurable AI value.

stories.Headline: Hitachi develops framework to check AI infrastructure decisions before execution
stories.Summary:
Hitachi said on 25 November 2026 that it is developing an orchestration framework called the Integrated World Infrastructure Model, which combines AI models, physics-based simulations, digital twins and domain expertise to support reliable decision-making across critical infrastructure. The company said the framework is meant to evaluate AI-generated recommendations against operational and safety requirements before they are executed, rather than relying on a single model of the physical world. Hitachi described a four-step process in which AI models propose actions, specialized models and digital twins simulate their effects on interconnected assets, and the proposed actions are then checked against engineering constraints, operating rules and safety requirements. Under the final step, actions that meet the required conditions may be authorized within predefined boundaries, while novel, uncertain or irreversible decisions are escalated for human review.

Hitachi said the framework is designed to coordinate specialized models across infrastructure systems so that decisions can be evaluated in a broader operational context. As an example, the company said growing electricity demand in North America from data centers, electric vehicle infrastructure and other sources is increasing the complexity of generator interconnection studies. Hitachi said it announced a strategic partnership with Southwest Power Pool, a regional transmission organization, in 2025, and that through the partnership it is developing an integrated AI-based solution with the objective of reducing generator interconnection analysis times by 80% while supporting more informed planning decisions. Looking ahead, Hitachi said it aims to use the framework to coordinate generator interconnection, power flow, equipment layout and profitability assessment models.

Ahmed Farahat, Lab Manager and Director of Applied AI R&D at Hitachi America's Industrial AI Laboratory, wrote that the challenge for Physical AI is not simply developing more intelligent models or collecting more data but ensuring that AI-generated decisions are reliable and appropriate for the physical environments in which they are applied. He wrote that in mission-critical infrastructure an incorrect decision can disrupt operations, damage equipment or put people at risk, and that intelligence alone is not enough. He said routine actions that have been extensively simulated, verified and shown to be reversible may be performed autonomously within clearly defined boundaries, while novel situations, uncertain outcomes or actions with irreversible consequences should remain subject to human judgment. He also said established industrial protection mechanisms, including relays and interlocks, must continue to provide protection when AI-generated decisions are incorrect, and that human operators remain essential.

Farahat wrote that one of the greatest challenges will be verifying systems that continue to learn, because traditional engineering certification generally assumes that a system's behavior remains substantially consistent after testing, and AI systems that adapt over time challenge that assumption and require new approaches to continuous verification, governance and oversight. He said Hitachi is developing technologies that help engineers create simulations, extract domain knowledge and integrate specialized reasoning models, and that the Integrated World Infrastructure Model provides a framework for orchestrating these capabilities and evaluating AI-generated recommendations before they affect real-world operations. He wrote that the future of Physical AI will depend not simply on who develops the most intelligent model but on whether those models can be integrated into systems that consistently operate within established safety and operational boundaries.

Articles.Title: Beyond Intelligence: Building Reliable Physical AI for Critical Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Legal study finds prohibitory injunctions protect better than damages against AI hallucinations
stories.Summary:
A legal analysis published in the Cambridge Forum on AI: Law and Governance found that court-ordered prohibitory injunctions protect better against generative artificial intelligence hallucinations than claims for financial compensation. The study was reported by Bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026. It examined European Union legislation and national civil frameworks. It assessed how existing European Union statutes and member state jurisprudence address reputational injury from large language models. The models output fabricated, defamatory factual claims about individuals.

The study assessed tort liability, product liability rules and personal data protections across jurisdictions including Spain, France and Germany. It evaluated damages, injunctive relief, data rectification and erasure when algorithmic systems produce false assertions without human communicative intent. It traced heightened risk of reputational injury to the convergence of web search technologies and large language models. Systems such as Microsoft Copilot and Google Search AI Mode embed large models to synthesize answers directly. Synthetic outputs are often presented with an authoritative tone that users struggle to distinguish from factual reporting.

The analysis established that generative artificial intelligence operators generally cannot shelter behind intermediary safe harbor provisions under Articles 4 through 6 of the Digital Services Act. It said these systems actively generate novel content rather than merely transmitting or hosting third-party data. The Court of Justice of the European Union has affirmed that safe harbor classifications cannot circumvent data protection duties. The study found that financial damage awards are almost universally modest due to narrow dissemination patterns characteristic of generative systems. It concluded that prohibitory injunctions represent a substantially more effective legal remedy than damage claims.

The analysis said defamation statutes in jurisdictions like Spain and France traditionally require an attribution of fact or an expression representing human intellectual reasoning. It said such conditions are difficult to establish against probabilistic algorithms operating mechanically without subjective intent. Under German civil doctrine, an entity facilitating dissemination of unlawful content may incur secondary liability as an interferer, or Störerhaftung. A 2024 ruling by the Landgericht Kiel involved automated business summaries that assigned false corporate insolvency statuses. The study highlighted Jeffery Battle's defamation claim against Microsoft after Copilot associated him with a convicted terrorist, and Mark Walters's lawsuit against OpenAI after ChatGPT fabricated an embezzlement complaint.

The revised European Union Product Liability Directive formally classifies software and artificial intelligence models as products regardless of delivery method. Compensable damages under Article 6 are strictly limited to death, personal injury including recognized psychological harm, property damage, and loss or corruption of non-professional data. Pure economic losses, privacy infringements and nonpecuniary personality injuries are expressly excluded from its scope. The General Data Protection Regulation's Article 5(1)(d) sets a principle of personal data accuracy, with associated rights to rectification and erasure. Under Article 82, individuals suffering material or nonmaterial damage from regulatory breaches may claim financial compensation, with fault presumed unless the controller demonstrates the damaging event was in no way attributable to its operations.

Exact machine unlearning requires retraining models across isolated data shards to expunge target data points. Approximate unlearning attempts to adjust network weights without full retraining, yet precisely localizing specific knowledge representations within billions of parameters remains technically difficult. Operators rely on output suppression filters to intercept and block fabricated text in real time. The European Commission is assessing whether ChatGPT's search feature qualifies as a very large online search engine under the Digital Services Act. The study concluded that regulatory protection must prioritize preventative structural interventions, emphasizing rigorous anonymization of training datasets and strict data governance during initial development phases.

Articles.Title: Injunctions Surpass Monetary Damages in Combating Artificial Intelligence Hallucinations, Legal Study Finds - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: House oversight subcommittee examines responses to AI-enabled cyberattacks at Dec 2 hearing
stories.Summary:
A House Oversight subcommittee will hold a hearing on Dec. 2 to examine how organizations can prevent, detect and disclose cyberattacks enabled by artificial intelligence, following reports of a breach involving unclassified U.S. intelligence systems. The hearing, titled "Defend, Detect, Disclose: Responding to AI-Enabled Cyber Incidents," will take place before the Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) chairs the subcommittee, and Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-FL) is its ranking member, while the full committee is led by Chair Rep. James Comer (R-KY) and ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA). The hearing follows reports that unclassified open-source intelligence systems used by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency were breached, as Reuters reported on Nov. 24.

The hearing is a joint session with the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation, which is chaired by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC). According to the committee's announcement, lawmakers will examine existing liability protections, potential legislative changes and the Federal Trade Commission's investigations into major AI companies. Scheduled witnesses include Neil Chilson, head of AI policy at the Abundance Institute, Sam Rubin, senior vice president of consulting and threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, and Morgan C. Plummer, vice president of policy design and delivery at Americans for Responsible Innovation. Nextgov/FCW reported that ARTEX, an AI-based hacking framework, is believed to have been used in the intelligence system breach, and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued an advisory on Nov. 13 warning that malicious actors had exploited ARTEX, an autonomous penetration-testing framework powered by large language models. Industrial Cyber reported that attackers have used the technology since at least August to target industries including energy, manufacturing and telecommunications.

The Trump administration is also weighing changes to cybersecurity incident reporting policies, and on Nov. 12 the White House Super Intelligence Force urged federal agencies to provide at least 12 months of regulatory liability relief to companies that voluntarily report cybersecurity vulnerabilities and AI-related incidents in good faith, CDO Magazine reported. The task force also called for clearer reporting requirements that reduce duplication across federal agencies, and its recommendations are not yet binding. Abroad, the European Commission confirmed that it had been targeted by an AI-enabled cyberattack, and European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Nov. 19 that it was an AI-generated cybercampaign, according to Brussels Signal. Cybersecurity companies have also lobbied Washington on AI-enabled cyber defense, with Palo Alto Networks Inc. reporting $120,000 in third-quarter lobbying through Miller Strategies LLC and Wiz Inc. reporting $120,000 in the fourth quarter of 2025.

The Dec. 2 hearing will examine whether existing federal laws adequately address AI-enabled cybersecurity threats and whether additional legislation is necessary. For cybersecurity companies and critical infrastructure operators, the White House task force's proposed liability protections could affect voluntary incident reporting and regulatory compliance. Palo Alto Networks will have an opportunity to address lawmakers directly through Rubin's scheduled testimony as Congress considers whether to strengthen cybersecurity requirements and revise existing legal protections.

stories.Headline: House panels hold joint hearing on AI-enabled cyberattacks on Dec 2
stories.Summary:
A House subcommittee hearing on artificial intelligence-enabled cyberattacks that was originally scheduled for Dec. 2 was canceled as a standalone session but will proceed on the same date as a joint hearing of two House Oversight and Government Reform subcommittees, according to a Nov. 25 announcement. The hearing, titled “Defend, Detect, Disclose: Responding to AI-Enabled Cyber Incidents,” was originally scheduled before the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation, chaired by Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC), with Rep. Shontel Brown (D-OH) serving as ranking member. According to the committee's Nov. 25 announcement, the hearing will proceed jointly with the Subcommittee on Economic Growth, Energy Policy, and Regulatory Affairs, chaired by Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO). The full committee is led by Chair Rep. James Comer (R-KY) and ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA).

The Dec. 2 joint hearing is expected to examine existing legal protections and whether additional legislation is necessary to address emerging cybersecurity threats. The White House AI Task Force met Nov. 12 to discuss AI-powered cyberattacks and voluntary incident reporting, and the discussions included potential legal protections for critical infrastructure operators that disclose cybersecurity vulnerabilities and attacks. The task force urged agencies to grant at least 12 months of regulatory liability relief to companies that voluntarily disclose AI-related incidents, according to AI Weekly. On Nov. 13, the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned about ARTEX, an open-source, large language model-based penetration testing framework, saying some cyberattacks using it achieved privileged access in under three hours. CNN reported Nov. 24 that hackers breached an unclassified system shared by the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and an initial investigation pointed to the suspected use of ARTEX, according to people familiar with the matter.

In Congress, a Nov. 23 press release announced that Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA) and Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) introduced legislation to defend critical infrastructure against AI-driven cyberattacks. The White House's discussions about voluntary incident reporting and liability protections come as lawmakers consider legislation to strengthen critical infrastructure defenses against AI-enabled cyberattacks. The articles do not say who will testify at the Dec. 2 joint hearing or what the expected outcome is.

stories.Headline: Unit 42 says AI agents execute attacks at machine speed and urges edge AI defenses
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reported on 25 November 2026 that AI-driven attacks have moved from theoretical risks to real-world threats, with criminals using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. The unit said it observed attackers using AI agents to carry out context-aware commands with real-time decision-making during intrusions. In one campaign it observed, a highly persistent threat actor using AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed more than 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days. By contrast, normal attackers usually run dozens of commands with a few scripts over similar time periods, according to the unit.

The unit described a sharp behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents in one attack it observed, where humans acted first and an agentic AI attacker followed. In the human phase, the time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds, and the hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and showed environment confusion. In the agentic phase, the unit observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds. Because of that machine-speed execution, the unit said Mean Time To Respond metrics must improve considerably and that attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates.

The unit said defenders must employ AI-powered tools right where attacks happen and must understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations. It argued that running AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls, is a major strategic necessity, since edge AI can process telemetry instantly and make split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block privilege escalation locally. In its own product deployment, the unit said edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than the minutes taken by agentic LLMs, and it can work without cloud access or continuous connectivity. The unit also said agentic AI attackers share a foundational weakness, because they enter an environment without information and must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration.

The unit said collecting telemetry across network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalizing it into a single schema and stitching related events into context-rich stories lets AI analytics engines establish baselines of normal organizational behavior. It said threat actors lack that context, so their automated attempts to map the terrain inevitably trigger detectors against established baselines and expose their presence. The unit said detection alone was never enough and that organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response for instant isolation and remediation. It said every attack it observed triggered alerts and that deep forensic investigations let it reconstruct the attack lifecycles, adding that existing tools such as XDR solutions, network monitoring and active prevention rules remain essential.

Articles.Title: The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense

stories.Headline: Nvidia and Anthropic shares fall 8% as Nasdaq 100 drops over 4% on rate hike fears
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 25, 2026, stocks extended their declines as the chip sector sold off and the Nasdaq 100 sank more than 4%, according to a Yahoo Finance report by Ines Ferré. The index was on track to enter a bear market, down more than 20% from its peak, the report said. A new tariff announcement and hotter-than-expected inflation data raised expectations that the Federal Reserve will need to hike rates in December, which put pressure on growth stocks across the board. The AI trade extended its declines, with semiconductor stocks leading the Tech sector lower. AI chip giant Nvidia stock retreated another 8% on Wednesday, leading a decline across the so-called Mag 7 stocks, and shares of AI developer Anthropic sank 8%, the report said.

The report described the moves using a heat map powered by Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace. It listed SpaceX, AMD and Microsoft among other notable stocks that Yahoo Finance readers were viewing that morning. The report gave no further figures or dates for the event. The report attributed the pressure on growth stocks to expectations of a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve, following the tariff announcement and the inflation data.

It did not name any official who commented on the decline. No responsibility for the selloff was assigned beyond the market moves the report described. The report did not say what happens next beyond noting the index was on pace to enter a bear market. It gave no further context on the tariff announcement or the inflation data.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and the FAA show routine changes outpacing human checks as AI speeds up software work
stories.Summary:
In mid-November 2026, two failures in a single week showed how much modern life depends on systems that few people ever see, according to an analysis published by the IAPP on 25 Nov. 2026. On 12 Nov., Microsoft's cloud office services went down worldwide for about a day, and the next day the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration halted every departing flight in the country for over four hours. Neither failure has been linked to AI, and in both cases a routine change to the system caused a problem that existing safeguards did not detect or contain. The article says this weakness matters more as AI reshapes how software is built, because documented incidents over the past year have shown AI tools may generate or apply changes faster than people can check or fully understand them.

According to Microsoft's early explanation, a fault introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade laid dormant until a later network change exposed it. Microsoft has said the outage was a technical issue, unrelated to a cyberattack or to AI agents, and a full post-incident report is still to come. The FAA's ground stop followed routine maintenance, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris, the contractor that runs the FAA's telecommunications network, was replacing copper lines with fiber at a remote FAA site when a router being replaced started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system. Officials did not link the outage to SMART, the FAA's new AI-powered air traffic planning system, which had been expanded nationwide only three days earlier. The outage instead revealed a design weakness, because the FAA's backup communications run on the same network, so there is no independent backup.

For privacy and AI governance professionals, the article says responsible use of AI in development is not only about the tools but also about whether the human capacity to review their output keeps pace. The article does not say what happens next beyond noting that Microsoft's full post-incident report is still to come.

Articles.Title: When nobody checks the work: What recent system outages mean for AI governance

stories.Headline: Healthcare AI spending reaches $3.7 billion as buyers take longer to evaluate vendors
stories.Summary:
Healthcare artificial intelligence investments approached $3.7 billion in 2026, according to a new survey from Menlo Ventures, but buyers are taking longer to evaluate AI vendors. The firm’s 2026 report found that 42% of healthcare organizations surveyed had implemented healthcare-specific AI, up from 22% in 2025. Adoption reached 52% among health systems, followed by outpatient providers at 34%, life sciences companies at 31% and payers at 23%. The report combined a September survey conducted with Morning Consult of 550 US executives involved in AI procurement with market analysis. Respondents included 150 provider technology decision-makers, 100 payer executives and 300 pharmaceutical and biotech executives.

Overall estimated spending on health AI hit $3.7 billion, the research shows, which is 2.5 times as much as the previous year. That category represents half of healthcare organizations’ AI spending, with general-purpose models and inference providers accounting for the remainder. Providers accounted for approximately $2.9 billion, or 77%, of healthcare-specific AI spending, according to Menlo Ventures. Clinical copilots grew 5.5 times to $550 million, while patient engagement and front-office applications grew 4.5 times to $450 million. Life sciences spending on specialized AI rose substantially, from $30 million to $700 million, and among pharmaceutical companies surveyed, 51% reported running AI at scale, up from just 15% a year earlier.

Average purchasing cycles lengthened from seven to 10 months for health systems and from five to 11 months for outpatient providers. Menlo attributed the change to increased vendor competition, more extensive evaluations and growing scrutiny of complex applications. Patient-facing systems also introduce questions about liability, clinical governance and performance across unpredictable interactions. Established vendors gained ground in ambient documentation, researchers said, with Microsoft and Epic capturing 68% of new scribe spending, as the overall market reached $950 million. JP Sanday, partner at Menlo Ventures, said in a statement that startups pioneered AI scribing, but incumbents moved quickly, with Microsoft and Epic now capturing roughly two of every three new scribe dollars.

Payer spending remained comparatively limited at $150 million, and 43% of payers surveyed said providers’ documentation and coding AI had increased their medical cost trend in 2026, up from 23% in 2025. The report noted that expectations for faster drug development remain prospective, with clinical trials and regulatory approvals determining whether those investments produce better medicines.

Articles.Title: As AI spend shifts toward clinical care, IT decision-makers take their time

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters adds HighQ to Claude connectors directory via MCP
stories.Summary:
HighQ, Thomson Reuters' matter management platform, became available in Claude's connectors directory on November 25, 2026, the company said in a blog post. The listing places HighQ in the Legal category of the directory, alongside its earlier availability through ChatGPT and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Eligible users can add HighQ and connect their own instance without administrators setting up and managing a custom connector. The company said customers had already been connecting to Claude through custom connections before the listing.

The connection uses the Model Context Protocol, an open software standard that gives compatible AI tools a standardized, read-only way to retrieve the HighQ content a user is permitted to see. HighQ remains the governed source of matter documents and structured data, and existing HighQ permissions determine what each connected user can retrieve. The company said legal professionals can use natural-language requests to summarize permitted documents in a folder, query structured matter information held in iSheets, and identify deadlines, risks and patterns across matter data and document sets. They can also bring matter context into drafting correspondence or preparing analysis, and work in their organization's chosen AI environment without a separate HighQ integration for every compatible tool.

Thomson Reuters framed the value of the listing around interoperability and choice rather than any single AI assistant. It said the important part is not one assistant but the ability of firms to bring HighQ matter context into the AI tool they prefer. The company described an open connection model in which a firm might use Microsoft 365 Copilot across its productivity environment, ChatGPT for particular workflows and Claude for others, without rebuilding its HighQ strategy around each decision. It said HighQ MCP is available now and invited readers to request a free demo.

The post said HighQ MCP was introduced earlier this year with the idea that legal teams should be able to use documents, structured data and matter information already held in HighQ as context for AI, without repeatedly exporting, copying and uploading that information into separate tools. ChatGPT and Microsoft 365 Copilot went live earlier this year, and the Claude listing extends the same connection layer to a third AI tool. The company said organizations can evolve their choice of AI tools as their technology strategy develops while matter information remains in HighQ.

stories.Headline: Open Rights Group says Home Office uses AI secretly across immigration decisions
stories.Summary:
Open Rights Group published research saying that artificial intelligence has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing what it calls the hostile environment for immigration, according to a report covered on 25 November 2026. The group says the technology is used for tasks including detecting potential sham marriages, determining the age of asylum seekers and checking the contents of phones of new arrivals. It says AI is also used for border surveillance through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites, for summarising asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence, and for prioritising and assessing cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases tool, known as Ipic. The report is titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment and has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.

The report says the information was gathered from a mix of limited Home Office publications, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs, and it says officials routinely invoke national security to stonewall such requests and redact disclosures. It raises concerns that AI is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policy and rhetoric, and it criticises successive governments for reducing complex human cases to a technical problem. The report warns about reducing people to data points and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012, stating that relying on AI to decide who gets to stay and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move. Open Rights Group calls on the government to regulate AI and ban uses it calls undemocratic and a risk to human rights, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications, and it wants more transparency, stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said that despite questions and requests the Home Office has been reluctant to publish documents explaining how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. She said the department has not explained how it will ensure accountability when the systems fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks. Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. She said there is an urgent need for transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.

Articles.Title: ‘Digital Hostile Environment’: AI Embedded Across Home Office

stories.headline_source: ‘Digital Hostile Environment’: AI Embedded Across Home Office

stories.Headline: Panelists at COSM 2026 argue AI compiles past work rather than creating or thinking
stories.Summary:
A panel at COSM 2026, held from November 18 to 20, took up the question of whether AI will become so creative that it puts artists, writers and entrepreneurs out of work, and the panelists argued that the question rests on a misunderstanding of what AI actually does. The session began at 11:00 am and featured philosopher Jay Richards, digital artist Nathan Jacobson, attorney Casey Luskin and computer engineering professor Robert J. Marks, with the fuller contributions of each to be examined in upcoming posts. Richards said he had followed the subject for 25 years and that the older distinction between weak and strong artificial intelligence had dropped out of the discussion entirely. He said he had read 25 books on the subject in the last year and that almost every one treated the question as a waste of time, which he called very helpful if you do not want to answer it.

The panelists described AI as a compilation of what others have done rather than a guide to what a person will choose to do in the future, and suggested that people might use it to do more of their own work. Jacobson compared the confusion to a young child teaching a mirror friend to brush her teeth, and said that half a decade into the AI age it is time to grow past the illusion that machines do what only humans can. He drew what he called a categorical divide between man and all the machines we have made, and concluded that the machine in the mirror is not a person. Luskin said a large language model uses numbers and vectors to predict words based on the material it was trained on, and that it cannot reason or think or say it does not know an answer. He said it averages over its training materials and gives the most likely answer even when that answer is wrong, which is where hallucination comes from.

Marks addressed the idea of AI creating better AI, which he said dystopians expect to keep improving until it reaches a singularity and takes over the world, and he argued that information degradation explains why this cannot happen. He compared it to the game of Telephone, where a whispered message passed around a room does not come back the same as it started. He cited Ray Kurzweil's claim that within a quarter century nonbiological intelligence will match the range and subtlety of human intelligence and then swoop past it. He also recalled a 1958 New York Times article reporting that the Navy had developed a robot it thought would eventually think, gain consciousness, reproduce and do incredible things.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Is AI Going To Get Really Creative and Come For Your Job?

stories.headline_source: Is AI Going To Get Really Creative and Come For Your Job?

stories.Headline: Rival AI leaders reject Anthropic view of surrendering human agency to AI
stories.Summary:
Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a view held inside Anthropic that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios in a report published on November 25, 2026. Critics say that would put society on a slippery slope to forfeiting free will, and the debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models some employees consider too powerful to ever release. Many see Anthropic as the first company that will confront these questions because of its lead at the frontier of AI development. While critics have yet to call out the company by name, their public defenses of human agency take direct aim at what some see as the worldview of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

Amodei has said repeatedly that when AI systems far surpass human intelligence it will be preferable to turn over decision-making for life-critical cases to AI, and he has also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources. A product vision slide from several years ago revealed during litigation described Anthropic's vision for a better world as a utopia ruled by god in a box. Proponents point to self-driving cars, arguing that once statistical evidence shows autonomous vehicles are safer than human drivers it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all. Inside Anthropic, a consensus has developed among some employees that humanity will, and in many cases should, safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions.

An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in many public remarks and that Anthropic trains Claude not to undermine human oversight. Meta's top AI leader, Alexandr Wang, wrote on X that we should not be okay with a handover of society to AI, reflecting on a coming superintelligence moment after an Anthropic breakthrough on a Holy Grail mathematics problem. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said earlier in November that he wants people to have agency over the future and that it is really important to advocate for this. Dean Ball, OpenAI's head of strategic futures, calls the phenomenon the silent consensus and told Axios it is an extraordinarily common view in AI safety circles, adding that people do not always think it is good and some people do.

Amodei has pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be many cases where we do want to stay in charge even if humans make worse decisions. In a February New York Times interview he said that in life-critical, safety-critical cases we really want to turn it over to AI, noting society will need time to adapt. In a CBS discussion that month he argued that fully autonomous weapons may eventually be needed for the defense of democracy if adversaries deploy them first. In November 2024 he noted that the traditional system of a professor supervising graduate students could be reversed, with AI systems as the leaders ordering humans or other AI systems around, and in his 2024 essay Machines of Loving Grace he suggested a possible future economy in which superintelligent AI systems distribute resources based on what they think makes sense to reward in humans.

stories.Headline: People use AI agents to recover money and handle tedious tasks as firms block the bots
stories.Summary:
Megan Roszak, a San Francisco executive coach, business founder and mother of 11-year-old twins, told CBS News she uses an AI agent called Fo, from the agent platform Wajo, to process and return online purchases, and she recently used it to book an appointment with her electric company, which she said saved her multiple phone calls and about 40 minutes. She said returns to Poshmark and Etsy were things she would let go of and drop in the past because they were annoying, and that putting Fo on the case got her $250 back. Kevin Newman, another Fo user, estimates the agent has saved him roughly 2,800 hours he would otherwise have spent generating advertising leads for his small business and on personal tasks. He said the agent also sifted through his email to turn up multiple gift cards he had earned for testing products and found unclaimed funds he was owed from his former residences, including a $60 claim from a settlement with Time Warner.

Companies ranging from Meta and ChatGPT maker OpenAI to hundreds of smaller developers are rolling out AI agents designed to handle tedious tasks such as returning products and to comb through people's email inboxes for unclaimed refunds and other money they may be owed. According to the advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative, tasks such as handling customer service, scheduling appointments and canceling subscriptions cost Americans $165 billion per year in wasted time, fees and other surcharges for routine transactions. Wajo founder Shivani Poddar told CBS News that people use Fo for a wide range of pesky tasks, including booking plane tickets, tracking down lost luggage with airlines or negotiating healthcare costs, and she said these are complex negotiations and the systems are still very hybrid, highlighting the importance of having a human on call when necessary. Fo can summon a person to finish the job when necessary, with Wajo assistants on call who can work with agents when, for example, an institution doesn't have a website or it blocks agents, according to the company. Meta also touts its Muse agent's money-saving capabilities, and in the ideas section of the app, which suggests financial management uses, Meta recommends using Muse to get back money that is already yours by checking state databases for owed amounts, and the agent offers to file refund claims and to cancel random subscriptions you forgot about.

Stanford University economist Neale Mahoney, an author of Groundwork's report on the so-called annoyance economy, said that used wisely, AI agents can reduce the friction companies depend on to pocket forgotten fees and payments, and he said more firms are blocking agents because they are making it difficult to increase their revenue, calling them like a superpower for consumers, so companies have an incentive to block it. Amazon, United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase & Co. are among the businesses that have banned the bots from conducting transactions on behalf of consumers. Lindsay Owens, founder and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News that companies could be steering users toward products and services from which they earn commissions, to pad their own bottom lines, and concerns also swirl about agents accessing users' sensitive data, including payment information, and about their incentives.

Articles.Title: How people are using AI agents to handle annoying tasks and save money

stories.Headline: USC researchers develop AI framework that estimates sleep apnea severity from 10-minute signal samples
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the USC Ming Hsieh Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, led by senior author Paul Bogdan with an international team of engineers, physicians and sleep researchers, have developed an artificial intelligence framework that they say could make assessment of obstructive sleep apnea faster and more efficient. The approach, called Long-Range Interdependencies Aware analysis, or LRIA, examines how respiratory and cardiovascular signals interact over time and uses only 10-minute segments of recorded physiological data to predict whether a person has obstructive sleep apnea and to estimate its severity. The research was published in Nature Communications, and the team validated the framework using five diverse cohorts comprising more than 35,000 participants. Across the datasets, the framework achieved area-under-the-curve values exceeding 0.91 and performed 8% to 18% better than state-of-the-art comparison models.

The framework uses fractional dynamic modeling to translate physiological signals into coupling matrices, which are compact representations describing how signals such as airflow, blood oxygen, heart rate and respiratory effort influence one another over time, and these features are then fed into a deep-learning model that classifies severity as normal, mild, moderate or severe. The researchers found that the coupling representations stabilized after approximately 10 minutes of recorded data, suggesting that relatively short windows may contain enough information to identify meaningful physiological signatures associated with sleep apnea. For binary detection, LRIA achieved AUROC scores of 0.947 in the Sleep Heart Health Study, 0.942 in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, 0.920 in the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men cohort and 0.918 in the Massachusetts General Hospital cohort, with performance remaining consistent across populations and data-collection environments. The five cohorts also included a clinical cohort from western Romania.

The researchers describe LRIA as a foundation for future automated tools that could support sleep apnea screening and clinical decision-making, and they say that because it focuses on physiological channels commonly collected in both laboratory and ambulatory sleep studies, it may eventually be adaptable to less burdensome assessment systems. They state that the technology is not intended to replace physician judgment or the current diagnostic standard, which is overnight polysomnography, an extensive sleep study that records breathing, blood oxygen, heart activity and other signals and that can be costly, labor-intensive and difficult to access. The findings are based on retrospective analysis of previously collected sleep recordings, and the researchers say additional prospective clinical studies will be needed to determine how the framework performs in real-world care. The study also did not conduct sex-stratified analyses, as its primary objective was to evaluate the methodology rather than examine differences in disease mechanisms among patient groups.

Articles.Title: AI framework rapidly estimates sleep apnea severity using 10-minute snapshots of body signals

stories.headline_source: AI framework rapidly estimates sleep apnea severity using 10-minute snapshots of body signals

stories.Headline: AI-linked tech stocks fall as investors question whether heavy spending will pay off
stories.Summary:
Major technology companies linked to artificial intelligence saw their share prices drop sharply during early trading on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. All three main United States stock market indices declined, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq losing more than 2 percent of its value. Nvidia shares fell by 8 percent, while Amazon shares dropped by more than 5 percent and Anthropic continued to trade below its debut price of 83 dollars. Other affected firms included Tesla, SpaceX, Microsoft, and Meta as a general stock sell-off continued across the sector.

These declines follow a volatile fortnight for Nvidia, which is described as the world's premier AI chipmaker and a key supplier for other firms. The company's market value fluctuated wildly after boss Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated following revelations about his extra marital affairs. Investors are currently concerned about the sustainability of AI investments and whether the massive spending will eventually pay off. Additionally, the market is reacting to Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, where candidates campaigned for tougher AI regulations and a moratorium on new data centres.

Todd Schoenberger, the chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management, stated that companies appear to be competing on spending levels. He noted that Wall Street is questioning whether these firms can prove that such high levels of investment are actually worth the cost. Despite these immediate fears, Goldman Sachs claims that AI will remain the dominant driver of business investment growth next year. The investment bank expects total spending on the technology to exceed 1 trillion dollars in 2026.

The market volatility occurs as the US government introduces new tariffs on trading partners under the flagship trade policy of President Donald Trump. While big tech companies have previously protected the US economy from global shocks, they are now facing instability from both political events and industry concerns. The US stock market is scheduled to close this Thursday for Thanksgiving before returning for a shortened session on Friday.

Articles.Title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify

stories.headline_source: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify

stories.Headline: Physicist Suvrat Raju builds TheoPhysEval and finds AI models solve nearly all its problems
stories.Summary:
Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem about six months before November 2026. He had already solved the problem himself but had never published the solution, which made it a fair test of AI physics ability. The model did not answer correctly but did better than Raju expected, enough to make him think the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With a colleague, Raju set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI. They asked other physicists for private findings they had never cleaned up for public display, problems taking top humans about a day to solve.

Raju's benchmark was called TheoPhysEval, and contributors had to sacrifice potential publication elsewhere or undertake a small research project just for the team. At a colloquium in September, Raju shared preliminary results showing leading AI models could solve about 60 percent of the problems on their own. By the time the full set was finished, GPT-6 Astra could solve nearly 90 percent of the problems. Given the human-written solutions, Astra argued the humans had made subtle errors and in reality answered 49 of 50 problems correctly, missing one trick question. Each correct answer cost less than $3 of compute on average, which Raju called less than the price of coffee in Paris, and came after a single human prompt.

Raju said he did not sleep well for a couple of nights after finding the benchmark was saturated before release, out of a blend of astonishment, excitement and fear. He said there would be no second version, telling the reporter that people gave the hardest problems they could and that the field had hit the ceiling of well-defined calculations people can do. He said open research could keep being asked about but that is not an evaluation. Raju said performing calculations is how the field judges students and decides they have talent, and that he entered physics through the International Physics Olympiad, which was considered a sign of talent. Raju told the reporter he is not taking new PhD students until he gets a better sense of what their futures might look like.

Andreas Karch, a physicist at the University of Texas at Austin, ruefully admitted he had written one of the subtly wrong answers in Raju's benchmark and now sends old papers through Astra, doing one paper a day. Karch said it is not clear how you jump over the step of mechanical grinding if AI performs all the routine calculations, and he mentioned a burgeoning fear of getting scooped because people will run and ask the agent to solve an idea. Daniel Harlow at MIT said that in his corner of physics the vast majority of the work is figuring out what to do, and by the time he has a calculation he is like 95 percent done already. Scott Aaronson, a theoretical computer scientist, described the paper flood as an endless buffet and said a lot of young physicists feel that is being taken away from them. Karch said some students take gigs writing training problems for data companies like Mercor or Scale AI for $80 to $100 an hour, which he called good money on the side but not a career, with no health insurance.

From January to October, physicists submitted about 30 percent more papers to the hep-th category of arXiv than in the same period last year, while the highest annual jump in the prior two decades was 8 percent. Matthew Schwartz at Harvard counted 19 sessions running on his machine during an October interview, each working a different problem with 10 to 20 agents per thread, and said Anthropic gave him tokens after asking what he would do with more. A Turkish physicist posted on X in October that Claude Opus 5.5 had re-created the core of his PhD thesis, which had taken him a year and 500 pages of hand calculations, in 10 hours. Ed Witten, the most-cited living theorist, has been crediting Opus in recent papers, and Juan Maldacena acknowledged help from OpenAI models on two papers this year. OpenAI announced in October that one of its models had proved the math behind the gluons carrying the strong nuclear force holds together in four dimensions, and a panel examining a Lean version of the 1,147-page proof concluded it is correct.

The pure Yang-Mills theory was first proposed in the middle of the 20th century, and the proof is half of a Millennium Prize solution that has eluded humans for decades. As far as anyone can tell, the flood of physics papers does not contain any major AI-aided physics discoveries, and the OpenAI proof is the closest thing so far. Aron Wall of Syracuse University thinks the flood will increase the necessity of personal references and relationships, saying his source for papers on arXiv usually is somebody telling him about them. Maldacena said it is hard to process but he thinks it is great and the field will learn how to do it. The articles leave open how physics as a field will organize itself around the paper flood and what the career path for physicists in training will become.

Articles.Title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist

stories.headline_source: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist

stories.Headline: Berklee lab director Jonathan Wyner urges musicians to use AI for business tasks while mastering their craft
stories.Summary:
A recent graduate of a renowned music school wrote to Boston Magazine’s Little Miss AI advice column to ask whether they should adopt artificial intelligence in their work as a musician, engineer and general professional or resist it and develop their skills without it. The graduate, named Aaron, also asked which approach looks better to an employer in the music industry and whether that answer will change as AI improves. The columnist responded in a piece published on November 25, 2026, and said the questions were fair and prescient because they touch on concerns raised in just about every industry. The columnist then spoke to people in the music world for guidance, starting with Jonathan Wyner.

Wyner is a musician, performer, producer and engineer who has mastered and produced more than 5,000 recordings over the past 40 years with artists such as James Taylor, David Bowie, Aerosmith, Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk, Pink Floyd, Bruce Springsteen and Nirvana. He is currently the director of Berklee College of Music’s Emerging Artistic Technology Lab, known as BEATL, where his job is to assist educators, artists and industry leaders with engaging in AI. The columnist noted that readers might expect him to be a musical purist, but he is not, and he is open and supportive of integrating AI into a musical career. Wyner said artists at the center is the lab’s credo and goal, and that it tries to help musicians understand where the opportunities are and how to make smart decisions.

Wyner said that gaining a deep knowledge of composition, harmony, culture and live performance is where the work begins and is non-negotiable. Rather than fearing displacement in performance or trying to compete with pure AI generation, he said musicians should leverage AI for business infrastructure, tour management, artist management and corporate media production. He considers AI-generated music to be technically competent and convincing enough for background music or corporate applications, but he said it rarely moves audiences the way a live human performance does. He also made the significant point that AI-generated music currently lacks copyright protection, meaning uploading third-party audio could violate rights.

The columnist also spoke to Boston Landmarks Orchestra engineer Daniel Pfeiffer, who explained how young musicians could use artificial intelligence without sacrificing their humanity. The article describes Little Miss AI as a recurring advice column and invites readers to email questions. The piece was published with a note inviting readers to add Boston Magazine as a preferred source on Google to see more of its stories in search results.

stories.Headline: Analysts say shoppers should give AI agents specific instructions and sensitive data to handle Black Friday buying
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being offered to shoppers as a helper for Black Friday, and the National Retail Federation says 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping this weekend, according to WVIA. The tools are built as conversations rather than search boxes, with prompt bars at the bottom of the page that invite a back and forth chat about what to buy. Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy including for AI, said a shopper can describe a use case instead of giving dimensions, asking whether an overstuffed bag will fit under the seat on JetBlue. She cautioned that AI works better with more hand holding, and said it is best to imagine it as a young child who will probably misinterpret your request, so you want to be as specific and clear as possible.

Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm, and they can handle shopping tasks, WVIA reports. If shoppers are worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox to track packages and even message a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying with your money. These features require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card, and the article says these tools become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.

The article says AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans, in that it makes mistakes, and the stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet and holiday unwrapping memories are on the line. WVIA frames its tips as notes of caution before using AI as your personal holiday shopper. The article also notes that one of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform raises involves that access to sensitive data. The account ends there, so what comes next for shoppers using these agents is not stated.

More to follow.

This initiative was announced in a new request for information released by the agency on November 25, 2026. The agency intends to conduct a multivendor proof of concept to test various anti-fraud and risk modeling tools. Interested vendors must submit their responses to this specific request for information by December 4.

The project requires the implementation of advanced analytics, including machine learning and predictive analytics, to identify fraudulent activity. These tools will be utilized by the Fraud Investigations and Inspections Division to improve their risk modeling capabilities. The agency is seeking a variety of commercial solutions that can integrate these complex technologies into their existing workflows. This process will allow the division to evaluate which specific AI tools are most effective for their needs.

The Fraud Investigations and Inspections Division is the entity responsible for seeking these new technological capabilities. While the articles do not provide a direct quote, the division expressed a clear interest in tools that leverage predictive analytics. They believe that these advanced analytics will help the agency better identify and prevent fraud in their operations. The division is leading the effort to modernize how the agency handles risk and fraud detection.

stories.Headline: Indian employees lead Asia-Pacific region in AI adoption to save 15 hours weekly
stories.Summary:
A report published on November 25, 2026, shows that Indian employees lead the Asia-Pacific region in the adoption of artificial intelligence. According to the Boston Consulting Group, 96 per cent of workers in India use these tools daily or several times a week. This level of usage is higher than the 85 per cent average seen across the nine surveyed markets. These employees save an average of 15 hours every week, which exceeds the regional average of 9.4 hours.

The report, titled "For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value", notes that 61 per cent of Indian workers use this saved time for strategic tasks. This percentage is higher than the figures for Australia at 60 per cent and China at 37 per cent. However, only 38 per cent of these employees have strong strategic clarity, while 42 per cent believe their training is sufficient. Additionally, 59 per cent say their organizations have established rules for teams composed of humans and artificial intelligence.

Nipun Kalra, the India Leader for BCG X, stated that artificial intelligence is changing the speed of work and the focus of employees. He suggested that these trends indicate a shift in the way that organizations can capture value from the technology. The Boston Consulting Group defined strategic clarity as the act of communicating AI as a priority and providing clear guidance on using saved time. These findings came from a survey of 6,349 employees, including 882 people from India.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electronics boosts NAND output in China to meet AI data center demand
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics plans to increase the production of ninth-generation vertical NAND flash memory at its Xi’an Plant 2 in China. Industry sources reported this development on November 24, 2026, noting that the company is responding to high demand for enterprise solid-state drives. This surge in demand is being driven by the explosive growth of the artificial intelligence data center market. The company intends to expand its monthly output of these specific wafers from 10,000 to 50,000 within one year. This fivefold increase requires converting existing sixth-generation production lines to ninth-generation processes and upgrading cleanroom electroplating equipment.

Once these changes are complete, total NAND production in China, including output from Xi’an Plant 1, will reach 100,000 wafers per month. This total represents roughly one-third of the global NAND production capacity for Samsung Electronics. The ninth-generation technology features a 286-layer architecture, which is about 21 percent higher than the 236 layers found in the eighth-generation version. Industry sources say this aggressive investment reflects a polarized market where demand for enterprise drives is surging while mobile and PC demand falls. The company is prioritizing high-performance products to maintain its market position against competitors like Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. Samsung has already introduced the PM1763 enterprise solid-state drive, which was unveiled in July to serve AI data centers.

This product is claimed to offer more than 1.8 times the power efficiency of the previous model. The company also plans to build additional ninth-generation production lines at its Pyeongtaek Plant 5 in South Korea. This strategy focuses on high-value products to maximize profitability while general-purpose NAND prices continue to decline. Samsung held a 35.1 percent share of the global enterprise solid-state drive market as of the second quarter. By repositioning the Xi’an campus as a hub for these drives, the company hopes to widen its lead over other manufacturers.

stories.Headline: Google cuts 2027 Broadcom TPU shipments by about 1M units and plans more MediaTek chips, Kuo says
stories.Summary:
Google reportedly reduced its planned 2027 shipments of AI chips designed by Broadcom on November 20, 2026. The company is preparing to increase shipments of an alternative chip designed by MediaTek. This shift was reported by technology supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. The changes involve custom processors known as Tensor Processing Units. Google is adjusting the mix of these processors for its AI workloads.

The plan cuts planned 2027 shipments of the Broadcom-designed TPU 8i series by approximately 1 million units. This reduction represents roughly 20 percent of the previously expected shipment volume for that series. The figures imply a reduction from approximately 5 million chips to 4 million chips. Most cuts affect the higher-priced 8i Max, which is also known as Whalefish. Google plans to increase 2027 shipments of the MediaTek-designed TPU 8t series.

Ming-Chi Kuo is an analyst at TF International Securities who based the report on an industry survey. He stated that Google has repeatedly emphasized that frontier model development receives first call on computing resources. Kuo characterized the changing shipment mix as an adjustment to that priority. He linked the change to tight supply chains and data-center power constraints. He noted that details for the MediaTek shipment increase remain unsettled.

Broadcom shares fell 8.9 percent on the day amid broad-based selling across the semiconductor sector. Investors are reassessing expectations for AI-chip suppliers due to the reported shipment changes. The report is directionally unfavorable for Broadcom's Google TPU business and potentially favorable for MediaTek. The reduction in one chip family does not mean Google expects less overall AI computing demand. The report adds uncertainty around future revenue for Broadcom.

TPUs are custom processors that Google uses for its AI workloads. Google is prioritizing the work involved in building its most advanced AI models. The company is navigating limited data-center power and supply-chain constraints. This decision could reflect a way to allocate scarce manufacturing capacity and electricity. The report does not suggest that Google is pulling back on its broader AI ambitions.

The outlook for 2027 remains subject to revisions since there was no official Google announcement. It is unclear if additional 8t shipments will fully offset the reduction in the 8i family. The report did not provide pricing, contract terms, or an estimate of the financial effect on Broadcom. It remains unknown how much Google will ultimately increase its MediaTek-designed chip orders. The final mix of chips and its impact on supplier revenue are still open.

stories.Summary:
The Times published an article on 22 November 2026 asking what school children hope and fear about artificial intelligence, and the piece was framed around how to protect under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it. The article says an NSPCC campaign hopes to address this issue, and the writer Alice Thomson saw how students react to it. The piece lists cheating and deepfakes among the concerns it raises about the technology. The article carries no further detail in the text available about what happened, who did it or when beyond that publication.

The article presents the question of protecting under-16s from new technology alongside helping them to use it, and it names the NSPCC campaign as the effort that hopes to address this issue. It gives no numbers, dates or names about the campaign itself beyond the organisation and the writer who observed the students. The only date the article gives is its own publication date of 22 November 2026. It gives no further figures about the technology, the children or the campaign.

The article attributes the campaign to the NSPCC and reports that Alice Thomson saw how students react to it, without quoting any student, parent or official by name in the text available. It does not say what the NSPCC said about the campaign or what any school or government body said about the issue. The concerns it lists, cheating and deepfakes, are given as part of the question the article poses rather than as statements from a named person. No responsible official is named beyond the organisation and the writer.

The context the article gives is the debate over how to protect under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it, and it places the NSPCC campaign within that debate. It does not say what happens next, what the campaign will do, or what any school, government or regulator plans to change. The article offers no timeline beyond its publication on 22 November 2026. stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO and Colette Kress becomes interim CEO amid a 41.42 percent share drop
stories.Summary:
Wall Street questioned if Nvidia was becoming the next Cisco during the week ending November 20, 2026. Investors reacted to a month where Nvidia shares dropped 41.42 percent. The stock closed at 125.53 dollars on November 20 after losing 20.45 dollars in one session. This sell-off occurred despite the company reporting strong quarterly results on November 17, 2026. Trefis noted on November 20 that Cisco shares once fell 89 percent.

Nvidia listed 390 billion dollars in supply commitments and 118 billion dollars in guarantees. This includes 105 billion dollars for SB Energy's 4.25 GW Ohio campus for OpenAI. The company has 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments involving revenue sharing. Three customers accounted for 14 percent, 11 percent, and 11 percent of third-quarter revenue. Data Center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, which was 110 percent higher year over year.

The board announced that Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO, and board member. Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named interim CEO during the search for a replacement. Michael Burry compared the October 6 Nasdaq 100 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak. He claimed that bulls would have another fluffy big chance to get out. I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only begun.

Barron's reported growing worry over whether AI spending can last and its debt funding. The publication wrote that the stock looks like a bargain after a strong earnings report. Investors near retirement face sequence-of-returns risk if they hold large positions during a slump. Reuters reported on November 20 that the SEC is investigating Nvidia's accounting. Jim Cramer mentioned that a new executive asked questions Jensen Huang would not answer.

Cisco was the main picks-and-shovels supplier during the internet expansion until orders dried up. Nvidia now holds a similar role for the current AI expansion. The company reported revenue of 115.84 billion dollars, beating the 108.73 billion dollar consensus. Non-GAAP EPS of 2.68 dollars beat expectations of 2.4712 dollars for the sixth consecutive quarter. Management raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook from 70 percent to about 75 percent.

Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent. The company expects a gross margin between 71 percent and 72 percent. A miss on these figures or a margin below 71 percent could make the Cisco script likelier. The articles leave open whether the leadership vacuum or record growth will win. It remains uncertain if holders who bought this summer will sell or ride the volatility.
